item.title: 上下文不可能无限长：Evoke 把场景几何搬进「外置、按相机索引的世界状态库」，于是能一直走下去 ｜ Alaya-EVOKE: From Linear-Scaling Supervision to Endless World
item.description:
一句话：三步、零 CFG，单张 H200 上每 2.11 秒产出 1.5 秒视频；关键是状态不在去噪器的上下文里。

要点：

  • 速度账很清楚：**3 步、零 CFG**，一次前向一步而不是两次，单张 H200 上每 2.11 秒产出 1.5 秒 384×640 视频——「少步数」不再以质量上限为代价
  • 核心结构：场景几何存在一个**外置、按相机索引的世界状态库（world state bank）**里，而不是塞进去噪器上下文；每次只检索当前视野需要的部分，因此会话再长上下文也有界
  • 它同时声称记得自己去过哪里、能在中途接受方向改变并继续，并在 WBench 上取得 SOTA（VBench-Long / VBench-2.0 上仍有竞争力）

为什么值得看：「记忆放哪」决定了世界模型能不能长期跑。Evoke 把状态外置，和昨天 WorldFoundry 的「持久状态」判据是同一件事的两面：状态归显式结构，生成只负责当前视野。零 CFG 又与 11-08 那篇 CFG 拆解蒸馏呼应——成本是从结构上省出来的。

中文摘要：Alaya-EVOKE 是一个三步、零 CFG 的交互式世界模型实现。它的关键不在于「更快」，而在于把**场景几何放在一个外置的、按相机索引的世界状态库里**，而不是放进去噪器的上下文：每次只检索当前视野需要的那部分，因此会话时间再长，上下文也保持有界——这是「无限长度」与「有限窗口」的区别所在。速度上，它用一次前向一步（而非 CFG 的两次）实现少步数，单张 H200 上每 2.11 秒产出 1.5 秒 384×640 视频；同时声称能记住去过哪里、支持中途转向，并在 WBench 上取得 SOTA。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：GitHub·AlayaLab（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

    Alaya-EVOKE: From Linear-Scaling Supervision to Endless World

A three-step, CFG-free world model that remembers where it has been, takes direction mid-flight,
and keeps going — 1.5 s of video every 2.11 s on a single H200.

✨ Highlights

  • 🏆 State of the art on WBench — as a three-step world model, while staying competitive in visual quality on VBench-Long and VBench-2.0.
  • ⚡ 3 steps, zero CFG. 1.5 s of 384×640 video every 2.11 s on one H200 — one forward per step, not two. Few-step speed without few-step ceilings.
  • 🌍 Endless, not windowed. Scene geometry lives in an external, camera-indexed world state bank instead of the denoiser's context. Only what the current view needs is retrieved, so the context stays bounded however long the session runs — no trading session length for memory.
  • 🎛️ Re-promptable mid-flight. Per-chunk conditioning lets you change the prompt while the rollout is running: the sky ignites, the storm rolls in, no cut and no restart.
  • 🧑‍🏫 A teacher rebuilt for the long horizon. Chunk-wise grouping, distant-frame retrieval and a linear-attention global state make its memory and compute grow linearly — which is what makes 30 s self-forced supervision affordable.

    • 📰 Latest News

  • 2026-09-12 — Interactive UI and inference optimizations. We release an interactive world-exploration UI that generates 1.5-second video chunks in 1.34 seconds on average on five H200 GPUs, at 640×384 resolution. UI guide and interface preview.
  • 2026-09-11 — Evoke-Turbo released. Our updated model achieves state of the art on WBench with an average score of 82.0, improving navigation, consistency, and physical plausibility. 🤗 Download Evoke-Turbo · WBench results
  • 2026-08-30 — Director Web UI. EVOKE now ships with a local Web UI for per-chunk prompting, dual-stick camera control, streaming previews, continuation, and revision branching. See the UI guide and interface preview.
  • 2026-08-14 — Day 0. Alaya-EVOKE entered the official WBench table and achieved state of the art in its release snapshot, one day after the first arXiv submission.

    • 🎬 Demos


    ▶  Watch the overview

    Every clip was produced by the launchers in this repo, on the data bundled in 

    examples/
    — no external dataset, no cherry-picking across seeds. The 
    Move
    / 
    Rot
    joystick is the camera-control HUD burned into 
    geo_pred.mp4
    .

    Re-prompting mid-rollout

    Per-chunk conditioning lets the prompt change while the rollout is running — no cut, no restart. Each schedule below switches at chunk 3 of 6 (213 frames, 8.9 s).

    scenethe prompt switches to
    frozen tundra, polar daylightan aurora ignites across the whole sky
    still mountain lake at nighta meteor shower opens overhead
    alien valley of crystal spiresan electrical storm arcs between the spires
    dormant ring megastructurethe gateway ignites, energy column rising
    MODE=segment NUM_CHUNKS=6 MAX_CASES=0 bash scripts/inference/infer_post_distill.sh

    Conditioning modes

    4 chunks each (141 frames, 5.9 s; t2v is 140).

    modeinputcamera
    v2v
    		reference video + pose trackyes — continues past the reference window
    i2v
    		single first frame + pose trackyes
    t2v
    		prompt onlyno — the engine forbids warp + t2v
    MODE=v2v NUM_CHUNKS=4 bash scripts/inference/infer_post_distill.sh   # or MODE=i2v / MODE=t2v

    The other two models

    Both run on the same bundled inputs as the demos above, so they are directly comparable.

    modelstepsnote
    stage1_camera_control
    		50, CFG 5.0the multi-step model that precedes distillation — not distilled, so it is sampled like an ordinary diffusion model. Same case as 
    v2v
    evoke_teacher
    		50, CFG 5.0the dual-expert DMD teacher sampled directly, same input image as 
    i2v
    ; no camera conditioning
    NUM_CHUNKS=4 bash scripts/inference/infer_stage1.sh
bash scripts/inference/infer_evoke_teacher.sh

    🧠 How it works

    The student is autoregressive over latent chunks (

    latent_window_size = 9
    ). Each chunk is laid out along the RoPE frame index as:

    prefix | long(16) | mid(2) | warp(W) | prev_short(1) | noise(W)
    tierwhat it is
    prefix
    		the frame-0 global anchor (i2v: the input image; v2v: the first latent of the reference video)
    long
    / 
    mid
    		multi-term parametric memory (
    history_sizes = [16, 2, 1]
    ) with coarser patch kernels — long 
    (4,8,8)
    , mid 
    (2,4,4)
    , everything else 
    (1,2,2)
    warp
    		the world state bank rendered into this view; its RoPE overlaps the noise window
    prev_short
    		the last latent of the previous chunk, the continuity anchor closest to the noise

    Every tier lives at the same latent resolution (

    res/8
    ); compression comes only from the patchify convolution kernel, and no low-resolution latents are stored. In the short tier 
    [prefix | warp | prev_short]
    the residual MLP and the per-stage compression act only on the warp frames in the middle.

    The world state bank itself has three operations: write — a monocular depth model estimates depth for the emitted chunk under its known poses, unprojected into a persistent point cloud; read — the current camera pose addresses the bank directly, with sources ranked by co-visibility, up to eight fused, and a batched z-buffered scatter returning a warped image plus a per-pixel visibility mask; and evict — an optional retention window, which hour-scale runs enable explicitly.

    ⚙️ Environment

item.title: 别再用「压缩连续帧」当动作标签：OnlyAct 从基础模型里抽动作表示，喂给视频世界模型 ｜ OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models
item.description:
一句话：动作标注稀缺又口径不一；常见替代是把相邻帧压成 latent，但这会逼 latent 只记「新信息」。

要点：

  • 瓶颈是动作监督：动作标签稀缺、分散在互不兼容的规格里，而且无法随着无标注视频语料一起扩展
  • 常见绕法是联合训练一个动作编码器把相邻帧压成 latent 动作，再让解码器用「上一帧 + 该 latent」重建下一帧——这等于强制 latent 只承载**新出现的信息**
  • 论文指出这种做法存在两处问题，并改为从基础模型中抽取动作表示（OnlyAct），而不是让 latent 自己扛下动作语义

为什么值得看：「latent 动作到底编码了什么」是世界模型训练里最含糊的一环：把新信息当动作，运动和外观变化就混在一起。改用基础模型给出的动作表示，等于给训练加了一个语义明确的监督源。

中文摘要：视频世界模型本可成为通用交互式模拟器，但训练被动作监督卡住：动作标签既稀缺、又分散在互不兼容的规格里，还无法随无标注视频语料一起扩展。常见的替代做法是联合训练动作编码器，把相邻两帧压缩成一个 latent 动作，再用「上一帧 + latent」重建下一帧——这种目标实际上强制 latent 只承载新出现的信息，于是运动与外观变化被混为一谈。OnlyAct 因此改为从基础模型中抽取动作表示，用语义更明确的监督源替代「压缩帧差」这条捷径，让世界模型学到的是动作而不是残差。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models

Abstract

Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning an action representation from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. This provides a more generalizable foundation for action representation. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. To this end, we propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol that probes action representations along three axes—action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality—across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with prior annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.

1 Introduction

Over the past few years, video generative models [10, 21, 34, 58] have reached unprecedented levels of realism. They are trained on vast quantities of video data and acquire broad priors over scene structure and dynamics, which has motivated their use well beyond video generation itself. A growing line of work explores how they can be turned into video world models by conditioning generation on action signals [11, 46, 20, 19]. Video world models have the potential to serve as general-purpose interactive simulators, with applications ranging from robotics to gaming.

Realizing this potential, however, hinges on action supervision. While unlabeled video is abundant, only a small fraction is paired with the actions that produced it, and the labels that do exist are fragmented across incompatible specifications, such as joint angles in robotics or controller inputs in games. Direct action conditioning therefore does not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus and does not transfer well across environments. To overcome this, latent-action models [43, 11] extract latent actions from unlabeled video in a self-supervised manner and use them to condition the video generator during pretraining. Real actions can then be mapped onto this latent space afterward with a small amount of labeled data [11, 19].

Latent-action models are typically trained from scratch as inverse-dynamics models: given a pair of consecutive frames, an action encoder infers a latent intended to capture the action, while a decoder reconstructs the next frame from the previous frame together with this latent. A bottleneck on the latent forces it to encode only what the decoder cannot recover from the previous frame alone, ideally isolating the action signal from scene content. This comes with two limitations: first, training the action space from scratch can prevent it from generalizing to unseen domains; second, tightening the bottleneck improves separation between action and scene at the cost of expressiveness, while loosening it preserves nuance at the cost of scene leakage, which can also hurt generalization when scene, embodiment, or dynamics shift.

In this work, we propose OnlyAct, an unlabeled action representation learning framework that takes a different starting point. Rather than learning the action representation from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model, V-JEPA 2 [4], and extract actions from it with contrastive learning. Pretrained on large-scale, diverse video, such a model encodes both what is in a scene and how it changes over time, so the action-relevant signal is already present in its embeddings, alongside scene content. We confirm this empirically: when a pair of consecutive frames is encoded as a two-frame clip, even the frozen V-JEPA 2 embedding carries more action information than latent-action models trained on the same data, as measured by a linear probe (Sec.4.1). However, it also carries more scene information (Sec.4.2), and its probing performance is unstable across domains. The main challenge is therefore not to learn an action representation from scratch, but to disentangle the action-relevant signal from scene content.

We do this by adapting the pretrained foundation model into an action encoder on unlabeled video with a contrastive objective and a lightweight low-rank adapter. Given two frames from a video, we form a positive example that keeps the motion but changes the scene: when the camera is static, we use optical flow to cut out the moving region and paste it, at a shifted location, onto the background of a different scene. Hard negatives are drawn from other frame pairs of the same video, where action provides the dominant axis of variation. Together, these signals shift the encoder embedding space toward action. Crucially, this is achieved without a reconstruction bottleneck: the objective reshapes the geometry of the pretrained space rather than compressing the action into a small code from which the next frame must be decoded.

The adapted encoder supports two main uses: transfer from demonstrations, and direct control with real actions. In the first, the encoder extracts a latent action from a pair of demonstration frames; this latent then conditions a video world model to reproduce the same action in a different scene. In the second, a small action-labeled dataset can be used to map an environment’s real actions onto the latent space, after which the video world model can be controlled directly through them.

Both uses require an action representation that captures rich and discriminative action dynamics, isolates the action signal from scene content so the same action transfers across scenes, and drives faithful action-conditioned video generation across different domains. We construct a unified evaluation protocol around these axes and benchmark against prior annotation-free latent-action methods and the frozen pretrained encoder on thirteen robot, camera-navigation, and game datasets, ten of which are unseen during adaptation, as well as on world-model training and fine-tuning across robot, navigation, game, and driving domains. Our representation is the most expressive on almost all datasets, matches the scene invariance of bottlenecked latent-action models, and yields world models with markedly better action transfer and controllability.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • 1.

    We introduce a new perspective on unlabeled action representation learning: rather than learning actions from scratch, we extract them from the representation space of a pretrained foundation model.

  • 2.

    We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework, built on flow-guided scene-swapped positives and same-video hard negatives, that disentangles action from scene without a reconstruction bottleneck and improves both action expressiveness and scene invariance over the frozen encoder.

  • 3.

    We introduce a unified evaluation protocol that systematically probes action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality, and show across robot, navigation, game, and driving benchmarks that our representations improve over prior annotation-free latent-action baselines.

    • Code and models will be released on our project page: runjiali-rl.github.io/onlyact/.

    2 Related Work

    Video World Models. Action-conditioned video world models have become a core approach for modeling environment dynamics in domains such as gaming and robotics. Existing methods typically obtain action information in one of two ways. The first assumes explicit action or intervention supervision, such as controller inputs, robot states, camera trajectories, or action prompts [3, 63, 1, 56, 67, 23, 53, 27, 46, 20, 40, 36, 54, 61, 47]. This provides a precise control interface, but the supervision is tied to particular environments, embodiments, or data-collection pipelines, and therefore does not naturally scale to uncurated in-the-wild video. The second introduces latent-action interfaces learned from video [11, 19, 18, 64, 49, 12], reducing the need for explicit labels but requiring a separate action-learning process. Current interactive video world models therefore face a trade-off between precise but environment-specific action supervision and scalable but separately learned latent actions. Our work is complementary: we use pretrained foundation-model representations as an effective starting point and ask whether they already contain transferable transition structure that can be extracted for world model pretraining.

    Latent Action Models from Video. A growing line of work learns latent actions from unlabeled video by jointly training an action encoder on frame pairs together with a future-frame decoder, with a bottleneck on the latent. Introduced by earlier work [16, 43, 42] and scaled by recent methods [11, 51, 64, 19, 18, 49, 12], these latents serve as proxy actions for controllable video generation or policy learning. The key limitation is generalization: because these encoders are trained from scratch with reconstruction objectives, the learned action space is shaped by the scenes, embodiments, and dynamics present in the training data. As a result, latents can encode scene-specific cues such as appearance, object identity, or viewpoint rather than the action itself, making transfer difficult when scene or embodiment shifts [15, 66]. Prior methods reduce this leakage with low-dimensional bottlenecks, discrete codebooks, or other architectural constraints, but these constraints come at the cost of reducing the resolution of the action space. A separate line of work augments reconstruction-based latent-action models with contrastive objectives, but relies on additional supervision such as action labels or kinematic trajectories [15, 66]. We instead start from a pretrained foundation model [4] and use a contrastive objective to extract action as a signal already present in its embeddings, neither learning the action space from scratch nor requiring additional supervision.

    Pretrained Representations. Pretrained visual representations [44, 38, 60, 39, 30, 68, 32, 9] provide strong and transferable features for downstream perception, control, and world modeling. Large-scale foundation models such as V-JEPA 2 [4] extend this to predictive spatio-temporal representations that support video understanding, and V-JEPA 2-AC further post-trains an action-conditioned predictor in this representation space for planning with robot actions. These works use pretrained representations to encode observations or predict future states, with actions, when needed, supplied as labels. We instead use the pretrained foundation model itself as an action encoder: encoding a frame pair as a short clip exposes the motion between the frames, and we adapt the encoder without labels so that this motion signal, rather than scene content, dominates its embedding space.

    3 Method

    Given a corpus of videos without action labels, each consisting of frames (o₁,…,o_T), our goal is to learn a latent action αₜ for each consecutive frame pair (oₜ,oₜ₊₁) and use these latent actions to pretrain an action-conditioned video world model G_ψ that predicts the next frame oₜ₊₁ from (o_1:t,α_1:t). Our pipeline has two stages: we first adapt a pretrained foundation model φ_θ on unlabeled video so that αₜ=φ_θ(oₜ,oₜ₊₁) isolates the action signal from scene content, and then freeze φ_θ and use the resulting action stream α_1:T-1 to train an auto-regressive video world model G_ψ. Following prior latent-action work [16, 11, 51, 64, 19], we define the action as the change between two frames that is caused by the agent or the camera, and treat what can be inferred from a single frame, such as appearance, layout, and object identity, as scene content. An overview of the training pipeline is provided in Fig.2. Once trained, G_ψ supports two control modes: action transfer and real-action control. Sec.3.1 introduces the foundation-model-based action encoder, Sec.3.2 details its contrastive adaptation, and Sec.3.3 describes the action-conditioned video world model.

    3.1 Frame-Pair Embeddings from a Foundation Model

    We instantiate the action encoder φ_θ with the encoder of V-JEPA 2 [4], a ViT-L foundation model pretrained on large-scale video. Because it is pretrained to model how video content evolves across space and time, the encoder represents motion, not only appearance, which makes it a natural starting point from which to extract action representations.

    Pair encoding.

    Given a frame pair (oₜ,oₜ₊₁), we stack the two frames into a two-frame clip and pass it through the encoder only; the V-JEPA 2 predictor is not used. Since the encoder groups every two frames into one spatio-temporal tubelet, the clip yields a single temporal slice of 16×16 patch tokens, and each token jointly observes both frames from the first layer onward. Motion is therefore fused into the representation from the start, rather than obtained by differencing two independently encoded frames. We average-pool the output tokens, apply a fixed linear projection to d=640 dimensions, and ℓ₂-normalize,

    αₜ = φ_θ(oₜ,oₜ₊₁) = (P h̄ₜ)/(∥P h̄ₜ∥₂), h̄ₜ = 1/N∑ₙ₌₁^Nh_t,n,

    where h_t,n is the n-th output token and P∈ℝ^640×1024 is a random projection that is fixed at initialization and never trained. A random linear projection approximately preserves the geometry of the pooled embedding, so P serves only to reduce dimensionality; all learning happens in the encoder.

    The frozen embedding already encodes substantial action information (Sec.4.1), but it is entangled with scene content: it leaks more scene information than latent-action models (Sec.4.2), and its action information degrades sharply on some domains. A low-dimensional reconstruction bottleneck is the standard remedy for scene leakage, but it trades scene invariance against action expressiveness and would discard the capacity that makes the pretrained space attractive in the first place. We therefore adapt φ_θ with a contrastive objective that reshapes its geometry without compressing it (Sec.3.2).

    3.2 Contrastive Action Adaptation

    Building on the encoder φ_θ of Sec.3.1, we now reshape its embedding space to better isolate action from scene while retaining the capacity of the pretrained representation. We frame this adaptation around two properties that we want the action embedding space to satisfy: action expressiveness and scene invariance. Without action labels, neither can be enforced directly, so we approximate both through a contrastive objective on positive and hard-negative pairs that are constructed from raw video. To avoid overwriting the general-purpose features acquired during pretraining, we keep the pretrained weights θ frozen and attach low-rank adapters [26] to the linear layers of every transformer block, yielding an update Δθ and the adapted encoder φ_θ+Δθ. With slight abuse of notation, we write φ_θ for this adapted encoder in the remainder of the paper, with the understanding that θ subsumes Δθ.

    Pair construction.

    For each training sample we draw an anchor pair, a positive pair, and a hard-negative pair. The anchor is a frame pair (oₜ,oₜ₊ₖ) from a video, with a small random offset k. The positiveg(oₜ,oₜ₊ₖ) should carry the same action in a different scene. We construct it with flow-guided scene swapping: we estimate the dense optical flow between the two frames with an off-the-shelf estimator [55], and threshold its magnitude to obtain the moving core region, i.e., the pixels that carry the action. We cut out this region from both frames and paste it onto the same background frame taken from a different scene of the same dataset, translating it in both frames by a common random offset. The pixels in motion are thus preserved exactly, while the scene, background, and absolute location of the motion are all replaced. This construction is only valid when the camera is static. When the camera moves, as in egocentric, hand-held, or driving video, the background motion is itself part of the action and cannot be swapped; in this case the positive falls back to the anchor pair under a different photometric augmentation. Both anchor and positive receive a color jitter that is shared between their two frames, so that inter-frame changes are not altered. The hard negative(o_t^′,o_t^′+k) is drawn from a non-overlapping time window of the same video: it shares the scene with the anchor but likely corresponds to a different action, so it cannot be told apart from the anchor by appearance. We write αₜ, αₜ⁺=φ_θ (g(oₜ,oₜ₊ₖ)), and αₜ⁻=φ_θ(o_t^′,o_t^′+k) for the embeddings of the anchor, positive, and hard negative, respectively.

    Contrastive objective.

    We organize these triplets into a candidate bank ℤ containing every anchor, positive, and hard negative in a batch of size N, and apply a symmetric InfoNCE objective [57] that pulls each anchor toward its matched positive and pushes it away from every other element of the bank in both directions,

    L_con = -1/2N∑ᵢ₌₁^N[\log(\exp (αᵢ^⊤αᵢ⁺/τ))/(∑_z∈ℤ∖{αᵢ}\exp (αᵢ^⊤z/τ))+\log(\exp (αᵢ^+⊤αᵢ/τ))/(∑_z∈ℤ∖{αᵢ⁺}\exp (αᵢ^+⊤z/τ))],

    where τ is a temperature. The same-video hard negatives in ℤ make the objective non-trivial: in contrast, random in-batch negatives from unrelated scenes would be easily separated by appearance alone, allowing the encoder to satisfy the loss without disentangling action from scene. The scene-swapped positives, in turn, prevent the encoder from separating the anchor from its hard negative by memorizing scene-specific cues, since the positive shares none of the anchor’s background.

    Inference.

    After adaptation, a latent action αₜ is obtained by a single forward pass of φ_θ on a frame pair. No labels, prompts, or trajectory-level optimization are required at inference. The adapted encoder φ_θ thus serves as a drop-in action encoder on arbitrary video, yielding the action stream α_1:t that conditions the video world model G_ψ (Sec.3.3).

    3.3 Action-Conditioned Video World Model

    We obtain the action-conditioned video world model G_ψ by adopting the autoregressive world model architecture of AdaWorld [19] and replacing its latent actions by our action stream. Given a trajectory (o₁,…,o_T), we apply the frozen action encoder of Sec.3.1 to consecutive frame pairs to form the action streamα_1:T-1 and use it as continuous action conditioning, with G_ψ predicting each next frame oₜ₊₁ from (o_1:t,α_1:t). Before entering G_ψ, our action embeddings are whitened by a fixed, parameter-free covariance equalization computed on the training data, while the baselines’ latent actions enter unchanged; whitening a baseline in the same way leads to the same conclusions (Appendix A.2). Otherwise, every action representation we compare uses exactly the same backbone, recipe, and data.

    Action injection and training objective.

    Following AdaWorld, the action representation conditions the denoiser through two pathways: it is concatenated with the CLIP image embedding to form the cross-attention context, and concatenated with the context-length embedding into the vector condition, which a label-embedding MLP maps and adds to the timestep embedding. One action vector is given per predicted transition, with no learned projection in between, and the action slots of the pretrained weights are zero-initialized. G_ψ predicts the next frame from up to six context frames, with the context length sampled uniformly from 1 to 6 during training, and is trained with the v-prediction objective under EDM noise scaling and loss weighting [31]. Each condition, including the action, is dropped with probability 0.1 to enable classifier-free guidance [24].

    Action transfer and real-action control.

    As illustrated in Fig.3, the trained pipeline supports two control modes that share the same autoregressive rollout of the video world model G_ψ but differ in how the conditioning action stream α_1:T-1 is obtained. For action transfer, we extract α_1:T-1ᵈᵉᵐᵒ by running the frozen action encoder φ_θ over a demonstration video and feed it to G_ψ together with an initial frame o₁ from a different scene. The model then reproduces the demonstrated action in the new scene without any action labels. For real-action control, we fine-tune on a small action-labeled set. Following [18], a small learned interface maps real actions into the latent-action space and replaces φ_θ at the input of G_ψ: one vector per discrete action, initialized at the mean latent action of its labeled clips, or, for continuous actions, a two-layer MLP first fitted to regress the latent actions of the labeled clips. The interface and the denoiser of G_ψ are then fine-tuned end-to-end (Appendix B.5). Because the latent-action space has already been shaped by large-scale unlabeled pretraining, only a modest amount of labeled data is required, and at inference time the mapped real actions serve as the conditioning stream.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate an action representation for action-conditioned video world models along three axes: (i) action expressiveness (Sec.4.2) — how well the embedding distinguishes different actions; (ii) scene invariance (Sec.4.3) — whether the embedding avoids encoding scene or future-state content that a video generator could exploit as a shortcut; and (iii) action-conditioned video generation quality (Sec.4.4) — how well the embedding serves as a conditioning signal for video generation, measured by fidelity, transferability, and controllability. On both seen and unseen benchmarks, OnlyAct is substantially more expressive than prior annotation-free latent-action baselines, matches their scene invariance, and yields world models with better action transfer and controllability. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B.1.

    4.1 Datasets and Baselines

    We evaluate OnlyAct on datasets both seen and unseen during encoder adaptation. The action encoder is adapted on 168K unlabeled frame-pair samples from nine video sources spanning robot manipulation, human and egocentric video, camera navigation, and games (Appendix B.2). Among our evaluation datasets, only LIBERO [37], DROID [33], and SpatialVID [59] contribute videos to this set (marked ∘ in the tables), and all other datasets are entirely unseen by the encoder. For action probing and scene leakage, we use thirteen datasets with action annotations: nine robot-manipulation datasets (LIBERO, DROID, RLBench [28], RoboCasa [45], DROID-IPRL [33], MetaWorld [65], MUTEX [52], Robosuite [70], and RoboDesk [29]), three camera-navigation datasets (SpatialVID, ARKitScenes [6], and RealEstate10K [69]), and Procgen [14] with 15 discrete actions. For action-conditioned video generation, we evaluate on LIBERO, RLBench, SpatialVID, and nuScenes [13], and further fine-tune with real actions on DMLab [7] and Minecraft from the TECO datasets [62], Habitat [50] in HM3D scenes [48], and nuScenes.

    We compare against two families of baselines. The first is latent-action models, namely DreamDojo [18] and AdaWorld [19]. Since their publicly released weights are not trained on our data, we retrain both on the same 168K training pairs as our encoder for a fair comparison (marked †). The second is the frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder [4], embedded in the same way as OnlyAct (Sec.3.1) but without contrastive adaptation, which isolates the effect of our adaptation from that of the pretrained backbone.

一句话：动作标注稀缺又口径不一；常见替代是把相邻帧压成 latent，但这会逼 latent 只记「新信息」。

要点：

  • 瓶颈是动作监督：动作标签稀缺、分散在互不兼容的规格里，而且无法随着无标注视频语料一起扩展
  • 常见绕法是联合训练一个动作编码器把相邻帧压成 latent 动作，再让解码器用「上一帧 + 该 latent」重建下一帧——这等于强制 latent 只承载**新出现的信息**
  • 论文指出这种做法存在两处问题，并改为从基础模型中抽取动作表示（OnlyAct），而不是让 latent 自己扛下动作语义

为什么值得看：「latent 动作到底编码了什么」是世界模型训练里最含糊的一环：把新信息当动作，运动和外观变化就混在一起。改用基础模型给出的动作表示，等于给训练加了一个语义明确的监督源。

中文摘要：视频世界模型本可成为通用交互式模拟器，但训练被动作监督卡住：动作标签既稀缺、又分散在互不兼容的规格里，还无法随无标注视频语料一起扩展。常见的替代做法是联合训练动作编码器，把相邻两帧压缩成一个 latent 动作，再用「上一帧 + latent」重建下一帧——这种目标实际上强制 latent 只承载新出现的信息，于是运动与外观变化被混为一谈。OnlyAct 因此改为从基础模型中抽取动作表示，用语义更明确的监督源替代「压缩帧差」这条捷径，让世界模型学到的是动作而不是残差。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models

Abstract

Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning an action representation from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. This provides a more generalizable foundation for action representation. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. To this end, we propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol that probes action representations along three axes—action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality—across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with prior annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.

1 Introduction

Over the past few years, video generative models [10, 21, 34, 58] have reached unprecedented levels of realism. They are trained on vast quantities of video data and acquire broad priors over scene structure and dynamics, which has motivated their use well beyond video generation itself. A growing line of work explores how they can be turned into video world models by conditioning generation on action signals [11, 46, 20, 19]. Video world models have the potential to serve as general-purpose interactive simulators, with applications ranging from robotics to gaming.

Realizing this potential, however, hinges on action supervision. While unlabeled video is abundant, only a small fraction is paired with the actions that produced it, and the labels that do exist are fragmented across incompatible specifications, such as joint angles in robotics or controller inputs in games. Direct action conditioning therefore does not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus and does not transfer well across environments. To overcome this, latent-action models [43, 11] extract latent actions from unlabeled video in a self-supervised manner and use them to condition the video generator during pretraining. Real actions can then be mapped onto this latent space afterward with a small amount of labeled data [11, 19].

Latent-action models are typically trained from scratch as inverse-dynamics models: given a pair of consecutive frames, an action encoder infers a latent intended to capture the action, while a decoder reconstructs the next frame from the previous frame together with this latent. A bottleneck on the latent forces it to encode only what the decoder cannot recover from the previous frame alone, ideally isolating the action signal from scene content. This comes with two limitations: first, training the action space from scratch can prevent it from generalizing to unseen domains; second, tightening the bottleneck improves separation between action and scene at the cost of expressiveness, while loosening it preserves nuance at the cost of scene leakage, which can also hurt generalization when scene, embodiment, or dynamics shift.

In this work, we propose OnlyAct, an unlabeled action representation learning framework that takes a different starting point. Rather than learning the action representation from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model, V-JEPA 2 [4], and extract actions from it with contrastive learning. Pretrained on large-scale, diverse video, such a model encodes both what is in a scene and how it changes over time, so the action-relevant signal is already present in its embeddings, alongside scene content. We confirm this empirically: when a pair of consecutive frames is encoded as a two-frame clip, even the frozen V-JEPA 2 embedding carries more action information than latent-action models trained on the same data, as measured by a linear probe (Sec.4.1). However, it also carries more scene information (Sec.4.2), and its probing performance is unstable across domains. The main challenge is therefore not to learn an action representation from scratch, but to disentangle the action-relevant signal from scene content.

We do this by adapting the pretrained foundation model into an action encoder on unlabeled video with a contrastive objective and a lightweight low-rank adapter. Given two frames from a video, we form a positive example that keeps the motion but changes the scene: when the camera is static, we use optical flow to cut out the moving region and paste it, at a shifted location, onto the background of a different scene. Hard negatives are drawn from other frame pairs of the same video, where action provides the dominant axis of variation. Together, these signals shift the encoder embedding space toward action. Crucially, this is achieved without a reconstruction bottleneck: the objective reshapes the geometry of the pretrained space rather than compressing the action into a small code from which the next frame must be decoded.

The adapted encoder supports two main uses: transfer from demonstrations, and direct control with real actions. In the first, the encoder extracts a latent action from a pair of demonstration frames; this latent then conditions a video world model to reproduce the same action in a different scene. In the second, a small action-labeled dataset can be used to map an environment’s real actions onto the latent space, after which the video world model can be controlled directly through them.

Both uses require an action representation that captures rich and discriminative action dynamics, isolates the action signal from scene content so the same action transfers across scenes, and drives faithful action-conditioned video generation across different domains. We construct a unified evaluation protocol around these axes and benchmark against prior annotation-free latent-action methods and the frozen pretrained encoder on thirteen robot, camera-navigation, and game datasets, ten of which are unseen during adaptation, as well as on world-model training and fine-tuning across robot, navigation, game, and driving domains. Our representation is the most expressive on almost all datasets, matches the scene invariance of bottlenecked latent-action models, and yields world models with markedly better action transfer and controllability.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • 1.

    We introduce a new perspective on unlabeled action representation learning: rather than learning actions from scratch, we extract them from the representation space of a pretrained foundation model.

  • 2.

    We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework, built on flow-guided scene-swapped positives and same-video hard negatives, that disentangles action from scene without a reconstruction bottleneck and improves both action expressiveness and scene invariance over the frozen encoder.

  • 3.

    We introduce a unified evaluation protocol that systematically probes action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality, and show across robot, navigation, game, and driving benchmarks that our representations improve over prior annotation-free latent-action baselines.

    • Code and models will be released on our project page: runjiali-rl.github.io/onlyact/.

    For each training sample we draw an anchor pair, a positive pair, and a hard-negative pair. The anchor is a frame pair (oₜ,oₜ₊ₖ) from a video, with a small random offset k. The positiveg(oₜ,oₜ₊ₖ) should carry the same action in a different scene. We construct it with flow-guided scene swapping: we estimate the dense optical flow between the two frames with an off-the-shelf estimator [55], and threshold its magnitude to obtain the moving core region, i.e., the pixels that carry the action. We cut out this region from both frames and paste it onto the same background frame taken from a different scene of the same dataset, translating it in both frames by a common random offset. The pixels in motion are thus preserved exactly, while the scene, background, and absolute location of the motion are all replaced. This construction is only valid when the camera is static. When the camera moves, as in egocentric, hand-held, or driving video, the background motion is itself part of the action and cannot be swapped; in this case the positive falls back to the anchor pair under a different photometric augmentation. Both anchor and positive receive a color jitter that is shared between their two frames, so that inter-frame changes are not altered. The hard negative(o_t^′,o_t^′+k) is drawn from a non-overlapping time window of the same video: it shares the scene with the anchor but likely corresponds to a different action, so it cannot be told apart from the anchor by appearance. We write αₜ, αₜ⁺=φ_θ (g(oₜ,oₜ₊ₖ)), and αₜ⁻=φ_θ(o_t^′,o_t^′+k) for the embeddings of the anchor, positive, and hard negative, respectively.

    Contrastive objective.

    We organize these triplets into a candidate bank ℤ containing every anchor, positive, and hard negative in a batch of size N, and apply a symmetric InfoNCE objective [57] that pulls each anchor toward its matched positive and pushes it away from every other element of the bank in both directions,

    L_con = -1/2N∑ᵢ₌₁^N[\log(\exp (αᵢ^⊤αᵢ⁺/τ))/(∑_z∈ℤ∖{αᵢ}\exp (αᵢ^⊤z/τ))+\log(\exp (αᵢ^+⊤αᵢ/τ))/(∑_z∈ℤ∖{αᵢ⁺}\exp (αᵢ^+⊤z/τ))],

    where τ is a temperature. The same-video hard negatives in ℤ make the objective non-trivial: in contrast, random in-batch negatives from unrelated scenes would be easily separated by appearance alone, allowing the encoder to satisfy the loss without disentangling action from scene. The scene-swapped positives, in turn, prevent the encoder from separating the anchor from its hard negative by memorizing scene-specific cues, since the positive shares none of the anchor’s background.

    Inference.

    After adaptation, a latent action αₜ is obtained by a single forward pass of φ_θ on a frame pair. No labels, prompts, or trajectory-level optimization are required at inference. The adapted encoder φ_θ thus serves as a drop-in action encoder on arbitrary video, yielding the action stream α_1:t that conditions the video world model G_ψ (Sec.3.3).

    3.3 Action-Conditioned Video World Model

    We obtain the action-conditioned video world model G_ψ by adopting the autoregressive world model architecture of AdaWorld [19] and replacing its latent actions by our action stream. Given a trajectory (o₁,…,o_T), we apply the frozen action encoder of Sec.3.1 to consecutive frame pairs to form the action streamα_1:T-1 and use it as continuous action conditioning, with G_ψ predicting each next frame oₜ₊₁ from (o_1:t,α_1:t). Before entering G_ψ, our action embeddings are whitened by a fixed, parameter-free covariance equalization computed on the training data, while the baselines’ latent actions enter unchanged; whitening a baseline in the same way leads to the same conclusions (Appendix A.2). Otherwise, every action representation we compare uses exactly the same backbone, recipe, and data.

    Action injection and training objective.

    Following AdaWorld, the action representation conditions the denoiser through two pathways: it is concatenated with the CLIP image embedding to form the cross-attention context, and concatenated with the context-length embedding into the vector condition, which a label-embedding MLP maps and adds to the timestep embedding. One action vector is given per predicted transition, with no learned projection in between, and the action slots of the pretrained weights are zero-initialized. G_ψ predicts the next frame from up to six context frames, with the context length sampled uniformly from 1 to 6 during training, and is trained with the v-prediction objective under EDM noise scaling and loss weighting [31]. Each condition, including the action, is dropped with probability 0.1 to enable classifier-free guidance [24].

    Action transfer and real-action control.

    As illustrated in Fig.3, the trained pipeline supports two control modes that share the same autoregressive rollout of the video world model G_ψ but differ in how the conditioning action stream α_1:T-1 is obtained. For action transfer, we extract α_1:T-1ᵈᵉᵐᵒ by running the frozen action encoder φ_θ over a demonstration video and feed it to G_ψ together with an initial frame o₁ from a different scene. The model then reproduces the demonstrated action in the new scene without any action labels. For real-action control, we fine-tune on a small action-labeled set. Following [18], a small learned interface maps real actions into the latent-action space and replaces φ_θ at the input of G_ψ: one vector per discrete action, initialized at the mean latent action of its labeled clips, or, for continuous actions, a two-layer MLP first fitted to regress the latent actions of the labeled clips. The interface and the denoiser of G_ψ are then fine-tuned end-to-end (Appendix B.5). Because the latent-action space has already been shaped by large-scale unlabeled pretraining, only a modest amount of labeled data is required, and at inference time the mapped real actions serve as the conditioning stream.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate an action representation for action-conditioned video world models along three axes: (i) action expressiveness (Sec.4.2) — how well the embedding distinguishes different actions; (ii) scene invariance (Sec.4.3) — whether the embedding avoids encoding scene or future-state content that a video generator could exploit as a shortcut; and (iii) action-conditioned video generation quality (Sec.4.4) — how well the embedding serves as a conditioning signal for video generation, measured by fidelity, transferability, and controllability. On both seen and unseen benchmarks, OnlyAct is substantially more expressive than prior annotation-free latent-action baselines, matches their scene invariance, and yields world models with better action transfer and controllability. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B.1.

    4.1 Datasets and Baselines

    We evaluate OnlyAct on datasets both seen and unseen during encoder adaptation. The action encoder is adapted on 168K unlabeled frame-pair samples from nine video sources spanning robot manipulation, human and egocentric video, camera navigation, and games (Appendix B.2). Among our evaluation datasets, only LIBERO [37], DROID [33], and SpatialVID [59] contribute videos to this set (marked ∘ in the tables), and all other datasets are entirely unseen by the encoder. For action probing and scene leakage, we use thirteen datasets with action annotations: nine robot-manipulation datasets (LIBERO, DROID, RLBench [28], RoboCasa [45], DROID-IPRL [33], MetaWorld [65], MUTEX [52], Robosuite [70], and RoboDesk [29]), three camera-navigation datasets (SpatialVID, ARKitScenes [6], and RealEstate10K [69]), and Procgen [14] with 15 discrete actions. For action-conditioned video generation, we evaluate on LIBERO, RLBench, SpatialVID, and nuScenes [13], and further fine-tune with real actions on DMLab [7] and Minecraft from the TECO datasets [62], Habitat [50] in HM3D scenes [48], and nuScenes.

    We compare against two families of baselines. The first is latent-action models, namely DreamDojo [18] and AdaWorld [19]. Since their publicly released weights are not trained on our data, we retrain both on the same 168K training pairs as our encoder for a fair comparison (marked †). The second is the frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder [4], embedded in the same way as OnlyAct (Sec.3.1) but without contrastive adaptation, which isolates the effect of our adaptation from that of the pretrained backbone.

item.title: 要在 3A 游戏里做 agent 评测：GTAGym 直接把真实商业游戏的任务包装成 RL 环境 ｜ GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
一句话：sim-to-real 需要足够复杂的测试场，而 3A 开放世界正好提供这种复杂度。

要点：

  • 出发点：sim-to-real 是训练真实世界 agent 的常用路径——先在模拟里训练，再迁移到物理环境
  • 在各类模拟环境中，**3A 开放世界游戏**提供了最丰富的测试场：任务复杂、世界开放、行为空间大
  • GTAGym 把真实 AAA 游戏里的任务包装成可用于评测与强化学习的环境，从而用商业级内容替代自制玩具环境

为什么值得看：评测环境决定了 agent 能力的上限。用商业 3A 游戏当环境，比自制小场景更接近真实复杂度——这条也反过来提醒：游戏引擎本身就是 AI 训练基础设施的一部分。

中文摘要：sim-to-real 是训练真实世界智能体的常见路径：先在模拟环境里训练，再迁移到物理环境。在各类模拟器中，AAA 开放世界游戏提供了格外丰富的测试场——任务复杂、世界开放、可选行为空间大，接近真实使用场景的难度。GTAGym 因此把真实商业 AAA 游戏中的任务整理成可用于评测与强化学习的环境，让 agent 训练与比较不再依赖自制的简化场景。对把这个方向当作数据来源的团队，这提示了一件事：游戏引擎本身就是 AI 训练基础设施。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

22footnotetext: Corresponding authors: wangyuxin@sii.edu.cn, xpqiu@sii.edu.cn.

1 Introduction

Building agents that can perceive, reason, and act in real-world environments as flexibly as humans is an ultimate goal of artificial general intelligence (AGI) [5]. Sim-to-real transfer is a common approach to developing real-world agent capabilities: models are trained in simulation and then transferred to physical environments [20, 15]. Among simulated environments, AAA open-world games offer a rich testbed: navigation, vehicle control, and interactions with moving characters require spatial understanding, temporal reasoning, and action execution [1, 18]. Vision-language models are increasingly deployed as agents that translate visual observations and natural-language goals into actions [22, 18]. Evaluating these agents requires measuring whether their actions achieve task goals over an extended interaction.

Existing work follows three broad directions: verifiable tasks in sandbox and purpose-built games [5, 13, 8], agents that act in commercial 3D worlds [18, 1, 19], and benchmarks that assess gameplay through visual trajectories or offline questions [25, 27, 21]. These directions advance task verification, realistic interaction, and broad coverage, respectively. Bringing them together requires an environment that preserves objectives from real AAA missions, verifies outcomes automatically, and generates new executable tasks for training. Table 1 compares these features across representative benchmarks.

We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework that decomposes main-story missions from GTA V [16] into reusable tasks defined by their goals, interaction stages, completion constraints, and dynamic behaviors. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, contains 103 online tasks across nine families of navigation, vehicle control, and dynamic interaction, plus 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. GTAVBench supplies textual task instructions; its GTAVBench-AGI branch presents them only in the first screenshot, as in-game objectives, and uses a harness with automatic context compression. A web server exposes a shared screenshot-and-action interface for parallel evaluation, with built-in evaluators checking online outcomes from engine states. The same framework samples task parameters within user-defined ranges to generate batches of RL environments with automatic reward and termination signals. Figure 1 summarizes GTAVBench-AGI performance with the Codex harness across the eleven evaluation categories.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We provide GTAGym, an environment for parallel evaluation of tasks derived from real AAA gameplay. Built-in evaluators determine task outcomes directly from engine states, removing the need for manual outcome judgments and bringing the programmatic task verification available in Minecraft platforms such as MineDojo [5] to tasks derived from GTA V missions.

  • •

    We construct GTAVBench from GTA V main-story missions and introduce its GTAVBench-AGI branch. The former supplies textual task instructions, while the latter presents goals in the initial game image and uses a harness with automatic context compression. The results reveal persistent weaknesses in completing these mission-derived tasks, particularly in aerial control, evasion and interception.

  • •

    We equip GTAGym with a scalable, template-based generator of reinforcement-learning task environments. Each template fixes the scene and task rules while exposing sampling parameters such as movement mode, route length, turn count, and actor speed. Users restrict their ranges or candidate sets to generate 3D and image-based shooting environments in batches, with automatic reward and termination signals to support RL training of exploration, control, and aiming skills.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Foundation-Model Agents for Video Games

    Foundation models combine visual perception, instruction following, and action selection to operate in commercial games. Cradle uses screenshots and keyboard–mouse control with planning, memory, and reflection modules, demonstrating main-story progression in Red Dead Redemption 2 [18]. SIMA learns instruction-following behavior across simulated 3D worlds, using ground-truth checks in research environments and OCR or human judgments in commercial games [1]; SIMA 2 extends this direction with higher-level reasoning and self-improvement [2]. Lumine trains an end-to-end vision-language policy for keyboard–mouse control in open worlds and uses human evaluation for its task benchmark [19]. OctoGTA instruments GTA V through scripting plugins, exposing game entities and programmatic action functions for visually guided task execution [23]. GTAGym instead reconstructs mission-derived tasks with engine-state evaluators and a shared screenshot-and-action interface, supporting parallel evaluation and RL environment generation.

    2.2 Multimodal Game Benchmarks

    Games have long served as testbeds for learning and evaluating interactive agents. Procgen studies RL generalization through procedurally generated levels [3], while MineDojo provides configurable Minecraft tasks and rewards for open-ended learning [5]. More recent benchmarks evaluate foundation-model agents across diverse games: lmgame-Bench studies perception, memory, and reasoning [7], Orak examines agent modules and fine-tuning across commercial games [14], and VideoGameBench measures visual gameplay progress and the effects of inference latency [25]. Specialized benchmarks such as LongPuzzleBench further test long-horizon decision-making in visual puzzles [26].

    Recent work also develops evaluation protocols for richer game environments. GameWorld provides state-verifiable browser tasks and parallel execution [13], while OmniGameArena introduces custom UE5 games for solo, competitive, and cooperative evaluation [8]. For commercial AAA games, GameVerse scores progress through VLM-based milestone matching and studies improvement from video reflection [27]; GameHorizon-Bench evaluates AAA gameplay offline, with its verifiable online track implemented in Minecraft [21]. Our work brings objectives extracted from GTA V main-story missions into an environment with built-in outcome checks, parallel web execution, and parameterized RL instance generation. Table 1 compares these features with prior benchmarks.

    3 GTAGym

    3.1 GTAVBench Task Suite

    GTAVBench and its GTAVBench-AGI branch share a task suite covering eleven dimensions of GTA-style gameplay, spanning navigation, vehicle control, dynamic interaction, and visual aiming. GTAGym provides the 3D evaluation environment, spanning urban, indoor, water, and aviation scenarios, with unified task initialization, interaction, and outcome verification. Native engine states enable automatic verification of online task outcomes.

    Figure 2 illustrates the task categories and representative objectives across the two tracks; Table 3 in Appendix A.1 summarizes their mission requirements. The online 3D track contains 103 tasks across nine dimensions. These categories organize the mission-derived goals, interaction stages, completion constraints, and dynamic behaviors that the environment implements. The image-based environments add 47 shooting and sniping tasks using source gameplay imagery, covering visual target localization and aiming. Together, the two tracks contain 150 tasks. This organization supports a capability-level assessment of agents, with results reported separately for the two tracks. Across both environment types, we group the eleven categories into navigation, interaction, and gun use.

    3.2 Task Construction

    Task extraction and specification.

    We manually decompose 75 GTA V main-story missions into subtasks based on collected walkthrough videos, each corresponding to a distinct stage in a mission. For each subtask, we specify the goal, required interaction order, completion constraints, and entity behaviors used to reconstruct it in our environment. These annotations and source game images support the construction of 150 benchmark tasks across eleven categories.

    Online scenario reconstruction.

    We build the 3D environment using Babylon.js and implement task controllers that expose task-specific states. Task specifications configure initial positions, destinations, vehicles, interaction objects, and moving actors. For navigation tasks, we manually trace paths on the source minimap and seek routes with comparable turn counts in the available city geometry. We add climbing surfaces and landing areas where required by the task. Dynamic-interaction tasks use predefined NPC behaviors and mechanics such as collision-induced slowdown. The resulting scenarios preserve the selected goals, interaction dependencies, and movement constraints while adapting their spatial layout to the evaluation environment.

    Image-based task construction.

    Shooting and sniping use a parallel construction process based on source game imagery. For shooting, we select gameplay frames and associate targets with annotated hit regions. For sniping, we capture images directly in GTA V to construct distinct unscoped and scoped views with magnification-dependent rendering.

    Template instantiation and verification.

    We instantiate each subtask description as a scenario template with an initial state, an instruction, a task budget, and executable success and failure predicates. The goal specifies the destination, target, or interaction outcome; stage transitions specify the required order of interactions. Completion predicates check movement mode, height or depth, target distance, and interaction events according to the task. For following and pursuit, a target controller executes a predefined route that the agent must track through visual observations. For evasion, pursuer controllers update detection and capture states as the agent moves freely. Section 3.4 describes how template parameters are sampled to generate RL environments in batches.

    3.3 Evaluation

    Shared interaction interface.

    GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI use the same task instances, action interface, and scoring rules, differing in instruction presentation and context management. Both branches follow a closed-loop screenshot–action protocol with keyboard–mouse control. By default, online 3D simulation pauses during inference and advances during action execution. The agent specifies a hold duration d∈(0,d_\max] for each key, with d_\max=1 second. Keys execute concurrently, and the turn duration is the longest scheduled hold. Section 5.4 examines alternative duration limits and evaluation without inference-time pausing. The image-based track uses the same action schema with its aiming interface. Complete trajectories are recorded for analysis. The action space is specified in Appendix A.3.

    GTAVBench.

    Following screenshot-based computer-use evaluation [22], agents use a fixed system prompt, a textual task instruction, and screenshot–reply history to generate JSON actions, which an adapter validates and executes. Online history is capped at ten pairs; exceeding the cap drops the oldest five while preserving the instruction. Image-based tasks retain the full history. See Appendix D for prompt and history details.

    GTAVBench-AGI.

    We introduce GTAVBench-AGI as a separate harness-based evaluation branch of GTAVBench. The task instruction appears only within the first screenshot, presenting the objective through the game view as in real gameplay. The agent must read the goal from the image and act through the same keyboard–mouse interface. As interaction history grows, the Codex harness automatically compresses the context supplied to the model [10].

    Scoring.

    Episodes terminate upon task success, task failure, or exhaustion of an applicable turn or game-time budget. We report category-level accuracy and overall accuracy micro-averaged over 150 tasks. Task-specific outcome conditions are detailed in Appendix A.2; model configurations are specified in Section 4.

    3.4 RL Environment Generation

    Templates and sampling ranges.

    Procedural environment generation provides a way to vary training instances and evaluate RL generalization [3]. To support controlled variation, GTAGym organizes environment generation around task templates. Each template T fixes the scene, available assets, interaction logic, evaluator, and episode budget. Users control variation within that template through numeric intervals or finite candidate sets ℂ:

    θ∼P_T(·|ℂ), 𝔼=G(T,θ;ξ),

    		(1)

    where θ contains sampled parameter values and ξ is the generation seed. Parameter definitions, sampling domains, and template-specific settings are provided in Appendix B.

    Batch generation for RL.

    The rule-based generator in GTAGym samples configurations subject to the user’s bounds and the template’s feasibility constraints. For example, a driving template can restrict route length to [200,500] meters and turn count to {2,3,4,5}. These constraints jointly determine eligible routes; the generator rejects incompatible configurations and reports when no feasible instance can be found. It constructs the full route and initial state from the accepted values, then saves the resolved configuration and seed for reuse. Instances share the screenshot–action interface and use task outcomes as sparse rewards, with success and failure ending an episode and budget exhaustion recorded as truncation. The evaluator uses engine-state predicates for 3D tasks and target-hit checks for image-based tasks. Repeated sampling generates batches of RL environments within the requested parameter ranges.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Models and Baselines

    We evaluate six models on GTAVBench under the conventional GUI protocol: GPT-6-Astra [12], GPT-6.1-Sol [11], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [4], GLM-5.3-Flash [24], Kimi-K3 [9], and Qwen3.8-27B. We additionally evaluate the GTAVBench-AGI branch using the Codex harness [10] under the protocol in Section 3.3. Additional model configurations are detailed in Appendix A.4. Navigation and interaction tasks allow up to 300 interaction rounds, while gun-use tasks allow up to 20. The human baseline evaluation protocol is described in Appendix A.5.

    4.2 Main Results

    Table 2 shows a substantial performance gap between the GPT models and the remaining models under both protocols. The best model configuration reaches 70.9% overall accuracy, 18.9 percentage points below the mean human accuracy of 89.8%.

    GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI.

    Compared with GTAVBench, the GTAVBench-AGI protocol increases overall accuracy for all six models by 0.9–10.0 percentage points. The gains are most consistent in navigation, while shooting and sniping show mixed changes across models.

    Dynamic control remains a bottleneck.

    Both GPT models reliably complete on-foot, indoor, and vertical navigation, yet struggle when success requires sustained regulation of vehicle motion or an evolving target relationship. Interception particularly separates Astra from the other models, while aerial navigation and evasion remain difficult across the evaluated configurations. To understand these differences, we examine task-specific failure modes in Section 5.1.

    Performance and output-token usage.

    Figure 3 compares task accuracy and mean output tokens per task across models and evaluation protocols. GPT models retain the strongest accuracy–token tradeoff: Astra without the harness uses the fewest output tokens, while Astra with Codex achieves the highest accuracy. The other models spend substantially more tokens without matching GPT’s task success; DeepSeek, for example, uses approximately 26× as many output tokens as Astra under the JSON protocol. Figure 8 in Appendix compares accuracy and token usage across reasoning-effort settings.

    4.3 Reinforcement Learning

    We study whether reinforcement learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [6] on generated on-foot environments improves task completion and transfers to other categories.

    Training environment generation.

    Using the generator in Section 3.4, we create 50 on-foot navigation instances, matching the benchmark category’s joint route-length and turn-count distribution and adding destination landmarks to some instances. The generated routes are spatially separated from the benchmark’s on-foot routes; all benchmark tasks remain excluded from training. Generation and optimization details are provided in Appendix B.1.

    Training.

    We train Qwen3.8-27B using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [17] inside the Codex harness. LoRA uses rank 32 and α=64 on the attention query and value projections, with a learning rate of 10⁻⁶. Each update samples eight rollouts for each of four tasks. For a rollout τ, we assign the terminal reward

    R(τ)=S+0.3(1-S)P(τ)-0.1·1_{N>100},(2)
    P(τ)=clip (1-(d_T)/(d₀),0,1).

    where S∈{0,1} indicates task success, d₀>0 and d_T are the initial and final traversable distances to the goal, and N counts interaction rounds. Distance progress rewards unsuccessful rollouts, while exceeding 100 rounds incurs a single 0.1 deduction. Distance estimation and scoring details appear in Appendix B.2.

    Results.

    Figure 4 compares mean accuracy across three seeds before and after RL training. Accuracy rises from 54.2% to 72.9% on held-out on-foot tasks and from 34.2% to 38.9% overall. Across OOD categories, accuracy rises from 31.8% to 34.8%, with gains in vertical navigation (46.7% to 73.3%) and aquatic navigation (57.6% to 69.7%). Road driving remains at 3.3%, aerial navigation and interception remain at 0%, and shooting accuracy drops from 73.6% to 68.1%. In blocked trajectories, the base model often repeats ineffective actions, while the trained model uses action feedback to switch strategies and resume progress.

    Transfer to native GTA V.

    We compare the base and RL-trained Qwen3.8-27B on 100 native GTA V navigation and interaction tasks through the same screenshot–action interface and Codex harness. Recorded success rises from 15% to 23%, as shown by the Real Game axis in Figure 4. Source missions and video-based human verification are detailed in Appendix B.3.

    5 Analysis

    We analyze failure modes, error recovery, harness trade-offs, and evaluation settings.

    5.1 Failure Mode Analysis

    Trajectory inspection reveals four recurring failure mechanisms. We contrast road-navigation behavior across models, then examine dynamic-control failures that persist even in frontier models. Table 11 in the appendix provides paired observations and executed actions for all four mechanisms.

    Mistimed steering. In road navigation, non-GPT models sometimes recognize an upcoming turn on the minimap but initiate steering too late or hold it too long for the current speed, overshooting the road. GPT models more effectively translate these cues into early braking and smaller heading corrections.

    Late descent correction. In aerial navigation, reaching the runway does not ensure a safe landing. In the illustrated GPT trajectory, reducing throttle fails to arrest a rapid descent; pitch correction follows too late to prevent a crash. Coordinating attitude, speed, and descent remains difficult even when the destination is correctly identified.

    Failure to sustain blocking. In interception, slowing the target through collision is only an intermediate step. The agent continues accelerating after impact and loses contact instead of braking to hold a blocking position, allowing the target to resume its route.

    Wall entrapment. In evasion, the agent continues applying forward throttle and steering against a wall after hitting a building, producing no displacement before eventually reversing. Such delays interrupt escape progress.

    Together, these cases expose difficulty anticipating motion and switching control strategies as the vehicle, target, or obstacle relationship changes.

    5.2 Error Recovery Across Models

    To study the recovery ability of different models, we manually identify and annotate the first task-relevant error in each trajectory. We group first errors into four capability categories: Perception, Planning, Calibration, and Regulation. Across 900 trajectories from six models, our analysis includes 565 with an identified and categorized first error. Figure 6 shows that Calibration and Regulation dominate, together accounting for 63.2% of assigned first errors. This concentration suggests a bottleneck in closed-loop control: calibrating action direction, magnitude, and duration, and adjusting maneuvers as motion and target states change. We then examine whether the agent subsequently recovers. Figure 6 shows that GPT models recover more reliably: Astra and Sol restore task progress within ten subsequent decisions in 65.7% and 49.3% of categorized first-error cases, compared with 21.6%–25.6% for the other models. In road-navigation trajectories, GPT models correct off-road deviations and rejoin the intended route, resuming progress after local control errors.

    5.3 Harness Trade-offs

    We study the instruction-presentation and context-management differences between GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI. Compared with the JSON runner’s ten-image window, the Codex harness preserves longer histories and uses textual summaries to maintain continuity. This provides memory of attempted strategies, explored rooms, and interaction feedback, helping agents revise their plans and avoid repeated ineffective actions. In motorcycle interception, GPT-6-Astra recalls a blocked approach and changes its maneuver before re-engaging; in indoor navigation, DeepSeek-Flash retains explored rooms and unsuccessful door interactions to guide further search. However, longer histories and compression can also preserve mistaken interpretations and weaken goal adherence. Kimi-K3 initially identifies a rooftop objective correctly but, after compression, substitutes a driving objective and later drops the original goal from its summary. GLM-5.3-Flash similarly carries reversed minimap-marker identities into subsequent decisions. These cases illustrate trajectory drift and goal loss around context handoffs.

    5.4 Effects of Evaluation Settings

    We examine how the timing settings of the online 3D evaluation protocol affect task completion. Both ablations use GPT-6.1-Sol with the Codex harness on the 103 online 3D tasks in GTAVBench-AGI. Figure 7 compares the four distinct settings across the two ablations.

    Maximum action duration.

    We compare three values of d_\max: 0.5 s, 1 s (default), and 2 s. The agent chooses each key’s duration within (0,d_\max]; simulation pauses during inference in all three conditions. Relative to the 1 s baseline (62.1%), reducing the cap to 0.5 s raises overall accuracy to 66.3%, while increasing it to 2 s lowers accuracy to 60.5%. Figure 7 shows the largest gains in following and interception, where shorter actions provide more frequent visual feedback. The tradeoff is more interaction and longer cumulative context: reducing the cap from 1 s to 0.5 s increases mean rounds from 62.6 to 121.2, input tokens from 4.32M to 11.20M, and output tokens from 4.27k to 7.66k. The mean maximum duration selected within an action increases with the allowed cap: 0.494, 0.916, and 1.468 s. At the 2 s cap, 66.6% of actions exceed 1 s, although shorter inputs remain available. This suggests that model does not reliably choose appropriate action durations under our interface.

    Evaluation without pausing.

    With d_\max=1 second, we let the simulation continue during model inference, releasing each key after its specified duration. Without pausing, overall accuracy drops by 22.3 percentage points to 39.8%. Following, interception, and police evasion fall to zero success, while on-foot and indoor navigation retain 100% accuracy and vertical navigation remains at 93.3% (Figure 7). This contrast points to inference latency as a bottleneck for dynamic interaction: after a short action ends, the environment continues evolving while the agent waits for its next decision. Targets can move beyond following range or reach their destinations, and police can capture the player before another corrective action is available. Tasks that tolerate waiting remain more tractable. Thus, real-time performance depends on whether the inference-and-action cycle is fast enough for the task’s response window.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented GTAGym, a web-server-based environment and framework for evaluation and RL on tasks derived from GTA V main-story missions. GTAVBench provides text-instructed evaluation, while its GTAVBench-AGI branch presents task goals only in the first screenshot and uses a harness with automatic context compression. Both support parallel task execution and automatic outcome verification through a unified interface. Experiments show that current agents remain limited in aerial control, evasion and interception. The environment generator in GTAGym complements GTAVBench by sampling numeric and categorical parameters within user-defined bounds under fixed templates, creating 3D and image-based shooting tasks with reward and termination signals for RL training. LoRA RL on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves Qwen3.8-27B’s task completion, with gains extending to unseen task categories and native GTA V missions. Together, these components provide a basis for evaluating and improving agents on tasks derived from real AAA gameplay.

    Acknowledgements

    We thank the developers and contributors of GTA_SZ for making their game environment openly available. Our reconstructed 3D environment builds on their work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Evaluation Details

    A.1 Task Categories and Mission Requirements

    Table 3 summarizes the eleven task categories and their mission requirements.

    A.2 Task-Specific Outcome Conditions

    The evaluator determines completion from engine states and task events for online tasks, and from annotated hit regions for image-based tasks. Success is binary: incomplete route progress, unfinished interactions, and partially cleared target sets receive no partial credit. Both evaluation branches use the same predicates; an agent’s declaration of completion cannot substitute for satisfying them.

    Road and On-Foot.

    The agent must enter the destination region using the required movement mode: driving for road tasks and walking for on-foot tasks. Default horizontal tolerances are 24 m and 3 m, respectively, with smaller task-specific regions for precise destinations. Arrival tests include the segment traversed between consecutive physics updates, so a fast vehicle crossing the region is not missed between frames. Walking arrivals require ground support and cannot be triggered during a jump or traversal animation. The displayed route and intermediate turns guide navigation without imposing mandatory checkpoints; physically feasible shortcuts are allowed. Vehicle-acquisition variants additionally require the agent to find and enter a vehicle. Their ground-truth reference sequence includes the initial walking and boarding stages. Driving into deep water initiates irreversible sinking and prevents arrival success.

    Vertical and Indoor.

    These templates add height and interaction requirements to arrival. For example, the pickup-to-rooftop task requires a grounded walking agent within 1 m of the goal and 0.15 m of the roof height; the ladder-to-rooftop task uses 1.1 m horizontally and 0.35 m vertically. Passing beneath an elevated goal does not complete it. Interior exits can use an oriented passage region instead of a small circular goal, and the agent must reach the correct floor. Required interactions are checked through explicit mission state: the bank task requires pressing E within 1.5 m of the cash interaction point, opening the exit shutter, and leaving the building. The cover task requires pressing Q between the cover and the rear wall, within 0.85 m of its interaction point, and completing the crouched pose. Other interiors can require an outward-and-return sequence before the final exit becomes valid.

    Following.

    The target follows its configured route while the evaluator checks the agent–target distance throughout the episode. The maximum horizontal separation is 20 m on foot and 200 m in road vehicles. Exceeding the applicable threshold causes immediate failure, whether the agent falls behind or moves too far ahead. Success occurs only after the target reaches its destination and the agent remains in the required movement state. Thus the agent must sustain following throughout the NPC’s traversal. Returning within range after a violation does not reverse a terminal failure.

    Interception.

    For ordinary vehicle targets, the agent must establish frontal collision contact and continue blocking the target. Success requires the target’s speed to remain at or below 3 m/s for 1.5 s while the agent remains ahead, with a collision gap below 2.5 m and its own speed at or below 4 m/s.
