Braking from a collision is integrated over time; a naturally slow corner does not satisfy the interception condition. Motorcycle targets instead require three distinct knockdowns, each caused by an impact with at least 2 m/s closing speed. Further hits count only after recovery and separation; the third knockdown completes after the visible fall is complete and the motorcycle slows to at most 1 m/s. A companion-recovery variant uses a separate predicate: the agent must align alongside the moving truck and complete the companion transfer. For these tasks, the target reaching its endpoint before completion causes failure, including ties within a physics update.

    Evasion.

    Evasion has no destination or prescribed route. Evasion has a fixed maximum duration of 180 simulated seconds. The agent succeeds by remaining outside every pursuer’s scanning sector for sixty consecutive simulated seconds within this limit. Each sector has a 12 m radius and a total angle of 90^∘. Any exposure resets the undetected timer; three continuous seconds inside the union of scanning sectors causes capture. Leaving all sectors resets the capture timer. Pursuers and their visible minimap sectors use the same sensing geometry.

    Aquatic.

    Completion depends on the water-task subtype. Swimming goals use a 3 m horizontal tolerance and a 0.8 m depth tolerance; the submerged-entry task, for example, requires a depth of 6±0.8 m. Boat-arrival tasks normally require successful boarding and arrival within 7 m of the destination. Swim-to-boat tasks instead end near the stern platform, while boarding tasks require the boarding transition itself. Shore-arrival tasks require grounded walking on land, above the water surface, within 2.5 m of the endpoint. The beaching variant additionally checks that the boat is grounded and its full footprint is on land. Shore-to-platform transport-choice variants accept surface arrival by swimming or boat. The submarine variant requires crossing the pipe mouth and reaching its interior goal section with valid depth, alignment, and hull clearance.

    Aerial.

    The agent must board the aircraft, take off, satisfy the configured aerial objective, and land at the designated recovery site. Flight waypoints are ordered three-dimensional gates, with radii of 65 m for planes and 16 m for helicopters. Approach objectives require coming within 60 m of the moving aircraft; hover objectives require three continuous seconds within 12 m of the target at a speed no greater than 3 m/s. Landing requires ground contact at the correct runway or helipad after a recorded takeoff and landing, speed at most 1.5 m/s, throttle below 5%, and two continuous seconds stopped. Helicopters must also be within 12 m of the designated landing point. Crashing, exiting the task aircraft, or leaving the allowed flight region causes failure. An aircraft-approach task also fails if the target leaves its task airspace before the approach condition is met.

    Shooting and Sniping.

    The evaluator transforms the reticle’s impact point back into the annotated image coordinate system, accounting for camera movement and scope magnification. Ordinary shooting tests the annotated target box and any required target-part mask; sniping tests the corresponding target polygons. In both cases, exclusion regions are removed from the accepted hit region, and head-specific tasks use the annotated head region. Single-target shooting and sniping allow one shot: a hit succeeds and a miss fails. In multi-target sniping, a task with K targets supplies exactly K bullets and requires K distinct valid hits. An unscoped shot, a miss, or a repeated hit on an already cleared target immediately fails a multi-target task. Single-target sniping uses seeded dispersion for unscoped fire where supported, while scoped fire uses a point impact.

    Interaction budgets and termination precedence.

    Online episodes allow up to 300 interaction rounds, and image-based tasks allow up to 20. Exhausting the round budget without success yields zero credit. Following requires the agent to maintain the required proximity until the NPC reaches its endpoint. Task-specific failures, including capture, aircraft destruction, and the target reaching its endpoint in Interception, take precedence over completion.

    A.3 Agent Action Space

    The agent controls the environment through a shared keyboard–mouse interface. Each response specifies one action object with a required keys array and an optional mouse object. Keyboard entries pair a key with its hold duration; mouse entries specify movement, scrolling, or button state changes. The conventional GUI agent emits this object as JSON text; the harness agent places it in game_step.action, alongside a unique request_id. Table 4 summarizes the interface.

    Keyboard inputs.

    The permitted keys are w, a, s, d, Shift, Control, Space, e, f, q, c, v, g, and Numpad4/5/6/8. Uppercase single-letter inputs and Ctrl are normalized to their canonical names. Each key appears at most once per response and has a finite duration d∈(0,d_\max], with a default limit of d_\max=1 second. For native 3D tasks, the duration is rounded upward to simulation frames at 60 Hz, and all specified keys start together or continue an existing hold. Keys are released independently as their durations expire; the turn duration is the maximum scheduled hold duration rather than their sum. There is no within-turn sequence of delayed key presses.

    Mouse inputs.

    All observations use a 1280×720 viewport. Mouse movement uses relative pixel displacement, with -640≤dₓ≤640 and -360≤d_y≤360; finite fractional values are permitted. Positive dₓ looks right and positive d_y looks up. Repeating a nonzero displacement changes the current view again. The aiming center in shooting and sniping remains at (640,360); native 3D tasks apply camera sensitivity rather than guaranteeing exact centering of an image point. The agent can also scroll up or down by one to six steps, or issue down/up events for the left and right buttons, with at most one event per button in a turn. Mouse inputs have no duration parameter and do not advance simulated time.

    Persistent input state.

    In native 3D tasks, keys held through the end of a turn remain held while inference is paused. Including the same key in the next response continues the hold; omitting it releases it before simulation resumes. Mouse buttons remain in their current state until an explicit release or episode cleanup. View orientation persists across turns, and no cursor coordinate is supplied as additional observation text. An empty keys array releases previous keyboard holds. With no mouse operation or wait, this produces a zero-time no-op that still consumes an interaction step. The optional wait_seconds field accepts a finite duration in (0,1] seconds with keys:[]. Instantaneous mouse operations occur first, then the simulation advances for the requested wait; image-based tasks consume a turn without advancing scene time. All held inputs are released when an episode ends.

    Example.

    The following native action first applies a relative mouse movement of 120 pixels right and 30 pixels up, then holds w for one second and Space for 0.1 seconds concurrently. The scheduled turn duration is one second, and the next screenshot is returned after execution or earlier task termination.

    {"keys": [{"key": "w", "duration_seconds": 1},{"key": "Space", "duration_seconds": 0.1}],"mouse": {"move": {"dx": 120, "dy": 30}}}

    Image-based aiming tasks.

    Shooting and sniping use the mouse portion of the same schema; agents are instructed to submit an empty keyboard array, and well-formed keyboard inputs are ignored by the executor. Ordinary shooting supports aiming movement and left-button down to fire. Sniping additionally supports right-button down/up for scope control, left-button up, and scrolling to adjust magnification. Each scroll step maps to 160 ms of the aiming engine’s zoom operation, without advancing a simulation clock. A shot terminates a single-target task; multi-target sniping continues until all targets are cleared or a failure occurs, as specified in Appendix A.2. Each response consumes one of the twenty available interaction steps. The prompt requests one aiming operation per turn; the current executor also accepts composite mouse inputs without an intermediate observation.

    Validation.

    Each action object is validated before execution. Unknown fields, duplicate keys or buttons, invalid durations, out-of-range mouse displacements, simultaneous movement and scrolling, and waiting with a nonempty keyboard array are rejected. For conventional GUI responses, the parser also accepts a single JSON code block enclosing the entire response, without surrounding explanation, although the prompt requests plain JSON.

    A.4 Model Configurations

    Table 6 lists the reasoning effort settings used for the results in Table 2 and Figures 1 and 3. Under both the JSON and Codex evaluation protocols, all models use a 1M-token context window, a maximum of 32,768 output tokens per response, and a sampling temperature of 0.7. Each configuration was evaluated using three independent random seeds.

    Reasoning-effort comparison.

    Figure 8 compares requested high and max effort for DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi under both protocols, using the same 150 task IDs and the token-accounting rules above. For these three models, each high result comes from one completed run; max retains the main-table aggregation. GPT-6-Astra and GPT-6.1-Sol are also shown at high as reference points using the main-table configurations and Figure 3 token measurements. These historical batches are not a controlled paired ablation. Higher requested effort does not consistently improve accuracy or reduce output-token usage.

    A.5 Human Evaluation

    We recruited three experienced players who had previously completed Grand Theft Auto V. Participants played directly through the task interfaces using standard gameplay controls. Each participant attempted all 150 benchmark tasks exactly once, with no prior exposure to those tasks. Table 2 reports the mean accuracy and population standard deviation (in percentage points) across the three participants. Overall accuracy weights all 150 tasks equally.

    Appendix B RL Environment Parameterization

    A template fixes the scene, available assets, task logic, outcome rules, and episode budget. For image-based shooting, it fixes an annotated image pool and the aiming interface. The parameters in Table 7 are numeric quantities or categorical choices whose sampling domains can be restricted by the user. Table 8 marks the parameters exposed by each template. Shared quantities use the same symbols across templates. All domains are intersected with the template’s valid locations, assets, and controller constraints. Positions use (x,y,z), with (x,z) spanning the horizontal plane and y giving vertical elevation; underwater depth is measured below the local water surface.

    Jointly feasible sampling.

    Numeric bounds and option sets constrain a distribution of samples within a fixed template. For a template supporting land and water transport, M={land,water} samples between these domains, while M={land} fixes land transport. Within a selected domain, U controls the concrete movement mode: land supports walking or driving, water supports swimming, diving, or boats, and air supports planes or helicopters, subject to template restrictions. For example, transport: [water] with movement: [boat] fixes boat navigation; movement: [swim, boat] allows either supported mode. If movement is omitted, the generator uses the template’s movement modes compatible with the transport restriction. Endpoint choices, path length, and turn count must admit a compatible route, and transport options must support the selected locations. The generator searches for valid routes and placements within these restrictions, rejects incompatible proposals, and reports failure if its generation budget is exhausted. Equal numeric bounds, a fixed location, or a singleton option set hold a parameter constant.

    Navigation and moving actors.

    Navigation templates use pₛ, p_g, ψ, ℓ, and k to generate the initial pose and reference route. Their transport domain is fixed: Road uses land, Aquatic uses water, and Aerial uses air. Road uses driving, while On-Foot, Vertical, and Indoor retain walking as their template-defined movement. Aquatic and Aerial expose u to select a concrete mode within their fixed water or air domain. Following and Evasion expose both m and u within their supported choices; Interception fixes land transport and driving. Elevation constraints on p_g and the template’s traversable geometry determine valid vertical, aquatic, and aerial routes. Following and Interception use the same start and heading parameters for the agent, but p_g, ℓ, and k describe the target route. The target starts at a valid location satisfying d and moves at the sampled speed v. Evasion instead samples n pursuers, with each pursuer’s speed and initial distance drawn within the specified v and d bounds. It imposes no destination or reference route on the agent. Pursuer identities, placement rules, sensing configuration, and behavior controllers are supplied by the template. Following-distance tolerances, interception conditions, and escape timers remain fixed template rules.

    Image-based sampling.

    The categorical choice i selects an existing image–target pair, preserving the correspondence between visible content and hit annotations. The generator then samples δ subject to the selected pair’s valid image bounds. Different pair choices and aiming offsets yield different shooting samples within the same template. Sniping is evaluation-only and is excluded from environment generation.

    From ranges to a concrete sample.

    As an illustrative evasion configuration, a user could restrict pursuer count to {1,2,3}, initial distance to [20,40] meters, and speed to [2,4] meters per second. A generation seed ξ controls the choices made within these bounds. The generator saves the sampled values, resolved route and actor placements or aiming state, and template and environment versions. These resolved values identify the concrete instance; the input ranges describe the family of instances from which it was sampled.

    B.1 On-Foot RL Training Setup

    Generated training split.

    We use generation seed 20261027 to construct 50 on-foot instances. Route lengths and turn counts follow the empirical joint distribution of the 16 benchmark on-foot tasks, with a 5% length tolerance for new routes. The resulting routes span 88.9–131.4 meters and zero to four turns; 19 instances include destination landmarks such as motorcycles, sedans, vans, or convertibles. The generator checks route feasibility using the movement controller and enforces spatial separation from the benchmark on-foot routes. Training and evaluation use distinct task instances within the same city and controllers.

    Optimization and interaction.

    We train rank-32 LoRA adapters with α=64 on the language model’s attention query and value projections; the vision encoder and base model weights remain frozen. GRPO uses AdamW with a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁶ and clipping ratio 0.2. Each update uses four tasks and eight rollouts per task, collecting 32 concurrent trajectories; optimization uses eight H200 GPUs. Training uses the native Codex history and automatic compaction, the same game rules. Instructions appear in the initial screenshot, and inference pauses the environment. The context window is 1M tokens, generation is capped at 32,768 tokens per response, actions at one second, and episodes at 300 interaction rounds.

    B.2 Reward Implementation Details

    We detail the terminal reward defined in Eq. 2 for the on-foot GRPO experiment.

    Normalized distance progress.

    Let P(τ) denote the clipped fractional distance reduction in Eq. 2. Normalization makes equal fractional reductions comparable across route lengths. Moving farther from the destination yields zero progress, and revisiting locations provides no accumulated bonus: only the final distance is used. The factor (1-S) applies the distance bonus only to unsuccessful rollouts. Thus a successful rollout receives either 1 or 0.9, while an unsuccessful rollout receives at most 0.3.

    Traversable-distance measurement.

    Distances are approximated on a one-meter, eight-neighbor walking grid using A* search with the environment’s collision and surface-height checks. The search is independent of the displayed purple route and permits physically feasible shortcuts. An unreachable or unsupported-height final position receives P=0. Distance computation failures are treated as invalid reward evidence, not as zero task progress. These measurements are host-side training signals and are not included in the agent’s observations.

    Round penalty and terminal scoring.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：sim-to-real 需要足够复杂的测试场，而 3A 开放世界正好提供这种复杂度。

要点：

  • 出发点：sim-to-real 是训练真实世界 agent 的常用路径——先在模拟里训练，再迁移到物理环境
  • 在各类模拟环境中，**3A 开放世界游戏**提供了最丰富的测试场：任务复杂、世界开放、行为空间大
  • GTAGym 把真实 AAA 游戏里的任务包装成可用于评测与强化学习的环境，从而用商业级内容替代自制玩具环境

为什么值得看：评测环境决定了 agent 能力的上限。用商业 3A 游戏当环境，比自制小场景更接近真实复杂度——这条也反过来提醒：游戏引擎本身就是 AI 训练基础设施的一部分。

中文摘要：sim-to-real 是训练真实世界智能体的常见路径：先在模拟环境里训练，再迁移到物理环境。在各类模拟器中，AAA 开放世界游戏提供了格外丰富的测试场——任务复杂、世界开放、可选行为空间大，接近真实使用场景的难度。GTAGym 因此把真实商业 AAA 游戏中的任务整理成可用于评测与强化学习的环境，让 agent 训练与比较不再依赖自制的简化场景。对把这个方向当作数据来源的团队，这提示了一件事：游戏引擎本身就是 AI 训练基础设施。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

22footnotetext: Corresponding authors: wangyuxin@sii.edu.cn, xpqiu@sii.edu.cn.

1 Introduction

Building agents that can perceive, reason, and act in real-world environments as flexibly as humans is an ultimate goal of artificial general intelligence (AGI) [5]. Sim-to-real transfer is a common approach to developing real-world agent capabilities: models are trained in simulation and then transferred to physical environments [20, 15]. Among simulated environments, AAA open-world games offer a rich testbed: navigation, vehicle control, and interactions with moving characters require spatial understanding, temporal reasoning, and action execution [1, 18]. Vision-language models are increasingly deployed as agents that translate visual observations and natural-language goals into actions [22, 18]. Evaluating these agents requires measuring whether their actions achieve task goals over an extended interaction.

Existing work follows three broad directions: verifiable tasks in sandbox and purpose-built games [5, 13, 8], agents that act in commercial 3D worlds [18, 1, 19], and benchmarks that assess gameplay through visual trajectories or offline questions [25, 27, 21]. These directions advance task verification, realistic interaction, and broad coverage, respectively. Bringing them together requires an environment that preserves objectives from real AAA missions, verifies outcomes automatically, and generates new executable tasks for training. Table 1 compares these features across representative benchmarks.

We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework that decomposes main-story missions from GTA V [16] into reusable tasks defined by their goals, interaction stages, completion constraints, and dynamic behaviors. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, contains 103 online tasks across nine families of navigation, vehicle control, and dynamic interaction, plus 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. GTAVBench supplies textual task instructions; its GTAVBench-AGI branch presents them only in the first screenshot, as in-game objectives, and uses a harness with automatic context compression. A web server exposes a shared screenshot-and-action interface for parallel evaluation, with built-in evaluators checking online outcomes from engine states. The same framework samples task parameters within user-defined ranges to generate batches of RL environments with automatic reward and termination signals. Figure 1 summarizes GTAVBench-AGI performance with the Codex harness across the eleven evaluation categories.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We provide GTAGym, an environment for parallel evaluation of tasks derived from real AAA gameplay. Built-in evaluators determine task outcomes directly from engine states, removing the need for manual outcome judgments and bringing the programmatic task verification available in Minecraft platforms such as MineDojo [5] to tasks derived from GTA V missions.

  • •

    We construct GTAVBench from GTA V main-story missions and introduce its GTAVBench-AGI branch. The former supplies textual task instructions, while the latter presents goals in the initial game image and uses a harness with automatic context compression. The results reveal persistent weaknesses in completing these mission-derived tasks, particularly in aerial control, evasion and interception.

  • •

    We equip GTAGym with a scalable, template-based generator of reinforcement-learning task environments. Each template fixes the scene and task rules while exposing sampling parameters such as movement mode, route length, turn count, and actor speed. Users restrict their ranges or candidate sets to generate 3D and image-based shooting environments in batches, with automatic reward and termination signals to support RL training of exploration, control, and aiming skills.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Foundation-Model Agents for Video Games

    Foundation models combine visual perception, instruction following, and action selection to operate in commercial games. Cradle uses screenshots and keyboard–mouse control with planning, memory, and reflection modules, demonstrating main-story progression in Red Dead Redemption 2 [18]. SIMA learns instruction-following behavior across simulated 3D worlds, using ground-truth checks in research environments and OCR or human judgments in commercial games [1]; SIMA 2 extends this direction with higher-level reasoning and self-improvement [2]. Lumine trains an end-to-end vision-language policy for keyboard–mouse control in open worlds and uses human evaluation for its task benchmark [19]. OctoGTA instruments GTA V through scripting plugins, exposing game entities and programmatic action functions for visually guided task execution [23]. GTAGym instead reconstructs mission-derived tasks with engine-state evaluators and a shared screenshot-and-action interface, supporting parallel evaluation and RL environment generation.

    2.2 Multimodal Game Benchmarks

    Games have long served as testbeds for learning and evaluating interactive agents. Procgen studies RL generalization through procedurally generated levels [3], while MineDojo provides configurable Minecraft tasks and rewards for open-ended learning [5]. More recent benchmarks evaluate foundation-model agents across diverse games: lmgame-Bench studies perception, memory, and reasoning [7], Orak examines agent modules and fine-tuning across commercial games [14], and VideoGameBench measures visual gameplay progress and the effects of inference latency [25]. Specialized benchmarks such as LongPuzzleBench further test long-horizon decision-making in visual puzzles [26].

    Recent work also develops evaluation protocols for richer game environments. GameWorld provides state-verifiable browser tasks and parallel execution [13], while OmniGameArena introduces custom UE5 games for solo, competitive, and cooperative evaluation [8]. For commercial AAA games, GameVerse scores progress through VLM-based milestone matching and studies improvement from video reflection [27]; GameHorizon-Bench evaluates AAA gameplay offline, with its verifiable online track implemented in Minecraft [21]. Our work brings objectives extracted from GTA V main-story missions into an environment with built-in outcome checks, parallel web execution, and parameterized RL instance generation. Table 1 compares these features with prior benchmarks.

    3 GTAGym

    3.1 GTAVBench Task Suite

    GTAVBench and its GTAVBench-AGI branch share a task suite covering eleven dimensions of GTA-style gameplay, spanning navigation, vehicle control, dynamic interaction, and visual aiming. GTAGym provides the 3D evaluation environment, spanning urban, indoor, water, and aviation scenarios, with unified task initialization, interaction, and outcome verification. Native engine states enable automatic verification of online task outcomes.

    Figure 2 illustrates the task categories and representative objectives across the two tracks; Table 3 in Appendix A.1 summarizes their mission requirements. The online 3D track contains 103 tasks across nine dimensions. These categories organize the mission-derived goals, interaction stages, completion constraints, and dynamic behaviors that the environment implements. The image-based environments add 47 shooting and sniping tasks using source gameplay imagery, covering visual target localization and aiming. Together, the two tracks contain 150 tasks. This organization supports a capability-level assessment of agents, with results reported separately for the two tracks. Across both environment types, we group the eleven categories into navigation, interaction, and gun use.

    3.2 Task Construction

    Task extraction and specification.

    We manually decompose 75 GTA V main-story missions into subtasks based on collected walkthrough videos, each corresponding to a distinct stage in a mission. For each subtask, we specify the goal, required interaction order, completion constraints, and entity behaviors used to reconstruct it in our environment. These annotations and source game images support the construction of 150 benchmark tasks across eleven categories.

    Online scenario reconstruction.

    We build the 3D environment using Babylon.js and implement task controllers that expose task-specific states. Task specifications configure initial positions, destinations, vehicles, interaction objects, and moving actors. For navigation tasks, we manually trace paths on the source minimap and seek routes with comparable turn counts in the available city geometry. We add climbing surfaces and landing areas where required by the task. Dynamic-interaction tasks use predefined NPC behaviors and mechanics such as collision-induced slowdown. The resulting scenarios preserve the selected goals, interaction dependencies, and movement constraints while adapting their spatial layout to the evaluation environment.

    Image-based task construction.

    Shooting and sniping use a parallel construction process based on source game imagery. For shooting, we select gameplay frames and associate targets with annotated hit regions. For sniping, we capture images directly in GTA V to construct distinct unscoped and scoped views with magnification-dependent rendering.

    Template instantiation and verification.

    We instantiate each subtask description as a scenario template with an initial state, an instruction, a task budget, and executable success and failure predicates. The goal specifies the destination, target, or interaction outcome; stage transitions specify the required order of interactions. Completion predicates check movement mode, height or depth, target distance, and interaction events according to the task. For following and pursuit, a target controller executes a predefined route that the agent must track through visual observations. For evasion, pursuer controllers update detection and capture states as the agent moves freely. Section 3.4 describes how template parameters are sampled to generate RL environments in batches.

    3.3 Evaluation

    Shared interaction interface.

    GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI use the same task instances, action interface, and scoring rules, differing in instruction presentation and context management. Both branches follow a closed-loop screenshot–action protocol with keyboard–mouse control. By default, online 3D simulation pauses during inference and advances during action execution. The agent specifies a hold duration d∈(0,d_\max] for each key, with d_\max=1 second. Keys execute concurrently, and the turn duration is the longest scheduled hold. Section 5.4 examines alternative duration limits and evaluation without inference-time pausing. The image-based track uses the same action schema with its aiming interface. Complete trajectories are recorded for analysis. The action space is specified in Appendix A.3.

    GTAVBench.

    Following screenshot-based computer-use evaluation [22], agents use a fixed system prompt, a textual task instruction, and screenshot–reply history to generate JSON actions, which an adapter validates and executes. Online history is capped at ten pairs; exceeding the cap drops the oldest five while preserving the instruction. Image-based tasks retain the full history. See Appendix D for prompt and history details.

    GTAVBench-AGI.

    We introduce GTAVBench-AGI as a separate harness-based evaluation branch of GTAVBench. The task instruction appears only within the first screenshot, presenting the objective through the game view as in real gameplay. The agent must read the goal from the image and act through the same keyboard–mouse interface. As interaction history grows, the Codex harness automatically compresses the context supplied to the model [10].

    Scoring.

    Episodes terminate upon task success, task failure, or exhaustion of an applicable turn or game-time budget. We report category-level accuracy and overall accuracy micro-averaged over 150 tasks. Task-specific outcome conditions are detailed in Appendix A.2; model configurations are specified in Section 4.

    3.4 RL Environment Generation

    Templates and sampling ranges.

    Procedural environment generation provides a way to vary training instances and evaluate RL generalization [3]. To support controlled variation, GTAGym organizes environment generation around task templates. Each template T fixes the scene, available assets, interaction logic, evaluator, and episode budget. Users control variation within that template through numeric intervals or finite candidate sets ℂ:

    θ∼P_T(·|ℂ), 𝔼=G(T,θ;ξ),

    		(1)

    where θ contains sampled parameter values and ξ is the generation seed. Parameter definitions, sampling domains, and template-specific settings are provided in Appendix B.

    Batch generation for RL.

    The rule-based generator in GTAGym samples configurations subject to the user’s bounds and the template’s feasibility constraints. For example, a driving template can restrict route length to [200,500] meters and turn count to {2,3,4,5}. These constraints jointly determine eligible routes; the generator rejects incompatible configurations and reports when no feasible instance can be found. It constructs the full route and initial state from the accepted values, then saves the resolved configuration and seed for reuse. Instances share the screenshot–action interface and use task outcomes as sparse rewards, with success and failure ending an episode and budget exhaustion recorded as truncation. The evaluator uses engine-state predicates for 3D tasks and target-hit checks for image-based tasks. Repeated sampling generates batches of RL environments within the requested parameter ranges.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Models and Baselines

    We evaluate six models on GTAVBench under the conventional GUI protocol: GPT-6-Astra [12], GPT-6.1-Sol [11], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [4], GLM-5.3-Flash [24], Kimi-K3 [9], and Qwen3.8-27B. We additionally evaluate the GTAVBench-AGI branch using the Codex harness [10] under the protocol in Section 3.3. Additional model configurations are detailed in Appendix A.4. Navigation and interaction tasks allow up to 300 interaction rounds, while gun-use tasks allow up to 20. The human baseline evaluation protocol is described in Appendix A.5.

    4.2 Main Results

    Table 2 shows a substantial performance gap between the GPT models and the remaining models under both protocols. The best model configuration reaches 70.9% overall accuracy, 18.9 percentage points below the mean human accuracy of 89.8%.

    GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI.

    Compared with GTAVBench, the GTAVBench-AGI protocol increases overall accuracy for all six models by 0.9–10.0 percentage points. The gains are most consistent in navigation, while shooting and sniping show mixed changes across models.

    Dynamic control remains a bottleneck.

    Both GPT models reliably complete on-foot, indoor, and vertical navigation, yet struggle when success requires sustained regulation of vehicle motion or an evolving target relationship. Interception particularly separates Astra from the other models, while aerial navigation and evasion remain difficult across the evaluated configurations. To understand these differences, we examine task-specific failure modes in Section 5.1.

    Performance and output-token usage.

    Figure 3 compares task accuracy and mean output tokens per task across models and evaluation protocols. GPT models retain the strongest accuracy–token tradeoff: Astra without the harness uses the fewest output tokens, while Astra with Codex achieves the highest accuracy. The other models spend substantially more tokens without matching GPT’s task success; DeepSeek, for example, uses approximately 26× as many output tokens as Astra under the JSON protocol. Figure 8 in Appendix compares accuracy and token usage across reasoning-effort settings.

    4.3 Reinforcement Learning

    We study whether reinforcement learning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [6] on generated on-foot environments improves task completion and transfers to other categories.

    Training environment generation.

    Using the generator in Section 3.4, we create 50 on-foot navigation instances, matching the benchmark category’s joint route-length and turn-count distribution and adding destination landmarks to some instances. The generated routes are spatially separated from the benchmark’s on-foot routes; all benchmark tasks remain excluded from training. Generation and optimization details are provided in Appendix B.1.

    Training.

    We train Qwen3.8-27B using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [17] inside the Codex harness. LoRA uses rank 32 and α=64 on the attention query and value projections, with a learning rate of 10⁻⁶. Each update samples eight rollouts for each of four tasks. For a rollout τ, we assign the terminal reward

    R(τ)=S+0.3(1-S)P(τ)-0.1·1_{N>100},(2)
    P(τ)=clip (1-(d_T)/(d₀),0,1).

    where S∈{0,1} indicates task success, d₀>0 and d_T are the initial and final traversable distances to the goal, and N counts interaction rounds. Distance progress rewards unsuccessful rollouts, while exceeding 100 rounds incurs a single 0.1 deduction. Distance estimation and scoring details appear in Appendix B.2.

    Results.

    Figure 4 compares mean accuracy across three seeds before and after RL training. Accuracy rises from 54.2% to 72.9% on held-out on-foot tasks and from 34.2% to 38.9% overall. Across OOD categories, accuracy rises from 31.8% to 34.8%, with gains in vertical navigation (46.7% to 73.3%) and aquatic navigation (57.6% to 69.7%). Road driving remains at 3.3%, aerial navigation and interception remain at 0%, and shooting accuracy drops from 73.6% to 68.1%. In blocked trajectories, the base model often repeats ineffective actions, while the trained model uses action feedback to switch strategies and resume progress.

    Transfer to native GTA V.

    We compare the base and RL-trained Qwen3.8-27B on 100 native GTA V navigation and interaction tasks through the same screenshot–action interface and Codex harness. Recorded success rises from 15% to 23%, as shown by the Real Game axis in Figure 4. Source missions and video-based human verification are detailed in Appendix B.3.

    5 Analysis

    We analyze failure modes, error recovery, harness trade-offs, and evaluation settings.

    5.1 Failure Mode Analysis

    Trajectory inspection reveals four recurring failure mechanisms. We contrast road-navigation behavior across models, then examine dynamic-control failures that persist even in frontier models. Table 11 in the appendix provides paired observations and executed actions for all four mechanisms.

    Mistimed steering. In road navigation, non-GPT models sometimes recognize an upcoming turn on the minimap but initiate steering too late or hold it too long for the current speed, overshooting the road. GPT models more effectively translate these cues into early braking and smaller heading corrections.

    Late descent correction. In aerial navigation, reaching the runway does not ensure a safe landing. In the illustrated GPT trajectory, reducing throttle fails to arrest a rapid descent; pitch correction follows too late to prevent a crash. Coordinating attitude, speed, and descent remains difficult even when the destination is correctly identified.

    Failure to sustain blocking. In interception, slowing the target through collision is only an intermediate step. The agent continues accelerating after impact and loses contact instead of braking to hold a blocking position, allowing the target to resume its route.

    Wall entrapment. In evasion, the agent continues applying forward throttle and steering against a wall after hitting a building, producing no displacement before eventually reversing. Such delays interrupt escape progress.

    Together, these cases expose difficulty anticipating motion and switching control strategies as the vehicle, target, or obstacle relationship changes.

    5.2 Error Recovery Across Models

    To study the recovery ability of different models, we manually identify and annotate the first task-relevant error in each trajectory. We group first errors into four capability categories: Perception, Planning, Calibration, and Regulation. Across 900 trajectories from six models, our analysis includes 565 with an identified and categorized first error. Figure 6 shows that Calibration and Regulation dominate, together accounting for 63.2% of assigned first errors. This concentration suggests a bottleneck in closed-loop control: calibrating action direction, magnitude, and duration, and adjusting maneuvers as motion and target states change. We then examine whether the agent subsequently recovers. Figure 6 shows that GPT models recover more reliably: Astra and Sol restore task progress within ten subsequent decisions in 65.7% and 49.3% of categorized first-error cases, compared with 21.6%–25.6% for the other models. In road-navigation trajectories, GPT models correct off-road deviations and rejoin the intended route, resuming progress after local control errors.

    5.3 Harness Trade-offs

    We study the instruction-presentation and context-management differences between GTAVBench and GTAVBench-AGI. Compared with the JSON runner’s ten-image window, the Codex harness preserves longer histories and uses textual summaries to maintain continuity. This provides memory of attempted strategies, explored rooms, and interaction feedback, helping agents revise their plans and avoid repeated ineffective actions. In motorcycle interception, GPT-6-Astra recalls a blocked approach and changes its maneuver before re-engaging; in indoor navigation, DeepSeek-Flash retains explored rooms and unsuccessful door interactions to guide further search. However, longer histories and compression can also preserve mistaken interpretations and weaken goal adherence. Kimi-K3 initially identifies a rooftop objective correctly but, after compression, substitutes a driving objective and later drops the original goal from its summary. GLM-5.3-Flash similarly carries reversed minimap-marker identities into subsequent decisions. These cases illustrate trajectory drift and goal loss around context handoffs.

    5.4 Effects of Evaluation Settings

    We examine how the timing settings of the online 3D evaluation protocol affect task completion. Both ablations use GPT-6.1-Sol with the Codex harness on the 103 online 3D tasks in GTAVBench-AGI. Figure 7 compares the four distinct settings across the two ablations.

    Maximum action duration.

    We compare three values of d_\max: 0.5 s, 1 s (default), and 2 s. The agent chooses each key’s duration within (0,d_\max]; simulation pauses during inference in all three conditions. Relative to the 1 s baseline (62.1%), reducing the cap to 0.5 s raises overall accuracy to 66.3%, while increasing it to 2 s lowers accuracy to 60.5%. Figure 7 shows the largest gains in following and interception, where shorter actions provide more frequent visual feedback. The tradeoff is more interaction and longer cumulative context: reducing the cap from 1 s to 0.5 s increases mean rounds from 62.6 to 121.2, input tokens from 4.32M to 11.20M, and output tokens from 4.27k to 7.66k. The mean maximum duration selected within an action increases with the allowed cap: 0.494, 0.916, and 1.468 s. At the 2 s cap, 66.6% of actions exceed 1 s, although shorter inputs remain available. This suggests that model does not reliably choose appropriate action durations under our interface.

    Evaluation without pausing.

    With d_\max=1 second, we let the simulation continue during model inference, releasing each key after its specified duration. Without pausing, overall accuracy drops by 22.3 percentage points to 39.8%. Following, interception, and police evasion fall to zero success, while on-foot and indoor navigation retain 100% accuracy and vertical navigation remains at 93.3% (Figure 7). This contrast points to inference latency as a bottleneck for dynamic interaction: after a short action ends, the environment continues evolving while the agent waits for its next decision. Targets can move beyond following range or reach their destinations, and police can capture the player before another corrective action is available. Tasks that tolerate waiting remain more tractable. Thus, real-time performance depends on whether the inference-and-action cycle is fast enough for the task’s response window.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented GTAGym, a web-server-based environment and framework for evaluation and RL on tasks derived from GTA V main-story missions. GTAVBench provides text-instructed evaluation, while its GTAVBench-AGI branch presents task goals only in the first screenshot and uses a harness with automatic context compression. Both support parallel task execution and automatic outcome verification through a unified interface. Experiments show that current agents remain limited in aerial control, evasion and interception. The environment generator in GTAGym complements GTAVBench by sampling numeric and categorical parameters within user-defined bounds under fixed templates, creating 3D and image-based shooting tasks with reward and termination signals for RL training. LoRA RL on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves Qwen3.8-27B’s task completion, with gains extending to unseen task categories and native GTA V missions. Together, these components provide a basis for evaluating and improving agents on tasks derived from real AAA gameplay.

    Acknowledgements

    We thank the developers and contributors of GTA_SZ for making their game environment openly available. Our reconstructed 3D environment builds on their work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Evaluation Details

    A.1 Task Categories and Mission Requirements

    Table 3 summarizes the eleven task categories and their mission requirements.

    A.2 Task-Specific Outcome Conditions

    The evaluator determines completion from engine states and task events for online tasks, and from annotated hit regions for image-based tasks. Success is binary: incomplete route progress, unfinished interactions, and partially cleared target sets receive no partial credit. Both evaluation branches use the same predicates; an agent’s declaration of completion cannot substitute for satisfying them.

    Road and On-Foot.

    The agent must enter the destination region using the required movement mode: driving for road tasks and walking for on-foot tasks. Default horizontal tolerances are 24 m and 3 m, respectively, with smaller task-specific regions for precise destinations. Arrival tests include the segment traversed between consecutive physics updates, so a fast vehicle crossing the region is not missed between frames. Walking arrivals require ground support and cannot be triggered during a jump or traversal animation. The displayed route and intermediate turns guide navigation without imposing mandatory checkpoints; physically feasible shortcuts are allowed. Vehicle-acquisition variants additionally require the agent to find and enter a vehicle. Their ground-truth reference sequence includes the initial walking and boarding stages. Driving into deep water initiates irreversible sinking and prevents arrival success.

    Vertical and Indoor.

    These templates add height and interaction requirements to arrival. For example, the pickup-to-rooftop task requires a grounded walking agent within 1 m of the goal and 0.15 m of the roof height; the ladder-to-rooftop task uses 1.1 m horizontally and 0.35 m vertically. Passing beneath an elevated goal does not complete it. Interior exits can use an oriented passage region instead of a small circular goal, and the agent must reach the correct floor. Required interactions are checked through explicit mission state: the bank task requires pressing E within 1.5 m of the cash interaction point, opening the exit shutter, and leaving the building. The cover task requires pressing Q between the cover and the rear wall, within 0.85 m of its interaction point, and completing the crouched pose. Other interiors can require an outward-and-return sequence before the final exit becomes valid.

    Following.

    The target follows its configured route while the evaluator checks the agent–target distance throughout the episode. The maximum horizontal separation is 20 m on foot and 200 m in road vehicles. Exceeding the applicable threshold causes immediate failure, whether the agent falls behind or moves too far ahead. Success occurs only after the target reaches its destination and the agent remains in the required movement state. Thus the agent must sustain following throughout the NPC’s traversal. Returning within range after a violation does not reverse a terminal failure.

    Interception.

    For ordinary vehicle targets, the agent must establish frontal collision contact and continue blocking the target. Success requires the target’s speed to remain at or below 3 m/s for 1.5 s while the agent remains ahead, with a collision gap below 2.5 m and its own speed at or below 4 m/s. Braking from a collision is integrated over time; a naturally slow corner does not satisfy the interception condition. Motorcycle targets instead require three distinct knockdowns, each caused by an impact with at least 2 m/s closing speed. Further hits count only after recovery and separation; the third knockdown completes after the visible fall is complete and the motorcycle slows to at most 1 m/s. A companion-recovery variant uses a separate predicate: the agent must align alongside the moving truck and complete the companion transfer. For these tasks, the target reaching its endpoint before completion causes failure, including ties within a physics update.

    Evasion.

    Evasion has no destination or prescribed route. Evasion has a fixed maximum duration of 180 simulated seconds. The agent succeeds by remaining outside every pursuer’s scanning sector for sixty consecutive simulated seconds within this limit. Each sector has a 12 m radius and a total angle of 90^∘. Any exposure resets the undetected timer; three continuous seconds inside the union of scanning sectors causes capture. Leaving all sectors resets the capture timer. Pursuers and their visible minimap sectors use the same sensing geometry.

    Aquatic.

    Completion depends on the water-task subtype. Swimming goals use a 3 m horizontal tolerance and a 0.8 m depth tolerance; the submerged-entry task, for example, requires a depth of 6±0.8 m. Boat-arrival tasks normally require successful boarding and arrival within 7 m of the destination. Swim-to-boat tasks instead end near the stern platform, while boarding tasks require the boarding transition itself. Shore-arrival tasks require grounded walking on land, above the water surface, within 2.5 m of the endpoint. The beaching variant additionally checks that the boat is grounded and its full footprint is on land. Shore-to-platform transport-choice variants accept surface arrival by swimming or boat. The submarine variant requires crossing the pipe mouth and reaching its interior goal section with valid depth, alignment, and hull clearance.

    Aerial.

    The agent must board the aircraft, take off, satisfy the configured aerial objective, and land at the designated recovery site. Flight waypoints are ordered three-dimensional gates, with radii of 65 m for planes and 16 m for helicopters. Approach objectives require coming within 60 m of the moving aircraft; hover objectives require three continuous seconds within 12 m of the target at a speed no greater than 3 m/s. Landing requires ground contact at the correct runway or helipad after a recorded takeoff and landing, speed at most 1.5 m/s, throttle below 5%, and two continuous seconds stopped. Helicopters must also be within 12 m of the designated landing point. Crashing, exiting the task aircraft, or leaving the allowed flight region causes failure. An aircraft-approach task also fails if the target leaves its task airspace before the approach condition is met.

    Shooting and Sniping.

    The evaluator transforms the reticle’s impact point back into the annotated image coordinate system, accounting for camera movement and scope magnification. Ordinary shooting tests the annotated target box and any required target-part mask; sniping tests the corresponding target polygons. In both cases, exclusion regions are removed from the accepted hit region, and head-specific tasks use the annotated head region. Single-target shooting and sniping allow one shot: a hit succeeds and a miss fails. In multi-target sniping, a task with K targets supplies exactly K bullets and requires K distinct valid hits. An unscoped shot, a miss, or a repeated hit on an already cleared target immediately fails a multi-target task. Single-target sniping uses seeded dispersion for unscoped fire where supported, while scoped fire uses a point impact.

    Interaction budgets and termination precedence.

    Online episodes allow up to 300 interaction rounds, and image-based tasks allow up to 20. Exhausting the round budget without success yields zero credit. Following requires the agent to maintain the required proximity until the NPC reaches its endpoint. Task-specific failures, including capture, aircraft destruction, and the target reaching its endpoint in Interception, take precedence over completion.

    A.3 Agent Action Space

    The agent controls the environment through a shared keyboard–mouse interface. Each response specifies one action object with a required keys array and an optional mouse object. Keyboard entries pair a key with its hold duration; mouse entries specify movement, scrolling, or button state changes. The conventional GUI agent emits this object as JSON text; the harness agent places it in game_step.action, alongside a unique request_id. Table 4 summarizes the interface.

    Keyboard inputs.

    The permitted keys are w, a, s, d, Shift, Control, Space, e, f, q, c, v, g, and Numpad4/5/6/8. Uppercase single-letter inputs and Ctrl are normalized to their canonical names. Each key appears at most once per response and has a finite duration d∈(0,d_\max], with a default limit of d_\max=1 second. For native 3D tasks, the duration is rounded upward to simulation frames at 60 Hz, and all specified keys start together or continue an existing hold. Keys are released independently as their durations expire; the turn duration is the maximum scheduled hold duration rather than their sum. There is no within-turn sequence of delayed key presses.

    Mouse inputs.

    All observations use a 1280×720 viewport. Mouse movement uses relative pixel displacement, with -640≤dₓ≤640 and -360≤d_y≤360; finite fractional values are permitted. Positive dₓ looks right and positive d_y looks up. Repeating a nonzero displacement changes the current view again. The aiming center in shooting and sniping remains at (640,360); native 3D tasks apply camera sensitivity rather than guaranteeing exact centering of an image point. The agent can also scroll up or down by one to six steps, or issue down/up events for the left and right buttons, with at most one event per button in a turn. Mouse inputs have no duration parameter and do not advance simulated time.

    Persistent input state.

    In native 3D tasks, keys held through the end of a turn remain held while inference is paused. Including the same key in the next response continues the hold; omitting it releases it before simulation resumes. Mouse buttons remain in their current state until an explicit release or episode cleanup. View orientation persists across turns, and no cursor coordinate is supplied as additional observation text. An empty keys array releases previous keyboard holds. With no mouse operation or wait, this produces a zero-time no-op that still consumes an interaction step. The optional wait_seconds field accepts a finite duration in (0,1] seconds with keys:[]. Instantaneous mouse operations occur first, then the simulation advances for the requested wait; image-based tasks consume a turn without advancing scene time. All held inputs are released when an episode ends.

    Example.

    The following native action first applies a relative mouse movement of 120 pixels right and 30 pixels up, then holds w for one second and Space for 0.1 seconds concurrently. The scheduled turn duration is one second, and the next screenshot is returned after execution or earlier task termination.

    {"keys": [{"key": "w", "duration_seconds": 1},{"key": "Space", "duration_seconds": 0.1}],"mouse": {"move": {"dx": 120, "dy": 30}}}

    Image-based aiming tasks.

    Shooting and sniping use the mouse portion of the same schema; agents are instructed to submit an empty keyboard array, and well-formed keyboard inputs are ignored by the executor. Ordinary shooting supports aiming movement and left-button down to fire. Sniping additionally supports right-button down/up for scope control, left-button up, and scrolling to adjust magnification. Each scroll step maps to 160 ms of the aiming engine’s zoom operation, without advancing a simulation clock. A shot terminates a single-target task; multi-target sniping continues until all targets are cleared or a failure occurs, as specified in Appendix A.2. Each response consumes one of the twenty available interaction steps. The prompt requests one aiming operation per turn; the current executor also accepts composite mouse inputs without an intermediate observation.

    Validation.

    Each action object is validated before execution. Unknown fields, duplicate keys or buttons, invalid durations, out-of-range mouse displacements, simultaneous movement and scrolling, and waiting with a nonempty keyboard array are rejected. For conventional GUI responses, the parser also accepts a single JSON code block enclosing the entire response, without surrounding explanation, although the prompt requests plain JSON.

    A.4 Model Configurations

    Table 6 lists the reasoning effort settings used for the results in Table 2 and Figures 1 and 3. Under both the JSON and Codex evaluation protocols, all models use a 1M-token context window, a maximum of 32,768 output tokens per response, and a sampling temperature of 0.7. Each configuration was evaluated using three independent random seeds.

    Reasoning-effort comparison.

    Figure 8 compares requested high and max effort for DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi under both protocols, using the same 150 task IDs and the token-accounting rules above. For these three models, each high result comes from one completed run; max retains the main-table aggregation. GPT-6-Astra and GPT-6.1-Sol are also shown at high as reference points using the main-table configurations and Figure 3 token measurements. These historical batches are not a controlled paired ablation. Higher requested effort does not consistently improve accuracy or reduce output-token usage.

    A.5 Human Evaluation

    We recruited three experienced players who had previously completed Grand Theft Auto V. Participants played directly through the task interfaces using standard gameplay controls. Each participant attempted all 150 benchmark tasks exactly once, with no prior exposure to those tasks. Table 2 reports the mean accuracy and population standard deviation (in percentage points) across the three participants. Overall accuracy weights all 150 tasks equally.

    Appendix B RL Environment Parameterization

    A template fixes the scene, available assets, task logic, outcome rules, and episode budget. For image-based shooting, it fixes an annotated image pool and the aiming interface. The parameters in Table 7 are numeric quantities or categorical choices whose sampling domains can be restricted by the user. Table 8 marks the parameters exposed by each template. Shared quantities use the same symbols across templates. All domains are intersected with the template’s valid locations, assets, and controller constraints. Positions use (x,y,z), with (x,z) spanning the horizontal plane and y giving vertical elevation; underwater depth is measured below the local water surface.

    Jointly feasible sampling.

    Numeric bounds and option sets constrain a distribution of samples within a fixed template. For a template supporting land and water transport, M={land,water} samples between these domains, while M={land} fixes land transport. Within a selected domain, U controls the concrete movement mode: land supports walking or driving, water supports swimming, diving, or boats, and air supports planes or helicopters, subject to template restrictions. For example, transport: [water] with movement: [boat] fixes boat navigation; movement: [swim, boat] allows either supported mode. If movement is omitted, the generator uses the template’s movement modes compatible with the transport restriction. Endpoint choices, path length, and turn count must admit a compatible route, and transport options must support the selected locations. The generator searches for valid routes and placements within these restrictions, rejects incompatible proposals, and reports failure if its generation budget is exhausted. Equal numeric bounds, a fixed location, or a singleton option set hold a parameter constant.

    Navigation and moving actors.

    Navigation templates use pₛ, p_g, ψ, ℓ, and k to generate the initial pose and reference route. Their transport domain is fixed: Road uses land, Aquatic uses water, and Aerial uses air. Road uses driving, while On-Foot, Vertical, and Indoor retain walking as their template-defined movement. Aquatic and Aerial expose u to select a concrete mode within their fixed water or air domain. Following and Evasion expose both m and u within their supported choices; Interception fixes land transport and driving. Elevation constraints on p_g and the template’s traversable geometry determine valid vertical, aquatic, and aerial routes. Following and Interception use the same start and heading parameters for the agent, but p_g, ℓ, and k describe the target route. The target starts at a valid location satisfying d and moves at the sampled speed v. Evasion instead samples n pursuers, with each pursuer’s speed and initial distance drawn within the specified v and d bounds. It imposes no destination or reference route on the agent. Pursuer identities, placement rules, sensing configuration, and behavior controllers are supplied by the template. Following-distance tolerances, interception conditions, and escape timers remain fixed template rules.

    Image-based sampling.

    The categorical choice i selects an existing image–target pair, preserving the correspondence between visible content and hit annotations. The generator then samples δ subject to the selected pair’s valid image bounds. Different pair choices and aiming offsets yield different shooting samples within the same template. Sniping is evaluation-only and is excluded from environment generation.

    From ranges to a concrete sample.

    As an illustrative evasion configuration, a user could restrict pursuer count to {1,2,3}, initial distance to [20,40] meters, and speed to [2,4] meters per second. A generation seed ξ controls the choices made within these bounds. The generator saves the sampled values, resolved route and actor placements or aiming state, and template and environment versions. These resolved values identify the concrete instance; the input ranges describe the family of instances from which it was sampled.

    B.1 On-Foot RL Training Setup

    Generated training split.

    We use generation seed 20261027 to construct 50 on-foot instances. Route lengths and turn counts follow the empirical joint distribution of the 16 benchmark on-foot tasks, with a 5% length tolerance for new routes. The resulting routes span 88.9–131.4 meters and zero to four turns; 19 instances include destination landmarks such as motorcycles, sedans, vans, or convertibles. The generator checks route feasibility using the movement controller and enforces spatial separation from the benchmark on-foot routes. Training and evaluation use distinct task instances within the same city and controllers.

    Optimization and interaction.

    We train rank-32 LoRA adapters with α=64 on the language model’s attention query and value projections; the vision encoder and base model weights remain frozen. GRPO uses AdamW with a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁶ and clipping ratio 0.2. Each update uses four tasks and eight rollouts per task, collecting 32 concurrent trajectories; optimization uses eight H200 GPUs. Training uses the native Codex history and automatic compaction, the same game rules. Instructions appear in the initial screenshot, and inference pauses the environment. The context window is 1M tokens, generation is capped at 32,768 tokens per response, actions at one second, and episodes at 300 interaction rounds.

    B.2 Reward Implementation Details

    We detail the terminal reward defined in Eq. 2 for the on-foot GRPO experiment.

    Normalized distance progress.

    Let P(τ) denote the clipped fractional distance reduction in Eq. 2. Normalization makes equal fractional reductions comparable across route lengths. Moving farther from the destination yields zero progress, and revisiting locations provides no accumulated bonus: only the final distance is used. The factor (1-S) applies the distance bonus only to unsuccessful rollouts. Thus a successful rollout receives either 1 or 0.9, while an unsuccessful rollout receives at most 0.3.

    Traversable-distance measurement.

    Distances are approximated on a one-meter, eight-neighbor walking grid using A* search with the environment’s collision and surface-height checks. The search is independent of the displayed purple route and permits physically feasible shortcuts. An unreachable or unsupported-height final position receives P=0. Distance computation failures are treated as invalid reward evidence, not as zero task progress. These measurements are host-side training signals and are not included in the agent’s observations.

    Round penalty and terminal scoring.

item.title: 离线逆渲染出的皮肤参数，游戏着色器用不上：这篇直接估计「屏幕空间次表面散射」参数，对着实时管线拟合 ｜ A Lightweight Differentiable Method for Real-Time Skin Rendering and Digitization
item.description:
一句话：路径追踪估出来的物理属性映射不到引擎里的近似着色器，这条直接估实时可用的 SSS 参数。

要点：

  • 断层讲得很准：皮肤的逆渲染通常依赖**离线路径追踪**估计物理属性，而这些结果无法直接映射到交互式应用（如游戏引擎）所用的近似着色器
  • 做法是直接估计**为实时渲染管线量身定制的次表面散射参数**，而不是先求出物理量再想办法近似
  • 技术上是一个可微的屏幕空间次表面散射（SSSS）框架，能同时优化空间变化的基础贴图与散射距离

为什么值得看：「离线好看、实时不能用」是皮肤渲染长期的分裂。把可微优化直接架在实时着色器的参数空间上，等于让数字人/皮肤资产的生产对着最终像素目标收敛，而不是对着物理量。

中文摘要：皮肤的逆渲染通常依赖离线路径追踪来估计物理属性，但这些结果无法直接映射到游戏引擎里使用的近似着色器——于是「物理正确」和「实时可用」长期是两套东西。这篇的做法是直接估计**面向实时渲染管线的次表面散射参数**：它提出一个轻量的可微屏幕空间次表面散射（SSSS）框架，能够联合优化空间变化的基础贴图与散射距离。这样优化目标从「物理量准不准」变成「实时着色器输出对不对」，对数字人与皮肤资产管线是更实际的目标函数。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

A Lightweight Differentiable Method for Real-Time Skin Rendering and Digitization

Abstract

Inverse rendering for skin typically relies on offline path tracing to estimate physical properties, which fail to map directly to the approximate shaders utilized in interactive applications, such as game engines. We bridge this gap by directly estimating subsurface scattering parameters tailored for real-time rendering pipelines. We introduce a differentiable Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) framework that enables the joint optimization of spatially varying base textures and scattering distances. To account for local variations in skin thickness, we estimate these parameters across distinct facial regions, generating a blended profile map ready for production runtime engines. Our pipeline utilizes a low-cost, single-light, single-view capture setup designed for accessible and practical appearance acquisition. Optimization is driven by a masked loss function targeting regions where subsurface scattering effects are dominant. We validate our approach on a real-world dataset of 45 individuals across the Monk Skin Tone Scale, ensuring demographic generalization. Furthermore, we complement this evaluation with synthetic data, a multi-light setup validating our single-light assumption, and a tilted-view configuration confirming angular consistency. Results demonstrate that our method effectively recovers scattering parameters from lightweight inputs, yielding realistic skin appearance directly compatible with standard real-time shaders.

1 Introduction

Accurately simulating human skin remains a significant challenge in computer graphics due to its physical complexity and the high sensitivity of the human visual system to facial appearance. As a layered, anisotropic, and spatially varying medium, skin involves intricate subsurface scattering, fine-scale geometric details, and directionally dependent light transport. To meet the computational constraints of interactive applications, the industry often relies on screen-space approximations rather than full volumetric path tracing. However, the perceptual sensitivity of observers ensures that even subtle rendering inaccuracies appear unnatural. Additionally, the global diversity of skin tones demands methods that generalize across the full spectrum of human pigmentation while maintaining both physical plausibility and real-time performance.

Traditional approaches for capturing skin optical properties often require sophisticated hardware, such as hyperspectral sensors or polarimetric imaging systems [23, 1, 32]. While these methods yield accurate results, they are typically expensive, restricted to controlled laboratory settings, and produce physical parameters (e.g., extinction coefficients) that do not map directly to real-time shaders. Furthermore, they often struggle to scale across the diverse facial expressions and skin tones encountered in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce a low-cost, replicable single-view, single-light capture setup. Our compact configuration facilitates the practical acquisition of skin appearance without requiring specialized environments.

Instead of estimating offline physical parameters like absorption or extinction coefficients through complex path-tracing intermediaries, we directly optimize the specific parameters used in real-time rendering pipelines. We ground our approach in the Bidirectional Subsurface Scattering Reflectance Distribution Function (BSSRDF), specifically utilizing the Burley Normalized Diffusion profile [6], the standard for real-time physically based skin shading. To enable optimization, we implement a differentiable version of the Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) algorithm incorporating this profile. This model provides control via the scattering distance parameter, which governs the distance light travels beneath the surface. Tuning this parameter manually is difficult due to its strong coupling with material appearance and the lack of direct visual references. Our approach automates this process by directly optimizing scattering distance textures from photographic data, enabling efficient and plausible appearance reconstruction.

Prior work frequently underexplores skin tone diversity, focusing primarily on mid-range tones and resulting in biased models that generalize poorly across lighter or darker skin. To address this limitation and drive representative skin modeling, we anchor our framework in the Monk Skin Tone Scale [35] (Fig. 2). Unlike traditional scales designed primarily for dermatological UV response (e.g., Fitzpatrick [14]), the Monk scale provides a perceptually balanced distribution covering the broad spectrum of human skin tones. Our primary goal is to leverage this scale to deliver a lightweight differentiable inverse rendering method that is physically grounded, equitable across diverse populations, and directly compatible with real-time production pipelines.

Our key contributions are:

  • 1.

    A lightweight, low-cost, single-light, single-view capture setup explicitly designed for the practical acquisition of facial skin patches across diverse skin tones.

  • 2.

    A differentiable rendering framework introducing a novel optimization stage to estimate state-of-the-art real-time scattering parameters directly from image data, bypassing complex path-tracing intermediaries.

  • 3.

    A masked loss formulation that isolates gradients within shadowed regions, where multiple scattering is physically dominant, ensuring accurate and stable optimization of subsurface parameters.

  • 4.

    A large dataset of calibrated facial skin patches and their estimated optical properties, sampled across the Monk Skin Tone Scale to drive equitable and representative skin modeling.

    • 2 Related Work

    In this section, we review prior work on skin rendering, categorizing approaches into subsurface scattering approximations, biophysical and material models, physical acquisition methods, and inverse rendering strategies.

    Subsurface Scattering Approximations. Realistic skin rendering requires simulating the complex transport of light through layers of varying opacity. As described by the BSSRDF [6], light transport in translucent media falls into three regimes: single scattering (thin materials), multiple scattering (thick materials), and intermediate scattering (turbid media) (Fig. 3). While full simulation is computationally expensive, most methods approximate the multiple scattering component to achieve visual plausibility [7]. The dipole model [27] remains a foundational approximation for offline rendering, modeling subsurface transport via virtual light source pairs. Subsequent improvements include the multipole method [11] for multi-layered materials and the directional dipole [13, 15], which introduces anisotropy to better capture detailed surface features. For higher precision, the quantized diffusion model [12] discretizes the diffusion process, offering finer control over scattering behavior.

    For real-time pipelines, scattering is typically separated into surface and subsurface components. Translucency effects (single scattering) are often approximated using thickness maps generated via inverted-normal ambient occlusion [3]. For multiple scattering, screen-space techniques are the standard. [28] and [29] approximate diffusion by convolving irradiance maps with weighted Gaussian kernels, while [8] proposed an exponential diffusion profile matching Monte Carlo simulations. Recently, neural approaches such as [43, 42] have proposed encoding scattering profiles into lightweight networks, though screen-space convolution remains the industry standard for its predictability and direct integration with standard shading models.

    Biophysical and Skin Material Models. Human skin exhibits significant spatial heterogeneity. Early measurement-based approaches [46] demonstrated that fixed scattering parameters fail to capture the variation between regions like the forehead, cheeks, and ears. [19] introduced layered models to account for epidermal and dermal variations, while [41] utilized region-based lookup tables, and [31] extended layered models to simulate cosmetics. Beyond empirical layers, recent biophysical models explicitly simulate physiological processes, such as sun-induced erythema and tanning [25], or multi-layer heterogeneous volume transport [44].

    While volumetric biophysical models offer high biological fidelity, they require computationally demanding Monte Carlo solvers. In contrast, we utilize the Disney 2015 BSSRDF [6] as our parametric foundation. While the earlier Disney BRDF [5]—widely referred to in the industry as Burley 12—provided a robust model for surface reflection, it lacked volumetric scattering controls. The 2015 extension, commonly known as Burley 15, introduces a physically derived scattering distance parameter that ensures energy conservation while supporting anisotropic diffusion. This balance of physical plausibility and artist-friendly control makes Burley 15 ideal for our optimization pipeline. Inspired by [50], we optimize a scalar scattering distance per facial region under this model and blend them at runtime to achieve anatomical fidelity without sacrificing real-time efficiency.

    Skin Appearance Acquisition. High-fidelity skin capture traditionally relies on complex hardware to separate reflectance components. Systems such as Light Stages [9], time-multiplexed lighting rigs [18], and polarization-based setups [33, 16] deliver ground-truth quality. Recent advances include spectral reconstruction methods [20] and single-shot polarized capture systems [38] that recover high-quality geometry and appearance. However, these methods require specialized equipment and controlled environments. In contrast, we focus on a lightweight acquisition regime to democratize skin reconstruction. Our differentiable framework optimizes scattering parameters from a single-view, single-light setup, eliminating the need for costly optical components or synchronized lighting arrays. Furthermore, this simplified pipeline remains robust across the full spectrum of human skin tones. This combination of hardware accessibility and tonal generalization provides a scalable solution for realistic digital human creation.

    Inverse Rendering for Material Estimation. Material estimation generally falls into learning-based or optimization-based categories. Learning-based methods [10, 53, 39] train neural networks to infer parameters from images, offering fast inference but often lacking generalization to out-of-distribution examples. Optimization-based methods minimize the reconstruction error between observed and rendered images. For example, [17] optimized spatially varying parameters for fabrics using a differentiable rasterizer. In the domain of skin, [1] and [32] have successfully estimated parameters from hyperspectral data. Most closely related to our work is [45], which performs inverse rendering for textured translucent appearance. However, while [45] focuses on general translucent objects, our pipeline is specialized for human skin, incorporating domain-specific constraints (such as the Monk scale and facial region masks) and directly optimizing the screen-space parameters used in game engines. Furthermore, while [44] estimates biological parameters from a pre-extracted albedo map for offline volume rendering, our framework optimizes directly from raw photographs under directional lighting, decoupling surface reflection (albedo, roughness, specular) and subsurface scattering for real-time screen-space execution.

    3 Overview and Rendering Model

    This section outlines our proposed pipeline for skin appearance estimation and describes the real-time rendering techniques integrated into our engine to simulate subsurface scattering.

    3.1 Overview

    Our approach builds upon the diffusion-based skin model introduced by [8], which extends Burley 12 with a subsurface scattering parameter s. We adopt Burley 15 model for its physical grounding and proven photorealism [17]. Unlike prior works that fix subsurface parameters to fit surface properties, we explicitly estimate the subsurface scattering terms that dominate skin appearance. We define the scattering distance as d=1/s (assuming a unit mean free path). We replace the standard uniform parameterization with an optimized homogeneous scattering parameter per facial region, which are then blended to create a spatially varying map for local anatomical variations.

    We focus on the human face due to its perceptual importance in recognition [4] and the significant variation in skin thickness that influences light diffusion [26]. Consequently, our acquisition targets facial skin patches.

    We utilize a single-view, single-light capture setup to extract skin data. To ensure representational diversity, we select subjects spanning the Monk Skin Tone Scale [35], capturing the optical variability caused by differing melanin and hemoglobin levels. Our proposed architecture proceeds in two sequential phases: first, we optimize a homogeneous scattering distance d for each individual skin patch; second, we generate a full facial scattering map by blending these values based on anatomical regions, similar to the profile blending in [50]. To execute this initial patch-fitting phase, our inverse rendering pipeline directly optimizes a spatially varying Burley 15 texture stack by backpropagating reconstruction errors through a differentiable rasterizer, extending the core optimization framework from [17]. The complete pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 4.

    This automated approach eliminates manual parameter tuning, driving skin rendering directly from photographic observations. Accordingly, the remainder of the paper details our acquisition protocol (Section 4.1), the tensorized scattering architecture (Section 4.2), implementation details (Section 5), and our experimental results and validation (Sections 6.1 and 6.2).

    3.2 Rendering Model

    We implement a custom real-time rendering engine using WebGL and Babylon.js [36]. This choice provides a broadly deployable, cross-platform verification environment that runs across a wide range of browsers and devices, including resource-constrained and low-end platforms, allowing us to assess whether the fitted scattering distances produce realistic and physically consistent appearances under practical cross-device rendering constraints. In addition to visualizing the final assets, the engine acts as a synthetic data generator, producing reference images with known ground-truth parameters to validate our optimization procedure.

    The shading model relies on two primary inputs: a thickness texture and a spatially varying scattering distance texture.
