    We evaluate our method qualitatively and quantitatively on both real and synthetic data to demonstrate its reconstruction fidelity, computational efficiency, and robustness across diverse skin tones. Our evaluation is structured into two main parts: (1) an analysis of fitting results on real facial patches across the Monk Skin Tone Scale, evaluating perceptual metrics, runtime benchmarks, and material plausibility (Section 6.1); and (2) a comprehensive validation study verifying parameter isolation via synthetic ground truth, assessing our shadow-masked loss through ablation, and benchmarking our single-light setup against a multi-light configuration (Section 6.2). Validation of angular consistency via tilted-view experiments is provided in Section 3 of the Supplementary Material.

    We built a dataset of 225 real skin patches from 45 participants across five facial regions using a single-light setup. A subset of 17 subjects (85 samples) was additionally captured using a multi-light setup for validation.

    Ethics, consent, and data handling

    . The acquisition protocol was reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Committee of our institution prior to data collection. All participants received written information describing the purpose and procedures of the study and provided written informed consent prior to participation, including consent for the processing of their personal data. Participation was voluntary, and participants could withdraw their consent at any time without adverse consequences. Skin images were associated with generic participant identifiers, while the correspondence between these identifiers and the contact information of the participants was stored separately under restricted access available only to the research team. Contact information was used solely when a participant needed to be contacted for a repeated acquisition. Only non-identifying skin-patch images were used for scientific dissemination, and any additional compatible research use requires prior anonymization. Personal data were handled according to applicable international regulations.

    6.1 Fitting Results

    We apply our inverse rendering pipeline to real facial skin patches sampled across the Monk Skin Tone Scale. We evaluate reconstruction quality using the perceptual metric FLIP [2], computed over masked regions to isolate the subsurface scattering halo. Fig. 12 shows representative examples from light, medium, and dark skin tones. The reconstructions closely match the input photographs, particularly in the shadowed transition regions where scattering dominates.

    We report complementary metrics—LPIPS [51], SSIM [52], and PSNR—in Table 2. While SSIM is sensitive to luminance variations in shadowed regions (resulting in lower scores), perceptual metrics like FLIP and LPIPS yield consistently low error values. This supports the perceptual plausibility of our reconstructions across the full skin tone spectrum.

    In addition to perceptual quality, we benchmark the computational efficiency of our pipeline. Because all skin patches are standardized to 480×360 px and evaluated under our fixed multi-stage schedule, runtime is deterministic across subjects. Table 3 details the stage-wise computational breakdown on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti (12 GB). Inverse optimization converges in under 3.5 minutes (198.4 s) per patch with a peak footprint of 9.4 GB during Stage 3 integration, confirming that our pipeline enables fast and accessible digitization on consumer desktop hardware.

    We visualize the optimized Burley 15 material stack alongside the auxiliary residual specular map in Fig. 13. The estimated textures are spatially smooth and consistent across the dataset. Utilizing a monocular depth-based normal prior, rather than relying on photometric cues, regularizes the single-view optimization, mitigating parameter instability across complex structures like the ear. While this depth prior acts as a low-frequency approximation that lacks sharp pore-level details—yielding smoother roughness maps—and screen-space shading partially bakes self-shadows into albedo across steep relief (e.g., ear folds), our multi-light validation confirms the scattering parameter d converges consistently. This demonstrates that subsurface optimization remains effectively decoupled from localized shadowing and micro-geometric inaccuracies.

    Crucially, the estimated scattering distance maps exhibit intuitive trends across the skin tone spectrum. As illustrated in Fig. 14, darker skin tones correspond to shorter scattering distances, consistent with the reduced subsurface light transport in melanin-rich tissue. These findings demonstrate the physical plausibility of our RGB-based optimizations without the need for hyperspectral data. Furthermore, our masking strategy effectively focuses supervision on shadowed regions, improving multiple scattering estimates in darker skin where the effect is subtle but directionally dependent.

    6.2 Validation

    Validation on Synthetic Skin Patches

    We validate our pipeline using synthetic skin patches rendered under known Burley parameters [6] with an identical sampling budget (N=128) to ensure numerical consistency during inverse optimization. In the first experiment, we fix all surface attributes (albedo, normals, roughness, IOR) and optimize only the scattering distance. This isolates the scattering estimation stage. As shown in Fig. 15, the estimated scattering maps (dₒₚₜ) closely match the reference ground truth (d_ref), and the rendered reconstructions are visually indistinguishable from the inputs.

    In the second experiment, we fix the scattering distance and vary the albedo across the ten synthetic tones of the Monk Scale to test robustness to pigmentation changes. While Figure 16 shows a representative subset, Section 4 of the Supplementary Material details the full 10-tone evaluation alongside the real-world dataset distribution (N=45) cross-referenced against participant self-assessments.

    Specular Isolation Validation

    Our pipeline employs a residual specular map to absorb high-frequency highlights, mitigating their leakage into the albedo map. To validate this strategy, we optimize a synthetic scene where the ground-truth decomposition between albedo and specular reflection is known. Fig. 17 compares the optimized residual map against the ground-truth specular contribution. The close resemblance confirms that our robust mean albedo computation effectively shields the diffuse component, allowing the residual map to accurately capture the specular response. Furthermore, this separation minimizes the risk of unmodeled specular energy corrupting other surface attributes, directly validating why our framework achieves highly stable and smooth roughness maps with suppressed artifact bleeding.

    Masked Loss Validation

    To isolate the contribution of our shadow-masked loss during Stage 3 (Mₒₚₜ=M), we performed an ablation study comparing this formulation against unmasked full-image loss supervision (Mₒₚₜ=1) under identical rendering conditions (Figure 18). In the unmasked setting, incident irradiance across directly illuminated stripes is orders of magnitude higher than within shadowed regions. Consequently, backpropagation gradients are dominated by surface reflectance components (diffuse albedo and specular highlights), introducing severe gradient competition against the subtle, low-frequency subsurface diffusion halo. The optimizer attempts to compensate for subtle direct-light discrepancies by skewing the scattering distance parameter d.

    Interestingly, while the relative spectral proportionality (dᵣ>d_g>d_b) is naturally preserved due to the lower absorption of melanin and hemoglobin at longer wavelengths, the unmasked optimization yields an artificially saturated and magnitude-shifted d. This magnitude shift truncates the diffusion tail along transition boundaries. In contrast, restricting the loss domain strictly to the binary shadow mask M decouples parameter estimation from direct surface illumination, forcing the objective function to evaluate the pure radial decay of multiple scattering. This targeted supervision eliminates parameter overcompensation, ensuring that the estimated parameter d yields a reconstruction closer to the reference capture, decreasing the perceptual FLIP error from 0.11 to 0.06 (45% reduction) in shadowed transition regions, and from 0.15 to 0.10 across the full patch.

    Comparison with Multi-Light Acquisition

    To evaluate robustness under real-world conditions, we compare our single-light results against a multi-light setup (three synchronized projectors). This configuration allows us to introduce an additional preliminary optimization stage to the pipeline. In this new Stage 1, we leverage the multi-light observations to specifically optimize and refine the initial Sobel-filtered normal map, improving geometric consistency before proceeding with the standard material estimation steps (now shifted to Stages 2, 3, and 4).

    We compare the scattering distance maps estimated from our standard single-light pipeline against those produced using this augmented four-stage multi-light configuration. Despite the improved geometric detail provided by the refined normals, the single-light method yields scattering distances that are visually and numerically consistent (mean L₁ difference <2%). As shown in Fig. 19, discrepancies are minimal and confined to occluded regions.

    Fig. 20 illustrates the material maps derived from the multi-light setup. By leveraging additional lighting data, this configuration improves the estimation of surface properties—particularly roughness—and better handles challenging facial regions such as the nose or ears. Although the setup is still constrained by the limited angular coverage of the three projectors, the multi-light approach provides more detailed material stacks. However, the recovered scattering distance parameters and the resulting rendering reconstructions are nearly identical to those produced by the single-view baseline. These results confirm that for the specific task of estimating subsurface scattering, our single-light, single-view approach remains both sufficient and robust.

    7 Conclusions

    We presented a lightweight differentiable inverse rendering pipeline for estimating subsurface scattering parameters of human skin directly from single-view, single-light captures. By optimizing the same parameters used in standard real-time shading models, our method establishes a direct bridge between physical acquisition and production-ready rendering pipelines, eliminating the need for complex optical setups or intermediate physical volumetric parameter conversion.

    Our experiments demonstrate that physically plausible scattering distances can be estimated from minimal input data. The recovered parameters produce a realistic skin appearance across a wide range of skin tones, exhibiting consistent numerical convergence in synthetic benchmarks and high perceptual reconstruction fidelity on real-world captures. The proposed shadow-aware loss formulation improves robustness in regions dominated by multiple scattering, enabling reliable estimation even under challenging pigmentation conditions. Furthermore, our dataset includes a diverse collection of calibrated skin samples aligned with the Monk Skin Tone Scale, supporting inclusive and scalable digital human modeling.

    A key result of this work is that production-ready subsurface scattering parameters can be estimated from an accessible capture setup without relying on laboratory-grade acquisition systems. Rather than requiring specialized hardware or complex measurement procedures, our approach makes the problem tractable through differentiable optimization, physically motivated parameterization, and carefully designed supervision. This substantially lowers the barrier to high-quality skin digitization while preserving compatibility with real-time rendering workflows.

    The method relies on a locally homogeneous scattering assumption, and monocular depth priors. These assumptions allow the inverse problem to remain practical while still producing parameters that are physically plausible and visually effective. In the single-light setting, the ambiguity between albedo and scattering is addressed through a multi-stage optimization strategy that stabilizes parameter recovery. In thin or highly translucent structures, such as nose cartilage or the ear helix, omitting explicit single-scattering optimization may lead to slightly larger estimated scattering distances, as the model explains missing translucency through the available parameters. Our regional blending scheme constrains these estimates within realistic ranges and preserves a consistent appearance across facial regions. Similarly, omitting non-local visibility handling causes residual self-shadows to be partially absorbed into the albedo in areas of steep relief.

    Future work can build on this foundation by jointly recovering additional scattering components, incorporating stronger learned priors, integrating differentiable visibility testing to resolve self-shadowing, and extending the capture protocol to less constrained environments. More flexible acquisition strategies could further improve the fidelity of reconstruction while maintaining the accessibility of the proposed setup.

    By combining accessible acquisition, differentiable optimization, physically grounded constraints, and validation across diverse skin tones, our method provides a scalable path toward realistic and inclusive digital human creation for real-time applications.

    1 Introduction

    This supplementary document provides extended validation, dataset analysis, and core implementation details supporting the main manuscript, organized as follows:

  • •

    Map Evolution Across Optimization Stages (Section 2): Illustrates the step-by-step visual progression of active and frozen maps across optimization stages, justifying our staged schedule in decoupling surface reflections and subsurface diffusion.

  • •

    Tilted View Validation (Section 3): Demonstrates the angular consistency and physical grounding of our 3D depth-aware optimization under varying camera orientations.

  • •

    Dataset across the Monk Scale (Section 4): Presents comprehensive synthetic validation across the full Monk Skin Tone Scale by isolating albedo variations under fixed scattering parameters, and evaluates real-world participant distributions by cross-referencing subjective self-identification against our objective color-matching algorithm via a unified confusion matrix.

  • •

    Replicability and Algorithmic Details (Section 5): Provides concrete pipeline blueprints, including RAW color calibration via Ridge Regression (Section 5.1), robust albedo initialization (Section 5.2), and our GPU shader (Section 5.3) and differentiable tensorized implementations (Section 5.4).

    • 2 Map Progression Across Optimization Stages

    To complement the optimization methodology described in the main manuscript, Figure 1 illustrates the step-by-step visual progression of active and frozen material maps across our three optimization stages.

    During Stage 1, freezing the albedo A_T forces the reconstruction loss to temporarily drive the active roughness map (ρ_T) to fit low-frequency diffuse shading gradients. In Stage 2, unfreezing A_T provides the direct path to resolve these diffuse reconstruction errors. As the albedo rapidly absorbs the spatial shading details, the reconstruction gradient on other maps vanishes. Consequently, the L₂ roughness prior smoothly regularizes ρ_T while leaving the residual specular map virtually unperturbed, matching its role as a buffer designed for unmodeled specular highlights rather than diffuse light transport.

    3 Tilted View Validation

    To verify that our frontal-view optimization yields physically grounded parameters rather than view-dependent overfitted solutions, we perform tilted-view cross-validation on both synthetic and real data. For synthetic targets, we optimize parameters independently from frontal and novel tilted views, verifying that the estimated scattering distance (dₒₚₜ) consistently matches the ground truth (d_ref). For real targets, we evaluate acquisitions of identical skin regions under varying camera angles. As shown in Fig. 2, estimated scattering distances remain invariant across orientations, yielding minimal reconstruction error.

    Our pipeline avoids 2D projection approximations by executing scattering calculations directly in 3D view space using the estimated geometric depth. This integration ensures that the Screen-Space Subsurface Scattering (SSSS) algorithm naturally accounts for surface curvature and perspective foreshortening. By computing physical distances rather than simple 2D pixel offsets, the model recovers orientation-invariant scattering profiles.

    4 Dataset across the Monk Scale

    Figure 3 presents the full synthetic validation workflow, confirming optimization stability across all ten Monk classes. By fixing the ground-truth scattering distance and varying only the target albedo, we verify that our method decouples scattering parameters independently of surface reflectance.

    Figure 4 cross-references participant skin tone self-assessments against our automatically computed baseline using a unified confusion matrix (N=45). As expected from a Mediterranean–Caucasian population, the sample distribution concentrates around intermediate Monk tones (3–6), highlighting the representative challenges of real-world skin digitization. For automated classification, the mean skin color is extracted from the neutral frontal-light capture to eliminate specular and shadow contamination, and subsequently mapped via CIE LAB distance to uniformly lit reference exemplars from the MST dataset.

    Discrepancies between computed tones and self-assessments in the matrix reveal inherent human perception biases and visual ambiguities when isolating pure albedo from overall lightness under casual observation. Furthermore, the original Monk scale is inherently perceptual, with reference colors defined under uncalibrated lighting conditions. Consequently, standardized computational environments and objective physical optimization pipelines are essential for consistent, illumination-invariant tone classification.

item.title: 布料的微观几何别真的画出来：DTM 把「随形变重组的微结构」编译进一张连续神经纹理 ｜ Deformable Texture Maps: Compiling Dynamic Microgeometry into Neural Textures
item.description:
一句话：粗粒度仿真能恢复微结构怎么动，但把它显式实例化并渲染出来太贵。

要点：

  • 问题定位准确：布料这类可变形材料的观感来自细尺度几何，而这些几何会**随形变重新排列**
  • 即便粗粒度仿真能高效恢复这种微结构，把微结构显式实例化再渲染仍然非常昂贵
  • DTM 提出一种表示：把形变驱动的微几何**编译成连续且紧凑的神经纹理**，用「纹理坐标 + 局部形变」映射到不透明度等固有属性图

为什么值得看：布料细节是「几何做不起、贴图又不跟着动」的典型。把微几何压进神经纹理、并把局部形变作为输入，等于在渲染时按需还原细节——这比换用更细的仿真网格便宜得多。

中文摘要：布料等可变形材料的外观，来自会随形变重新排列的细尺度几何。粗粒度的仿真模型虽然能高效恢复这类微结构如何运动，但把它显式实例化出来再渲染，成本依然很高。Deformable Texture Maps（DTM）因此提出一种表示：把形变驱动的微几何**编译成一张连续、紧凑的神经纹理**，由纹理坐标与局部形变共同映射到描述不透明度等固有属性的图。这样渲染阶段不必真的构建微几何，而是在需要的地方按形变还原细节，把「细看要真、算起来要省」这对矛盾挪到了表示层解决。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

Deformable Texture Maps: Compiling Dynamic Microgeometry into Neural Textures

Abstract

Deformable material surfaces, such as cloth, owe their appearance to fine-scale geometries that restructure under deformation. Even when coarse simulation models efficiently recover this microstructure, explicitly instantiating and rendering it remains expensive. We introduce Deformable Texture Maps (DTM), a representation that compiles deformation-driven microgeometry into a continuous and compact neural texture. Our model maps texture coordinates and local deformations to intrinsic maps describing opacity, surface normals, depth, and material identity. This captures the occlusion and visibility changes generated by deformation. At runtime, these maps provide a common texture-space representation of deformation-driven fine-scale structure that can be evaluated directly on coarse deforming surfaces. Since our representation encodes geometric attributes rather than radiance, lighting and material response remain decoupled from the learned model. This allows us to apply relighting, as well as shading and material editing without retraining. We further introduce a persistent texture-space rendering strategy that caches these intrinsic maps and selectively updates them as deformation changes. This effectively decouples neural evaluation from frame rendering and enables their reuse across frames and conventional rendering effects. We demonstrate our approach on yarn-based textiles, where non-linear material stretch and shear induce apply changes in yarn geometry spacing and occlusion. We build our model by, first, sweeping tileable yarn patches through deformation space, then, rendering the resulting detailed geometry into a canonical texture-space, and finally, compressing the resulting maps into a single neural representation. Our resulting model can be evaluated directly on arbitrary coarse garment meshes and integrated with conventional shading pipelines. Our results demonstrate a compact and flexible representation of deformation-driven fine-scale structure while keeping appearance authorable at render time.

1 Introduction

Materials with complex fine-scale structure—threads, fibers, scales, pores—derive their detailed appearance from fine-scale geometric details that are expensive to represent and render explicitly. As they are deformable materials, this structure then evolves with stretching, compression and shear, to generate or close gaps, changing surface orientations. Faithfully reproducing these effects is challenging as it requires capturing fine-scale geometries under deformation.

Textiles are a critical and challenging instance of this problem. The appearance of woven and knitted fabrics emerges from large numbers of interlocking yarns whose spatial arrangement changes as the cloth deforms. Yarn-level methods capture this structure explicitly and can further reconstruct fiber-scale detail for rendering [MXF∗19, YKJM12], while homogenized models recover detailed yarn configurations from the deformation of a coarse cloth surface modeled with shells [SNW20, SNW21]. Recent methods further demonstrate that deformation-dependent yarn geometries can be reconstructed and rendered at interactive rates [HSW∗25] (30ms/frame, fullHD). However, these approaches retain the fine-scale geometry as part of the runtime representation, coupling reconstruction and rendering to the represented microgeometry. Surface-based fabric appearance models take the opposite approach, avoiding explicit yarn geometry [ZHB∗24, KAYM26], but represent static states rather than deformation-driven changes in spacing and occlusion. More recently, Kalinov et al.[KLHW26] demonstrate deformation-dependent texture content using physics-inspired procedural rules. Their approach prescribes classes of texture behavior under deformation rather than deriving appearance from an underlying deforming microgeometry.

We introduce Deformable Texture Maps (DTM), a representation that compiles deformation-driven microgeometry into a continuous, compact neural texture. Our key insight is that when fine-scale geometry is determined by local deformation, its rendering-relevant properties can be represented directly in material space as functions of that deformation. This turns dynamic microgeometry rendering into deformation-conditioned texture evaluation.

We demonstrate DTM on yarn-based textiles. We sample a tileable yarn model across in-plane stretch and shear, map the resulting configurations to a common material-space domain, and render intrinsic maps describing coverage, surface normal, depth, and material identity. A coordinate-based neural model compresses these samples into a continuous representation that is evaluated directly on coarse deforming meshes at runtime. Because its content is learned from the underlying deformed geometry, DTM captures changes in spacing, orientation and visibility, including yarn structures that become exposed or occluded during deformation.

Importantly, DTM represents intrinsic geometric information rather than final radiance. Lighting and material response are applied only after evaluating the neural texture, using conventional shading. This separation keeps appearance authorable: lighting, BRDF parameters, and the visual properties assigned to different yarns can be changed without retraining the neural representation. The texture-space representation also enables neural evaluation to be decoupled from frame rendering. We cache predicted maps persistently in material space and selectively update them as deformation changes, allowing the remaining rendering pipeline to reuse conventional textures across frames and rendering operations.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    Deformable Texture Maps, a continuous, compact neural representation of deformation-driven microgeometry as intrinsic texture-space fields conditioned on local deformation.

  • •

    A canonicalization and data-generation pipeline for yarn-based textiles that samples deformation-dependent yarn geometry, maps each configuration to a shared material-space domain, and renders tileable intrinsic maps for learning.

  • •

    A persistent texture-space rendering framework that decouples neural evaluation from frame rendering through selective deformation-dependent updates and cross-frame reuse, while exposing conventional maps to downstream rendering.

    • We will publish the dataset and models upon publication.

    2 Deformable Texture Maps

    Overview

    Our method replaces runtime reconstruction and rendering of deformation-dependent microgeometry with neural evaluation of deformation-conditioned intrinsic neural fields. Assuming that fine-scale geometry is determined by local deformation, we generate detailed geometry offline, map it to a common material-space domain, and compile its rendering-relevant properties into a continuous neural texture T. We formalize T as

    T:[0,1]²×D→ℝ⁸, (u,d)↦(α,n,h,c),

    		(1)

    where u∈[0,1]² denotes a coordinate in the canonical material domain and d∈D denotes the local deformation state (D≃ℝ³, see Sec. 2.1). The outputs comprise opacity α – derived from the fractional coverage of the microgeometry, surface normal n, depth h, and a three-channel material-identity code c. Because these fields encode geometry rather than radiance, lighting and material response remain separate from the learned representation and can be modified without retraining.

    An overview of the method is presented in Figure . We instantiate this representation for yarn-based textiles using the homogenized yarn model of Sperl et al.[SNW21]. First, we sweep a yarn patch through deformation space, reconstruct and canonicalize the resulting microgeometry, and render the target intrinsic fields (Section2.1). Second, we fit the deformation-conditioned neural texture T to these samples (Section2.2). Finally, at runtime, we evaluate T on a coarse deforming cloth mesh and shade the predicted fields using conventional material and lighting models (Section3).

    2.1 Microgeometry Compilation

    We generate data for T by sweeping a tileable yarn configuration through deformation space and converting each resulting microgeometry state into a common material-space representation. For each deformation state, we simulate the yarn configuration, construct renderable geometry, canonicalize it to the rest-space tile footprint, and render the resulting intrinsic fields.

    Simulation

    Starting from a planar tile containing the rest-pose yarn splines, we sample a Cartesian grid of deformation states d=(sₓ,s_y,sₐ)∈[m,M]²×[-1,1] (m/M being the minimum/maximum stretch values captured during simulation). Each state applies the in-plane deformation gradient

    F(d)=\beginpmatrix1+sₓ&sₐ (1+s_y) 0&(1+s_y)√1-sₐ²\endpmatrix,

    		(2)

    Defining sₐ as the sine of the shear angle (sₐ=sin(α)) keeps the norm of the second column equal to 1+s_y, allowing shear to change its orientation without introducing additional stretch. We use F(d) to prescribe the macroscopic deformation and obtain the corresponding relaxed yarn configuration with MADYPG [SNW21], running physical relaxation until equilibrium. Each resulting configuration therefore associates a deformation state d with a detailed set of yarn centerlines.

    Meshing

    MADYPG yields periodic deformed yarn centerlines as a result of homogenization. To obtain renderable surface geometry, we construct a generalized cylinder with a fixed circular cross-section around each rest-pose centerline. For each deformation state, we displace its vertices by the rest-to-deformed centerline offsets, expressed in the adapted frame featuring the smallest torque along the centerline. We enforce consistency of this frame across the tile boundaries so that the resulting surface geometry remains periodic and tileable. To preserve geometry crossing the periodic boundaries during rendering, we replicate the resulting yarn tile over a 3×3 neighborhood, render it orthographically, and retain the central tile (Figure 1). The surrounding copies provide the portions of yarn geometry crossing into the central tile, ensuring seamless boundaries.

    Canonicalization

    The deformed yarn geometry has a spatial footprint that varies with the deformation state d, whereas our neural texture is defined over a fixed material-space domain. We therefore pull each configuration back to the rest-space tile by applying F(d)⁻¹ to the deformed geometry before rasterization. This transformation canonicalizes the sampling domain without undoing the simulated yarn rearrangement, preserving deformation-dependent changes in spacing, occlusion, and visibility. As a result, all deformation states are represented over a common texture-space footprint and sampled at a consistent spatial density. This is illustrated in Figure 2.

    Rendering

    We rasterize each canonicalized yarn configuration into the intrinsic maps used to train T.The render pass produces four maps indexed by the canonical texture coordinate u: alpha α, representing fractional yarn opacity coverage α; surface normal n; depth h; and material identity c.

    Although positions are rasterized in the canonical domain, the normal map should describe the yarn surface in the deformed configuration. We therefore lift the in-plane deformation to three dimensions as F̃=diag(F,1), apply F̃ to the canonicalized mesh vertices, and recompute smooth vertex normals on the resulting deformed mesh. These normals are interpolated at the corresponding rasterized surface points and stored as the target normal map. Thus, canonicalization provides a common spatial domain while retaining the deformation-dependent surface orientation used for shading.

    Finally, each texel together with its deformation state defines a training sample (u,d,α,n,h,c).

    2.2 Deformation-Conditioned Neural Texture

    Recent neural texture compression methods combine learned latent textures with lightweight MLP decoders to reconstruct material maps efficiently at runtime [LA25, Lau26]. In our setting, however, the target maps must additionally vary continuously with deformation. We therefore directly parameterize the joint material-coordinate and deformation domain with a coordinate-based network [SMB∗20, TSM∗20]. To model high-frequencies we combine a fixed Fourier encoding with sinusoidal activations. We compare this choice against alternative coordinate-network [GJ24][AMDT26] architectures in supplemental material. Let p=(u,d) denote the concatenated texture coordinate and deformation state. Our neural texture is

    T=S∘γ, (α,n,h,c)=S(γ(p)),

    		(3)

    where γ independently maps each component p to

    γ(p)=(p, \sin(2^ℓπp), \cos(2^ℓπp))_ℓ=0^L-1.

    		(4)

    The resulting features are concatenated and processed by the SIREN S, which jointly predicts the eight channels of the four target maps.

    Fourier features expose multiple frequency bands directly to the network, complementing the periodic activations of SIREN. We evaluate the contribution of this encoding against a bare SIREN at matched parameter budgets in the supplemental material.

    We train all maps jointly using

    L=∑_f∈{α,n,h,c}MSE(f̂,f),

    		(5)

    Here, f̂ denotes the network prediction of target map f at the same texture coordinate and deformation state. Each MSE is averaged over the channels of its map, giving equal weight to the four maps losses. Material identity is represented by a continuous three-dimensional code c; at inference, predictions are decoded to the material ID associated with the nearest codeword.

    3 Runtime Rendering

    The simplest integration of DTM evaluates the neural texture on demand in the fragment shader. While straightforward, our early experiments showed that this unoptimized strategy results in poor performance. A more advanced strategy is to query the network only at visible surface samples every frame, using deferred shading. The coarse mesh is rasterized into screen-space buffers (a G-Buffer) containing texture coordinates, per-vertex deformation parameters (sₓ,s_y,sₐ), and a coverage mask. The network is then evaluated in GPU batches over covered pixels, and the predicted opacity, normals, depth, and material ID are stored for shading in a subsequent pass. This substantially reduces redundant neural evaluations, but remains coupled to screen-space visibility and inherits limitations of deferred shading for effects requiring multiple or partially occluded surface samples, such as transparency. We instead adopt a persistent texture-space strategy inspired by decoupled shading [BJ22], separating neural evaluation from frame rendering, and sparse virtual textures [Bar08]

    3.1 Texture-Space Caching

    Our primary rendering strategy follows [BJ22] and exploits the UV parameterization of the DTM to cache network predictions in texture space (Figure 3). As the predicted material maps are independent of lighting and viewing direction, they can be reused across frames and selectively updated as the cloth deforms. This trades texture memory for fewer neural evaluations and decouples network evaluation from per-frame rendering.

    To obtain deformation inputs at texture resolution, we rasterize the coarse mesh in UV space, interpolating the per-vertex parameters (sₓ,s_y,sₐ) into a deformation texture. For each texel selected for neural evaluation, we sample this texture with bilinear filtering and combine the resulting deformation state with the local yarn-texture coordinate as input to the network. The resulting predictions are stored directly in material textures.

    We decompose the UV space into pages, to which we assign a constant Level of Detail (LoD, see "Camera-dependent resolution" in Figure 3), which allows us baking high-resolution texture outputs in close-up regions while remaining memory friendly. To ensure an adequate final texel ratio on screen after shading, we determine a target resolution for each triangle based on its projected area and the screen resolution. All triangles are processed in a first pass, and each UV-page is assigned with a rasterization LoD corresponding to the maximum of selected LoDs for all triangles projecting on said page. Triangles falling outside the camera frustrum are marked as discarded: they do not influence the pages’ LoDs and are not baked, as they are not visible on screen. Once the pages’ LoDs are set up, the neural texture is baked at adapted resolution over the UV-space.

    Representing the network output as dynamically updated textures allows standard rendering techniques to access the predicted maps without further neural evaluations. In particular, we use forward rendering to handle transparency, while parallax mapping, flyaway fibers, and fuzz shells repeatedly reuse the cached maps. Table 1 details the differences between the two rendering strategies.

    3.2 Cache Update Strategy

    Because the cache stores texture maps, changes in lighting or viewpoint do not by themselves require new neural predictions at a fixed texture resolution. We exploit this reuse with a deformation-triggered update policy and a configurable update schedule.

    Deformation-triggered invalidation.

    For each coarse-mesh vertex v, we compare its current deformation dᵥ=(sₓ,s_y,sₐ) with a stored reference d̂ᵥ. We mark the affected texture regions for reevaluation when

    \lVertdᵥ-d̂ᵥ\rVert_∞>τ,

    where τ is a tolerance in the original deformation coordinates, without per-component normalization. On a threshold crossing, we advance the vertex’s reference to its current deformation and mark all row groups in the affected regions as pending. Selecting one row group for an update leaves the others pending; the reference therefore records a detected change, rather than a common state of all cached texels. Comparing against this reference allows small successive changes to trigger an update once their net departure exceeds τ.

    Update scheduling.

    We set a target update frequency fᵤ independently of the rendering frame rate and cycle through G groups of texture rows during motion. With G=2, successive scheduled updates alternate between even and odd rows. If updates occur at the target rate without interruption, each group receives an update opportunity every G/fᵤ seconds. This is a nominal scheduling interval, not a bound on prediction age: thresholding can suppress updates, and batching or deferred submissions can delay them. Initialization and forced refreshes bypass row interleaving; a settling refresh also uses full row coverage before unchanged deformation can be reused without further updates. The supplementary material details these exceptions and the runtime settings.

    Quality and responsiveness.

    Skipped texels retain their cached intrinsic fields, while their rendered appearance can still change with lighting, viewpoint, and coarse-mesh motion. The tolerance τ controls deformation-space differences and does not bound appearance error. Reduced update frequency and row interleaving can delay changes in the predicted yarn fields and leave neighboring rows representing different deformation states. Evaluating these approximations requires comparison with full per-frame texture-space updates at the same resolution, so that errors due to update scheduling are separated from representation and sampling errors.

    3.3 Yarn Shading and Cloth Effects

    The cached neural maps are used as conventional material textures to render the coarse cloth. Alpha determines yarn coverage, normals provide local surface orientation, and the material ID selects the corresponding shader parameters. We use Lambertian diffuse and GGX specular reflection, while depth and alpha support view-dependent relief and local occlusion.

    Our maps-based representation enable additional yarn-scale effects without further neural evaluations. Parallax mapping uses depth to produce view-dependent yarn relief, while fuzz is approximated with thin shell layers anchored to the yarn surface. Sparse flyaway fibers are represented as tapered ribbons, with alpha selecting their roots, depth positioning them on the yarns, and normals guiding their orientation [LPFH01]. Further implementation details are provided in the supplementary material.

    Reconstruction fidelity across five yarn structures using a width of 128, we measure PSNR (dB) for alpha, normals and depth and report the proportion of material IDs that are correctly reconstructed. For all columns, higher is better (↑).

    Storage cost and reconstruction quality on rib. We compare our neural models with ASTC block compression of the ground-truth textures and lossless texture references, illustrating the trade-off between storage and representation quality PSNR of in-distribution samples. We compare different widths of our Fourier-SIREN network, among which best scores are bold, second best underlined; we highlight the trade-off that we use in practice.

    4 Results

    In this section we evaluate DTM accuracy and performance (Section 4.1), appearance control (Sections 4.2 and 4.3), and end-to-end rendering performance (Section 4.4).

    Experimental Setup.

    We evaluate DTM on five yarn structures spanning woven and knitted configurations: rib, basket, stockinette, honeycomb, and satin. Unless stated otherwise, each structure uses an independently trained Fourier-SIREN of width 128, trained for 30,000 steps on a discrete lattice of deformation states. All models sample an 8×8×8 lattice of deformation states with sₓ,s_y∈[-0.2,1.0] and sₐ∈[-0.7,0.7] for a total of 512 states. Full implementation details are provided in the supplementary material. Throughout the quantitative tables, alpha, normals, and depth are measured by PSNR (dB), and material ID by classification accuracy (%). Normals are also evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively using lambertian renders and FLIP metric  [ANAM∗20].

    4.1 Model Accuracy and Performance

    We evaluate reconstruction accuracy across five yarn structures and sampled deformation states. We compare against the ground-truth (GT) maps, which are estimated from the original geometry.

    Table 2 reports accuracy for each map. Depth and material identity achieve the highest reconstruction accuracy, while alpha and normals have less precision. Figure 4 shows these differences qualitatively by shading the predicted normals with a Lambertian model. The error is measured using FLIP[ANAM∗20]. DTM preserves the overall yarn structure even under large deformations.

    We show in Table 3 how DTM performs at different model sizes. We compare per-map quality against texture compression approaches such as ASTC, performed over the entire training dataset (See supplementary for further evaluations). Using our selected parameters (Fourier SIREN width set to 128, yellow row), our approach provides quality between the ones of ASTC (8×8) and ASTC (12×12), for a 42x-to-94x storage memory reduction.

    In Figure 5, we also compare our method with a naïve baseline that blends in image space the neighboring stored textures. Linear texture blending superimposes yarn boundaries from neighboring states, producing visible ghosting, whereas DTM produces a more coherent intermediate configuration closer to the ground truth.

    4.2 Garment-level Examples

    We evaluate DTM on simulated coarse garment meshes and cloth patches. We compute per-triangle stretch and shear in local material coordinates, average these quantities at mesh vertices using area weights, and interpolate the resulting deformation parameters across the surface to condition the tileable neural material. Figure 6 illustrates the importance of deformation-dependent coverage: stretching alters the yarn arrangement and the openings through which the backlight is visible. Unlike naive texture scaling, DTM captures these structural changes through its deformation-conditioned opacity field. The resulting effect reflects changes in yarn coverage, rather than light transmission through the yarns.

    4.3 Editability

    Because DTM predicts intrinsic maps rather than final radiance, lighting and material appearance can be edited without retraining. Figure 7 shows how predicted material identities enable palette edits that consistently follow yarn groups across the textile. The predicted maps can also be combined with conventional rendering effects, including parallax relief, fuzzy shells, and flyaway fibers, without modifying the learned representation (Figure 8). We also demonstrate real-time relightability and pallette edits with fixed models in various animated scenarios (see Teaser ).

    4.4 Real-Time Renderer Evaluation

    We evaluate the complete renderer to measure how texture-space reuse affects performance under deformation and camera motion. We compare per-fragment screen-space deferred neural evaluation with our texture-space approach, using the same neural model, shading settings, and 1920×1080 output resolution. Our texture-space approach only schedules cache updates when cloth elements are being actively deformed and reuses previously evaluated maps when deformation remains unchanged. We enable all of the optimization techniques discussed in Section 3 such as update scheduling, selective updates to changed tiles, and adaptive virtual textures, we set a max resolution of 4k for the highest quality virtual texture and we define 5 LODs in total which we swap based on approximate texture texel to viewport pixel footprint.

    The benchmark alternates stationary intervals with cloth stretching and a camera zoom during stretching. We measure GPU-finished application frames per second with browser-driven scheduling and vsync disable, we also allow up to three frames in flight. Figure 9 reports performance over the interaction sequence.

    In this benchmark, we evaluate the performance profile of each method: In the case of the screen-space deferred approach, we can see that the framerate scales with amount of pixels on screen that require a DTM network evaluation. Comparatively, in our approach, we can see that we achieve considerably higher framerate in the rest sections of the benchmark, this is because once we calculate that deformation state, we can keep reusing the results and only update the minor changes. We drop in framerate as the fabric starts moving and we require cache updates. We also show the performance behavior of zooming in in both cases, in screens-pace deferred, performance drops expectedly because we fill the entire viewport with pixels that need network evaluations, in our approach we also drop in framerate briefly because, as we zoom in, we start swapping to higher quality LODs and calculating them into the cache. As soon as we finish we get a spike again of framerate.

    5 Ablations

    We evaluate the main design choices of DTM through ablations of the neural representation (Section 5.1) and our texture-cache runtime rendering strategy (Section 5.2).

    5.1 Neural Model

    We ablate the architecture, training budget, and frequency initialization of our neural representation. At approximately matched parameter counts, Fourier-SIREN achieves the highest reconstruction quality among the evaluated architectures (Table 4). We perform various runs per architecture, sweeping over multiple learning rates and architecture specific parameters. For our Fourier-SIREN network, increasing the training budget improves reconstruction quality with diminishing returns beyond 30k steps (Figure 10), which we use throughout our experiments. (see supplementary material for more details).

    Reconstruction quality of six neural architectures on rib with approximately 64k parameters each.

    5.2 Runtime Rendering

    We evaluate our rendering approach along with all the approximations and optimizations discussed in 2 by measuring the end-to-end FPS across multiple scenarios in our Three.js WebGPU renderer implementation. We progressively enable various optimizations and measure the impact that they have on performance. (see the supplementary for the full study)

    6 Limitations

    Source fidelity and material scope.

    DTM inherits the limitations of the microgeometry used for training. Our textile instantiation uses MADYPG centerlines with fixed-radius cylindrical geometry, omitting effects such as cross-sectional flattening, multi-ply rearrangement, and contact-induced compression. The representation itself is not tied to this geometry model: richer microgeometry [GNCM∗25] could be used provided that deformation-conditioned training maps can be generated. Similarly, although we evaluate DTM only on yarn-based textiles, the same formulation could apply to other materials whose microgeometry can be parameterized by local deformation, such as skin.

    Generalization.

    Each DTM is trained for a single microstructure over a bounded deformation domain. We demonstrate interpolation between sampled deformation states, but not extrapolation beyond this domain or transfer across yarn structures. Moreover, our deformation descriptor captures local in-plane stretch and shear, but not effects such as bending or localized compression. Future work could explore shared representations conditioned on microstructure and richer local deformation descriptors.

    Surface representation.

    DTM trades the generality of explicit 3D microgeometry for a compact, surface-attached representation. The predicted opacity, normal, depth, and material-identity maps capture local yarn structure and relief, but do not fully describe the geometry or optical behavior of the underlying microstructure. As a result, the current representation cannot reproduce effects that require full 3D geometry or volumetric light transport, such as complex silhouettes, deep visibility, transmission, and multiple scattering. Our current shading model is also limited to a generic Cook–Torrance BRDF and does not model yarn-direction-dependent reflectance. Finally, scale-dependent filtering remains unresolved: filtering heterogeneous maps requires different treatment of continuous, directional, and categorical quantities.

    7 Conclusion

    We presented Deformable Texture Maps, a continuous, compact neural representation that turns dynamic microgeometry rendering into deformation-conditioned texture evaluation. Our data-generation pipeline maps deformed yarn geometry to a shared texture-space domain and produces tileable intrinsic maps for learning. We demonstrated DTM on 5 woven and knitted textiles, capturing changes in yarn arrangement, coverage, and visibility under stretch and shear.

    Our rendering framework evaluates the learned maps on coarse deforming cloth meshes, avoiding explicit yarn geometry at runtime. Lighting and material response remain independent of the learned representation, supporting relighting and runtime yarn-material editing without retraining. We have shown interactive frame rates under various cloth deformation scenarios along with multiple optimization methods to achieve higher performance at the cost of minor quality loss and latency.

    While we have demonstrated DTM in the particularly challenging setting of deformable textiles, the underlying representation is not inherently limited to fabrics. Our results highlight the broader potential of deformation-conditioned neural textures as a compact alternative to explicitly representing fine-scale geometry on deforming surfaces. We believe this opens an interesting direction for extending the approach to other materials and structures in which microscopic geometric changes are driven by macroscopic deformation.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：粗粒度仿真能恢复微结构怎么动，但把它显式实例化并渲染出来太贵。

要点：

  • 问题定位准确：布料这类可变形材料的观感来自细尺度几何，而这些几何会**随形变重新排列**
  • 即便粗粒度仿真能高效恢复这种微结构，把微结构显式实例化再渲染仍然非常昂贵
  • DTM 提出一种表示：把形变驱动的微几何**编译成连续且紧凑的神经纹理**，用「纹理坐标 + 局部形变」映射到不透明度等固有属性图

为什么值得看：布料细节是「几何做不起、贴图又不跟着动」的典型。把微几何压进神经纹理、并把局部形变作为输入，等于在渲染时按需还原细节——这比换用更细的仿真网格便宜得多。

中文摘要：布料等可变形材料的外观，来自会随形变重新排列的细尺度几何。粗粒度的仿真模型虽然能高效恢复这类微结构如何运动，但把它显式实例化出来再渲染，成本依然很高。Deformable Texture Maps（DTM）因此提出一种表示：把形变驱动的微几何**编译成一张连续、紧凑的神经纹理**，由纹理坐标与局部形变共同映射到描述不透明度等固有属性的图。这样渲染阶段不必真的构建微几何，而是在需要的地方按形变还原细节，把「细看要真、算起来要省」这对矛盾挪到了表示层解决。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-11

本期推送：2026-11-12

Deformable Texture Maps: Compiling Dynamic Microgeometry into Neural Textures

Abstract

Deformable material surfaces, such as cloth, owe their appearance to fine-scale geometries that restructure under deformation. Even when coarse simulation models efficiently recover this microstructure, explicitly instantiating and rendering it remains expensive. We introduce Deformable Texture Maps (DTM), a representation that compiles deformation-driven microgeometry into a continuous and compact neural texture. Our model maps texture coordinates and local deformations to intrinsic maps describing opacity, surface normals, depth, and material identity. This captures the occlusion and visibility changes generated by deformation. At runtime, these maps provide a common texture-space representation of deformation-driven fine-scale structure that can be evaluated directly on coarse deforming surfaces. Since our representation encodes geometric attributes rather than radiance, lighting and material response remain decoupled from the learned model. This allows us to apply relighting, as well as shading and material editing without retraining. We further introduce a persistent texture-space rendering strategy that caches these intrinsic maps and selectively updates them as deformation changes. This effectively decouples neural evaluation from frame rendering and enables their reuse across frames and conventional rendering effects. We demonstrate our approach on yarn-based textiles, where non-linear material stretch and shear induce apply changes in yarn geometry spacing and occlusion. We build our model by, first, sweeping tileable yarn patches through deformation space, then, rendering the resulting detailed geometry into a canonical texture-space, and finally, compressing the resulting maps into a single neural representation. Our resulting model can be evaluated directly on arbitrary coarse garment meshes and integrated with conventional shading pipelines. Our results demonstrate a compact and flexible representation of deformation-driven fine-scale structure while keeping appearance authorable at render time.

1 Introduction

Materials with complex fine-scale structure—threads, fibers, scales, pores—derive their detailed appearance from fine-scale geometric details that are expensive to represent and render explicitly. As they are deformable materials, this structure then evolves with stretching, compression and shear, to generate or close gaps, changing surface orientations. Faithfully reproducing these effects is challenging as it requires capturing fine-scale geometries under deformation.

Textiles are a critical and challenging instance of this problem. The appearance of woven and knitted fabrics emerges from large numbers of interlocking yarns whose spatial arrangement changes as the cloth deforms. Yarn-level methods capture this structure explicitly and can further reconstruct fiber-scale detail for rendering [MXF∗19, YKJM12], while homogenized models recover detailed yarn configurations from the deformation of a coarse cloth surface modeled with shells [SNW20, SNW21]. Recent methods further demonstrate that deformation-dependent yarn geometries can be reconstructed and rendered at interactive rates [HSW∗25] (30ms/frame, fullHD). However, these approaches retain the fine-scale geometry as part of the runtime representation, coupling reconstruction and rendering to the represented microgeometry. Surface-based fabric appearance models take the opposite approach, avoiding explicit yarn geometry [ZHB∗24, KAYM26], but represent static states rather than deformation-driven changes in spacing and occlusion. More recently, Kalinov et al.[KLHW26] demonstrate deformation-dependent texture content using physics-inspired procedural rules. Their approach prescribes classes of texture behavior under deformation rather than deriving appearance from an underlying deforming microgeometry.

We introduce Deformable Texture Maps (DTM), a representation that compiles deformation-driven microgeometry into a continuous, compact neural texture. Our key insight is that when fine-scale geometry is determined by local deformation, its rendering-relevant properties can be represented directly in material space as functions of that deformation. This turns dynamic microgeometry rendering into deformation-conditioned texture evaluation.

We demonstrate DTM on yarn-based textiles. We sample a tileable yarn model across in-plane stretch and shear, map the resulting configurations to a common material-space domain, and render intrinsic maps describing coverage, surface normal, depth, and material identity. A coordinate-based neural model compresses these samples into a continuous representation that is evaluated directly on coarse deforming meshes at runtime. Because its content is learned from the underlying deformed geometry, DTM captures changes in spacing, orientation and visibility, including yarn structures that become exposed or occluded during deformation.

Importantly, DTM represents intrinsic geometric information rather than final radiance. Lighting and material response are applied only after evaluating the neural texture, using conventional shading. This separation keeps appearance authorable: lighting, BRDF parameters, and the visual properties assigned to different yarns can be changed without retraining the neural representation. The texture-space representation also enables neural evaluation to be decoupled from frame rendering. We cache predicted maps persistently in material space and selectively update them as deformation changes, allowing the remaining rendering pipeline to reuse conventional textures across frames and rendering operations.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    Deformable Texture Maps, a continuous, compact neural representation of deformation-driven microgeometry as intrinsic texture-space fields conditioned on local deformation.

  • •

    A canonicalization and data-generation pipeline for yarn-based textiles that samples deformation-dependent yarn geometry, maps each configuration to a shared material-space domain, and renders tileable intrinsic maps for learning.

  • •

    A persistent texture-space rendering framework that decouples neural evaluation from frame rendering through selective deformation-dependent updates and cross-frame reuse, while exposing conventional maps to downstream rendering.

    • We will publish the dataset and models upon publication.

    2 Deformable Texture Maps

    Overview

    Our method replaces runtime reconstruction and rendering of deformation-dependent microgeometry with neural evaluation of deformation-conditioned intrinsic neural fields. Assuming that fine-scale geometry is determined by local deformation, we generate detailed geometry offline, map it to a common material-space domain, and compile its rendering-relevant properties into a continuous neural texture T. We formalize T as

    T:[0,1]²×D→ℝ⁸, (u,d)↦(α,n,h,c),

    		(1)

    where u∈[0,1]² denotes a coordinate in the canonical material domain and d∈D denotes the local deformation state (D≃ℝ³, see Sec. 2.1). The outputs comprise opacity α – derived from the fractional coverage of the microgeometry, surface normal n, depth h, and a three-channel material-identity code c. Because these fields encode geometry rather than radiance, lighting and material response remain separate from the learned representation and can be modified without retraining.

    An overview of the method is presented in Figure . We instantiate this representation for yarn-based textiles using the homogenized yarn model of Sperl et al.[SNW21]. First, we sweep a yarn patch through deformation space, reconstruct and canonicalize the resulting microgeometry, and render the target intrinsic fields (Section2.1). Second, we fit the deformation-conditioned neural texture T to these samples (Section2.2). Finally, at runtime, we evaluate T on a coarse deforming cloth mesh and shade the predicted fields using conventional material and lighting models (Section3).

    2.1 Microgeometry Compilation

    We generate data for T by sweeping a tileable yarn configuration through deformation space and converting each resulting microgeometry state into a common material-space representation. For each deformation state, we simulate the yarn configuration, construct renderable geometry, canonicalize it to the rest-space tile footprint, and render the resulting intrinsic fields.

    Simulation

    Starting from a planar tile containing the rest-pose yarn splines, we sample a Cartesian grid of deformation states d=(sₓ,s_y,sₐ)∈[m,M]²×[-1,1] (m/M being the minimum/maximum stretch values captured during simulation). Each state applies the in-plane deformation gradient

    F(d)=\beginpmatrix1+sₓ&sₐ (1+s_y) 0&(1+s_y)√1-sₐ²\endpmatrix,

    		(2)

    Defining sₐ as the sine of the shear angle (sₐ=sin(α)) keeps the norm of the second column equal to 1+s_y, allowing shear to change its orientation without introducing additional stretch. We use F(d) to prescribe the macroscopic deformation and obtain the corresponding relaxed yarn configuration with MADYPG [SNW21], running physical relaxation until equilibrium. Each resulting configuration therefore associates a deformation state d with a detailed set of yarn centerlines.

    Meshing

    MADYPG yields periodic deformed yarn centerlines as a result of homogenization. To obtain renderable surface geometry, we construct a generalized cylinder with a fixed circular cross-section around each rest-pose centerline. For each deformation state, we displace its vertices by the rest-to-deformed centerline offsets, expressed in the adapted frame featuring the smallest torque along the centerline. We enforce consistency of this frame across the tile boundaries so that the resulting surface geometry remains periodic and tileable. To preserve geometry crossing the periodic boundaries during rendering, we replicate the resulting yarn tile over a 3×3 neighborhood, render it orthographically, and retain the central tile (Figure 1). The surrounding copies provide the portions of yarn geometry crossing into the central tile, ensuring seamless boundaries.

    Canonicalization

    The deformed yarn geometry has a spatial footprint that varies with the deformation state d, whereas our neural texture is defined over a fixed material-space domain. We therefore pull each configuration back to the rest-space tile by applying F(d)⁻¹ to the deformed geometry before rasterization. This transformation canonicalizes the sampling domain without undoing the simulated yarn rearrangement, preserving deformation-dependent changes in spacing, occlusion, and visibility. As a result, all deformation states are represented over a common texture-space footprint and sampled at a consistent spatial density. This is illustrated in Figure 2.

    Rendering

    We rasterize each canonicalized yarn configuration into the intrinsic maps used to train T.The render pass produces four maps indexed by the canonical texture coordinate u: alpha α, representing fractional yarn opacity coverage α; surface normal n; depth h; and material identity c.

    Although positions are rasterized in the canonical domain, the normal map should describe the yarn surface in the deformed configuration. We therefore lift the in-plane deformation to three dimensions as F̃=diag(F,1), apply F̃ to the canonicalized mesh vertices, and recompute smooth vertex normals on the resulting deformed mesh. These normals are interpolated at the corresponding rasterized surface points and stored as the target normal map. Thus, canonicalization provides a common spatial domain while retaining the deformation-dependent surface orientation used for shading.

    Finally, each texel together with its deformation state defines a training sample (u,d,α,n,h,c).

    2.2 Deformation-Conditioned Neural Texture

    Recent neural texture compression methods combine learned latent textures with lightweight MLP decoders to reconstruct material maps efficiently at runtime [LA25, Lau26]. In our setting, however, the target maps must additionally vary continuously with deformation. We therefore directly parameterize the joint material-coordinate and deformation domain with a coordinate-based network [SMB∗20, TSM∗20]. To model high-frequencies we combine a fixed Fourier encoding with sinusoidal activations. We compare this choice against alternative coordinate-network [GJ24][AMDT26] architectures in supplemental material. Let p=(u,d) denote the concatenated texture coordinate and deformation state. Our neural texture is

    T=S∘γ, (α,n,h,c)=S(γ(p)),

    		(3)

    where γ independently maps each component p to

    γ(p)=(p, \sin(2^ℓπp), \cos(2^ℓπp))_ℓ=0^L-1.

    		(4)

    The resulting features are concatenated and processed by the SIREN S, which jointly predicts the eight channels of the four target maps.

    Fourier features expose multiple frequency bands directly to the network, complementing the periodic activations of SIREN. We evaluate the contribution of this encoding against a bare SIREN at matched parameter budgets in the supplemental material.

    We train all maps jointly using

    L=∑_f∈{α,n,h,c}MSE(f̂,f),

    		(5)

    Here, f̂ denotes the network prediction of target map f at the same texture coordinate and deformation state. Each MSE is averaged over the channels of its map, giving equal weight to the four maps losses. Material identity is represented by a continuous three-dimensional code c; at inference, predictions are decoded to the material ID associated with the nearest codeword.

    3 Runtime Rendering

    The simplest integration of DTM evaluates the neural texture on demand in the fragment shader. While straightforward, our early experiments showed that this unoptimized strategy results in poor performance. A more advanced strategy is to query the network only at visible surface samples every frame, using deferred shading. The coarse mesh is rasterized into screen-space buffers (a G-Buffer) containing texture coordinates, per-vertex deformation parameters (sₓ,s_y,sₐ), and a coverage mask. The network is then evaluated in GPU batches over covered pixels, and the predicted opacity, normals, depth, and material ID are stored for shading in a subsequent pass. This substantially reduces redundant neural evaluations, but remains coupled to screen-space visibility and inherits limitations of deferred shading for effects requiring multiple or partially occluded surface samples, such as transparency. We instead adopt a persistent texture-space strategy inspired by decoupled shading [BJ22], separating neural evaluation from frame rendering, and sparse virtual textures [Bar08]

    3.1 Texture-Space Caching

    Our primary rendering strategy follows [BJ22] and exploits the UV parameterization of the DTM to cache network predictions in texture space (Figure 3). As the predicted material maps are independent of lighting and viewing direction, they can be reused across frames and selectively updated as the cloth deforms. This trades texture memory for fewer neural evaluations and decouples network evaluation from per-frame rendering.

    To obtain deformation inputs at texture resolution, we rasterize the coarse mesh in UV space, interpolating the per-vertex parameters (sₓ,s_y,sₐ) into a deformation texture. For each texel selected for neural evaluation, we sample this texture with bilinear filtering and combine the resulting deformation state with the local yarn-texture coordinate as input to the network. The resulting predictions are stored directly in material textures.

    We decompose the UV space into pages, to which we assign a constant Level of Detail (LoD, see "Camera-dependent resolution" in Figure 3), which allows us baking high-resolution texture outputs in close-up regions while remaining memory friendly. To ensure an adequate final texel ratio on screen after shading, we determine a target resolution for each triangle based on its projected area and the screen resolution. All triangles are processed in a first pass, and each UV-page is assigned with a rasterization LoD corresponding to the maximum of selected LoDs for all triangles projecting on said page. Triangles falling outside the camera frustrum are marked as discarded: they do not influence the pages’ LoDs and are not baked, as they are not visible on screen. Once the pages’ LoDs are set up, the neural texture is baked at adapted resolution over the UV-space.

    Representing the network output as dynamically updated textures allows standard rendering techniques to access the predicted maps without further neural evaluations. In particular, we use forward rendering to handle transparency, while parallax mapping, flyaway fibers, and fuzz shells repeatedly reuse the cached maps. Table 1 details the differences between the two rendering strategies.

    3.2 Cache Update Strategy

    Because the cache stores texture maps, changes in lighting or viewpoint do not by themselves require new neural predictions at a fixed texture resolution. We exploit this reuse with a deformation-triggered update policy and a configurable update schedule.

    Deformation-triggered invalidation.

    For each coarse-mesh vertex v, we compare its current deformation dᵥ=(sₓ,s_y,sₐ) with a stored reference d̂ᵥ. We mark the affected texture regions for reevaluation when

    \lVertdᵥ-d̂ᵥ\rVert_∞>τ,

    where τ is a tolerance in the original deformation coordinates, without per-component normalization. On a threshold crossing, we advance the vertex’s reference to its current deformation and mark all row groups in the affected regions as pending. Selecting one row group for an update leaves the others pending; the reference therefore records a detected change, rather than a common state of all cached texels. Comparing against this reference allows small successive changes to trigger an update once their net departure exceeds τ.

    Update scheduling.

    We set a target update frequency fᵤ independently of the rendering frame rate and cycle through G groups of texture rows during motion. With G=2, successive scheduled updates alternate between even and odd rows. If updates occur at the target rate without interruption, each group receives an update opportunity every G/fᵤ seconds. This is a nominal scheduling interval, not a bound on prediction age: thresholding can suppress updates, and batching or deferred submissions can delay them. Initialization and forced refreshes bypass row interleaving; a settling refresh also uses full row coverage before unchanged deformation can be reused without further updates. The supplementary material details these exceptions and the runtime settings.

    Quality and responsiveness.

    Skipped texels retain their cached intrinsic fields, while their rendered appearance can still change with lighting, viewpoint, and coarse-mesh motion. The tolerance τ controls deformation-space differences and does not bound appearance error. Reduced update frequency and row interleaving can delay changes in the predicted yarn fields and leave neighboring rows representing different deformation states. Evaluating these approximations requires comparison with full per-frame texture-space updates at the same resolution, so that errors due to update scheduling are separated from representation and sampling errors.

    3.3 Yarn Shading and Cloth Effects

    The cached neural maps are used as conventional material textures to render the coarse cloth. Alpha determines yarn coverage, normals provide local surface orientation, and the material ID selects the corresponding shader parameters. We use Lambertian diffuse and GGX specular reflection, while depth and alpha support view-dependent relief and local occlusion.

    Our maps-based representation enable additional yarn-scale effects without further neural evaluations. Parallax mapping uses depth to produce view-dependent yarn relief, while fuzz is approximated with thin shell layers anchored to the yarn surface. Sparse flyaway fibers are represented as tapered ribbons, with alpha selecting their roots, depth positioning them on the yarns, and normals guiding their orientation [LPFH01]. Further implementation details are provided in the supplementary material.

    Reconstruction fidelity across five yarn structures using a width of 128, we measure PSNR (dB) for alpha, normals and depth and report the proportion of material IDs that are correctly reconstructed. For all columns, higher is better (↑).

    Storage cost and reconstruction quality on rib. We compare our neural models with ASTC block compression of the ground-truth textures and lossless texture references, illustrating the trade-off between storage and representation quality PSNR of in-distribution samples. We compare different widths of our Fourier-SIREN network, among which best scores are bold, second best underlined; we highlight the trade-off that we use in practice.

    4 Results

    In this section we evaluate DTM accuracy and performance (Section 4.1), appearance control (Sections 4.2 and 4.3), and end-to-end rendering performance (Section 4.4).

    Experimental Setup.

    We evaluate DTM on five yarn structures spanning woven and knitted configurations: rib, basket, stockinette, honeycomb, and satin. Unless stated otherwise, each structure uses an independently trained Fourier-SIREN of width 128, trained for 30,000 steps on a discrete lattice of deformation states. All models sample an 8×8×8 lattice of deformation states with sₓ,s_y∈[-0.2,1.0] and sₐ∈[-0.7,0.7] for a total of 512 states. Full implementation details are provided in the supplementary material. Throughout the quantitative tables, alpha, normals, and depth are measured by PSNR (dB), and material ID by classification accuracy (%). Normals are also evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively using lambertian renders and FLIP metric  [ANAM∗20].

    4.1 Model Accuracy and Performance

    We evaluate reconstruction accuracy across five yarn structures and sampled deformation states. We compare against the ground-truth (GT) maps, which are estimated from the original geometry.

    Table 2 reports accuracy for each map. Depth and material identity achieve the highest reconstruction accuracy, while alpha and normals have less precision. Figure 4 shows these differences qualitatively by shading the predicted normals with a Lambertian model. The error is measured using FLIP[ANAM∗20]. DTM preserves the overall yarn structure even under large deformations.

    We show in Table 3 how DTM performs at different model sizes. We compare per-map quality against texture compression approaches such as ASTC, performed over the entire training dataset (See supplementary for further evaluations). Using our selected parameters (Fourier SIREN width set to 128, yellow row), our approach provides quality between the ones of ASTC (8×8) and ASTC (12×12), for a 42x-to-94x storage memory reduction.

    In Figure 5, we also compare our method with a naïve baseline that blends in image space the neighboring stored textures. Linear texture blending superimposes yarn boundaries from neighboring states, producing visible ghosting, whereas DTM produces a more coherent intermediate configuration closer to the ground truth.

    4.2 Garment-level Examples

    We evaluate DTM on simulated coarse garment meshes and cloth patches. We compute per-triangle stretch and shear in local material coordinates, average these quantities at mesh vertices using area weights, and interpolate the resulting deformation parameters across the surface to condition the tileable neural material. Figure 6 illustrates the importance of deformation-dependent coverage: stretching alters the yarn arrangement and the openings through which the backlight is visible. Unlike naive texture scaling, DTM captures these structural changes through its deformation-conditioned opacity field. The resulting effect reflects changes in yarn coverage, rather than light transmission through the yarns.

    4.3 Editability

    Because DTM predicts intrinsic maps rather than final radiance, lighting and material appearance can be edited without retraining. Figure 7 shows how predicted material identities enable palette edits that consistently follow yarn groups across the textile. The predicted maps can also be combined with conventional rendering effects, including parallax relief, fuzzy shells, and flyaway fibers, without modifying the learned representation (Figure 8). We also demonstrate real-time relightability and pallette edits with fixed models in various animated scenarios (see Teaser ).

    4.4 Real-Time Renderer Evaluation

    We evaluate the complete renderer to measure how texture-space reuse affects performance under deformation and camera motion. We compare per-fragment screen-space deferred neural evaluation with our texture-space approach, using the same neural model, shading settings, and 1920×1080 output resolution. Our texture-space approach only schedules cache updates when cloth elements are being actively deformed and reuses previously evaluated maps when deformation remains unchanged. We enable all of the optimization techniques discussed in Section 3 such as update scheduling, selective updates to changed tiles, and adaptive virtual textures, we set a max resolution of 4k for the highest quality virtual texture and we define 5 LODs in total which we swap based on approximate texture texel to viewport pixel footprint.

    The benchmark alternates stationary intervals with cloth stretching and a camera zoom during stretching. We measure GPU-finished application frames per second with browser-driven scheduling and vsync disable, we also allow up to three frames in flight. Figure 9 reports performance over the interaction sequence.

    In this benchmark, we evaluate the performance profile of each method: In the case of the screen-space deferred approach, we can see that the framerate scales with amount of pixels on screen that require a DTM network evaluation. Comparatively, in our approach, we can see that we achieve considerably higher framerate in the rest sections of the benchmark, this is because once we calculate that deformation state, we can keep reusing the results and only update the minor changes. We drop in framerate as the fabric starts moving and we require cache updates. We also show the performance behavior of zooming in in both cases, in screens-pace deferred, performance drops expectedly because we fill the entire viewport with pixels that need network evaluations, in our approach we also drop in framerate briefly because, as we zoom in, we start swapping to higher quality LODs and calculating them into the cache. As soon as we finish we get a spike again of framerate.

    5 Ablations

    We evaluate the main design choices of DTM through ablations of the neural representation (Section 5.1) and our texture-cache runtime rendering strategy (Section 5.2).

    5.1 Neural Model

    We ablate the architecture, training budget, and frequency initialization of our neural representation. At approximately matched parameter counts, Fourier-SIREN achieves the highest reconstruction quality among the evaluated architectures (Table 4). We perform various runs per architecture, sweeping over multiple learning rates and architecture specific parameters. For our Fourier-SIREN network, increasing the training budget improves reconstruction quality with diminishing returns beyond 30k steps (Figure 10), which we use throughout our experiments. (see supplementary material for more details).

    Reconstruction quality of six neural architectures on rib with approximately 64k parameters each.

    5.2 Runtime Rendering

    We evaluate our rendering approach along with all the approximations and optimizations discussed in 2 by measuring the end-to-end FPS across multiple scenarios in our Three.js WebGPU renderer implementation.
