However, existing methods still rely on relatively limited split spaces, typically dominated by surface-based or planar operations, and on intermediate shaping rewards that are only weakly aligned with hexahedral meshability. As a result, they struggle to resolve feature misalignment in CAD models, often leaving decompositions that remain unmeshable.

    III Method

    DecompRL treats CAD model decomposition as a sequential decision process over an evolving decomposition frontier. At each step, the agent considers one active solid, generates candidate split operations from the B-Rep of that active solid, filters out infeasible candidates, and selects one valid split for execution. The selected split may produce multiple child solids, which are then inserted back into the frontier for subsequent decisions. This process continues until no further useful split remains or the step budget is reached. Fig. 3 shows the overall pipeline.

    III-AProblem Setup

    We formulate CAD decomposition as a decision-making process with branching transitions. Fig. 4 shows the local frontier expansion induced by a single split that produces multiple child solids. At decision step t, the environment considers one active solid, denoted by Bₜ, and generates a raw candidate pool Cₜ={cₜ¹,…,cₜ^Kₜ} from that solid.

    The policy observation combines three parts: a global state representation sₜ of the active solid, an encoded candidate set Xₜ whose elements xₜⁱ are computed from each candidate together with the global state context, and a binary validity mask mₜ∈{0,1}^Kₜ whose i-th entry indicates whether candidate cₜⁱ remains admissible after filtering. The observation passed to the policy is therefore

    oₜ=(sₜ,Xₜ,mₜ).

    		(1)

    In the remainder of the paper, candidate pool refers to the raw generated operations Cₜ, while candidate set refers to the masked candidates presented to the policy after feasibility filtering and encoding.

    Given this observation, the policy selects one valid candidate index iₜ∼π_θ(·|oₜ), which is then mapped to the executed geometric action aₜ. A valid split under aₜ may produce multiple child solids and these children are inserted into the decomposition frontier and become future decision targets. An episode terminates when no splittable node remains or the step budget is reached.

    III-BAction Space and Candidate Generation

    Our action space consists of geometric split candidates constructed from the active solid rather than a fixed list of abstract actions. At decision step t, candidate generation produces the raw pool

    Cₜ=G(Bₜ)=\bigcupₖCₜ⁽ᵏ⁾,

    		(2)

    where G(·) denotes the candidate generation procedure and Cₜ⁽ᵏ⁾ denotes the subset produced by candidate family k. The raw candidate pool Cₜ is then formed by merging these family-specific candidates before feasibility filtering.

    The candidate families are chosen to cover different blocking conflicts commonly encountered in hexahedral meshing, including planar, symmetry, O-grid, feature gap, and rotation splits. Here a candidate family denotes an operator class; at each decision step, geometry-specific proposal procedures instantiate these families on the current active solid Bₜ to form a solid-specific raw candidate set ℂₜ. A planar split cuts the CAD model with a plane, which may coincide with a surface face or be an interior plane defined by three points, as shown in Fig. 5(a). A symmetry split partitions the model along its symmetry plane. It is well suited for symmetric blocks, especially ring-like structures, as shown in Fig. 5(b). O-grid splits improve mesh quality for circular structures and are particularly effective for resolving internal conflicts in intersecting cylindrical structures, such as T-junctions. They are also suitable for decomposing cylindrical and spherical blocks, as shown in Fig. 5(c). A feature-gap split can be viewed as a special case of planar splitting. It separates nearby misaligned features by placing the cutting plane at the intermediate plane between them, as shown in Fig. 5(d). The rotation split follows a cylindrical surface and separates the features on that surface from the cylindrical body, as shown in Fig. 5(e). It is particularly effective for resolving sweep direction conflicts in ring-like structures. Together, these families provide complementary coverage for different forms of feature misalignment.

    Feature-gap construction. Local feature walls are grouped using opening relationships and topological adjacency, excluding common exterior faces that would otherwise connect unrelated features. Their projected extents are examined along geometrically determined separation directions. Overlapping intervals of all identified features are merged, so an intervening feature is not overlooked. A cutting plane is placed at the midpoint of a separation band satisfying the scale-dependent minimum-gap requirement, with its normal aligned with the separation direction. Candidates undergo geometric validity checks and deduplication, and at most five are retained for policy selection. Figure 6 illustrates this procedure for a transverse rectangular through-hole and vertical cylindrical through-holes: the midpoint plane crosses the connecting material while avoiding the hole features.

    Before action selection, the raw candidate pool is filtered by feasibility checks to remove invalid or degenerate operations. Feasibility filtering is summarized by a binary mask

    m_t,i=\begincases1,&cₜⁱpasses the enabled checks, 0,&otherwise,\endcases

    		(3)

    so that only feasible candidates are passed to the policy. Here m_t,i=1 if candidate cₜⁱ passes all geometric validity checks (non-degenerate volume, valid topology, and non-self-intersecting result), and 0 otherwise. The checks remove candidates that violate geometric validity, minimum size or thickness constraints. As a result, the policy scores a compact set of feasible and structurally meaningful split options.

    III-CState and Candidate Encoding

    To make candidate selection depend on both global topological structure and local geometric property, we encode the observation with two complementary branches: one for the active solid and one for each candidate split. The state branch represents the active solid through a global representation derived from the boundary representation (B-Rep):

    sₜ=ψₛₜₐₜₑ(Bₜ),

    		(4)

    where ψₛₜₐₜₑ(·) combines a graph-level embedding from the AAGNet B-Rep graph encoder [30] with an explicit 9-dimensional state descriptor of the active solid. The graph-level embedding provides learned B-Rep geometric/topological context from face attributes and face-adjacency relations, whereas the 9D state descriptor supplies fixed-size global geometric statistics. We initialize the AAGNet backbone from the released MFInstSeg-pretrained weights and keep it frozen during RL training; its machining-feature recognition heads are not used as a trainable component of DecompRL.

    Each candidate split is encoded as

    xₜⁱ=φ(cₜⁱ,sₜ),

    		(5)

    where φ(·) combines a fixed-dimensional explicit candidate descriptor with candidate-associated local geometric/B-Rep context. The explicit descriptor records the candidate type, orientation, normalized relative position, and candidate-specific geometric attributes, while the local context describes the region of the active solid relevant to that candidate. The encoded candidate set is

    Xₜ={xₜ¹,…,xₜ^Kₜ}.

    		(6)

    The state representation sₜ provides the global geometric/topological context shared by all candidates of the current active solid, whereas each xₜⁱ describes one instantiated candidate through its explicit candidate descriptor together with candidate-associated local geometric/B-Rep context. The actor therefore evaluates every candidate conditionally on the same global state. Different candidate families retain a common explicit descriptor layout; entries corresponding to non-applicable candidate-specific attributes are set to zero.

    The actor evaluates each candidate using the global state encoding and its candidate encoding, and the resulting scores are normalized with a feasibility mask:

    π_θ(i|sₜ,Xₜ,mₜ)=MaskedSoftmax({f_θ(sₜ,xₜʲ)}ⱼ₌₁^Kₜ, mₜ)ᵢ,

    		(7)

    where f_θ is the actor scoring network. Infeasible candidates receive zero probability.

    The policy action at step t is the selection of one feasible instantiated candidate cₜⁱ from the solid-specific candidate set, rather than the selection of an action-family label alone. Each candidate already specifies the geometry needed to instantiate its split, while the actor learns to rank these candidates under the current state. The critic evaluates the same candidate-conditioned decisions through twin Q-networks Q_φ₁(sₜ,xₜⁱ) and Q_φ₂(sₜ,xₜⁱ), taking their minimum to reduce value overestimation, and a separate state value network V_ν(sₜ) with its target counterpart V_ν̄(sₜ) supports the tree backup described in Section III-E. During training, the candidate index iₜ is sampled from the masked policy, whereas during inference the highest-probability feasible candidate is selected.

    Feature dimensions

    In the reported configuration, the explicit 9D state descriptor included in sₜ contains the bounding-box scales (bₓ,b_y,b_z), diagonal length, volume, number of faces, number of edges, number of solids, and a binary multi-solid indicator Iₘᵤₗₜᵢ=1[N_solid>1]. This state-side descriptor summarizes global properties of the active solid and is distinct from the 9 candidate-specific geometric attributes defined below. The explicit candidate descriptor in xₜⁱ is 56-dimensional, consisting of a 41-dimensional one-hot encoding for candidate type, a 3D axis or surface-normal descriptor, a 3D normalized relative-position descriptor, and 9 candidate-specific attributes. These are the solid-cutter indicator, normalized candidate-associated length, generator-provided score, gap-family indicator, normalized gap size, normalized associated area, normalized radius, and two sweep-related slots. With D denoting the active-solid bounding-box diagonal, length, gap size, area, and radius are encoded as ℓ_c/D, g/D, A/D², and r/D, respectively. The solid-cutter indicator is 1 when a candidate is marked as using a volumetric cutting tool and 0 otherwise; it does not indicate execution success. The score previously termed confidence is supplied by the generator and is not a calibrated success probability. The gap-family indicator identifies gap-type candidates. Attributes not supplied by a generator are encoded as zero.

    III-DReward Design

    We design the reward to favor decompositions that remain geometrically regular and better aligned with hexahedral meshing. The geometric reward is composed of five terms (Eq. 8):

    rₜᵍᵉᵒ=∑_k∈{V,E,G,L,M}w̄ₖ q_k,t, w̄ₖ=(wₖ)/(∑ⱼwⱼ),

    		(8)

    where the five reward terms are defined over the child blocks generated by the selected split.

    The first two terms, q_V,t and q_E,t, measure angular regularity. Specifically, q_V,t evaluates face-corner angle quality: the in-face angle formed by adjacent boundary directions in the local face plane/tangent plane; it is not a 3D solid angle. The term q_E,t evaluates the dihedral angle between adjacent face normals along a shared edge. For curved edges where the dihedral varies spatially, we evaluate the adjacent face normals at a representative point near the curve center and use their included angle as a local edge measure, rather than integrating or taking the worst angle over the entire edge. In each case, the reward combines the mean angle quality of the generated child blocks with a relative quality-preservation term that compares scalar child and parent angle-quality references. This comparison does not measure geometric or topological similarity between the child and parent blocks. For these two terms, we use the shared template (Eq. 9)

    ℚ(μ,c,p)=0.5 μ+0.5 \min ((c/p+ε)²,1),

    		(9)

    and instantiate (Eq. 10)

    q_V,t=ℚ(αₜᵐᵉᵃⁿ,Aₜᶜʰⁱˡᵈ,Aₜᵖᵃʳ),(10)
    q_E,t=ℚ(βₜᵐᵉᵃⁿ,Dₜᶜʰⁱˡᵈ,Dₜᵖᵃʳ),

    where αₜᵐᵉᵃⁿ and βₜᵐᵉᵃⁿ denote the mean face-corner angle and dihedral-angle quality scores over the generated child blocks, respectively. The terms Aₜᶜʰⁱˡᵈ and Aₜᵖᵃʳ denote the child and parent face-corner angle-quality reference terms, while Dₜᶜʰⁱˡᵈ and Dₜᵖᵃʳ denote the corresponding child and parent dihedral-angle quality reference terms. The preservation term is one-sided and saturates at 1 when the child reference is equal to or better than the parent reference; it only decreases when the split degrades the corresponding quality measure. Thus, structural changes such as those intentionally introduced by an O-grid operation are not penalized simply for differing from the parent.

    The extreme-geometry term q_G,t (not to be confused with the candidate generator G) acts as a relative degeneracy guard. It discourages a split from introducing substantially worse short-edge, poor face-shape/aspect, or small-face-area conditions in the generated children (Eq. 11):

    q_G,t=0.25 η_t,len+0.5 η_t,aspect+0.25 η_t,area,(11)
    η_t,x=clip (((g_t,xᶜʰⁱˡᵈ)/(g_t,xᵖᵃʳ+ε))²,0,1), x∈{len,aspect,area},

    Here the compared quantities are scalar lower-bound geometric-quality measures rather than descriptors of the overall child shape or topology. The score reaches 1 when the corresponding child quality is preserved or improved relative to the parent and decreases only when the split creates a worse degeneracy. The internal coefficients 0.25/0.5/0.25 are fixed heuristic design weights rather than values obtained from test-set optimization or a dedicated hyperparameter search. The face-shape/aspect term receives the larger weight to emphasize narrow or strongly distorted faces, while the short-edge and small-area terms provide complementary indicators of scale-related degeneracy.

    The term q_L,t encourages simpler face-boundary topology by rewarding decompositions whose child blocks contain fewer B-Rep faces with internal face-boundary loops (Eq. 12). Here an internal face-boundary loop means an inner trimming loop of a face in addition to its outer boundary; it is not a direct count of 3D holes or tunnels in the solid:

    q_L,t=1/Nₜ∑ᵢ₌₁^Nₜ((F_t,no_loop⁽ⁱ⁾)/(\max(F_t,total⁽ⁱ⁾,1)))²,

    		(12)

    where Nₜ is the number of generated child blocks, F_t,no_loop⁽ⁱ⁾ denotes the number of faces with no inner boundary loop in child block i, and F_t,total⁽ⁱ⁾ denotes the total number of faces in child block i.

    Finally, the meshability term (q_M,t) provides a meshability-oriented signal through the mean of the child-block meshability indicators (Eq. 13)

    q_M,t=1/Nₜ∑ᵢ₌₁^Nₜz_t,iᵐᵉˢʰ,

    		(13)

    where z_t,iᵐᵉˢʰ∈{0,1} is the operational meshability indicator assigned to child block B_t,i, defined as

    z_t,iᵐᵉˢʰ=I [c_sweep(B_t,i)∨cₘₐₚ(B_t,i)∨c_submap(B_t,i)],

    		(14)

    where c_sweep, cₘₐₚ, and c_submap denote the supported sweep, map, and submap compatibility checks, respectively. Thus, q_M,t is the mean of binary meshability indicators at the child-block level and serves directly as a continuous feasibility signal for the set of child blocks. The positive weights wₖ are raw coefficients, while w̄ₖ denotes the normalized weight used in reward aggregation. The child-level indicator is intentionally binary because Map, Submap, and Sweep are treated as alternative supported compatibility routes rather than ordered quality levels; satisfying several predicates does not automatically imply a higher-quality block than satisfying one valid predicate. The split-level score q_M,t is nevertheless graded through the fraction of generated children that satisfy at least one supported compatibility condition.

    Fig. 7 shows the geometric intuition behind the main reward terms: Fig. 7 (a)–(b) illustrate better and worse dihedral angle configurations for q_E, Fig. 7 (c) shows an extreme geometry case penalized by q_G, and Fig. 7 (d) shows how reducing internal loops improves q_L.

    To handle invalid actions, stopping behavior, and depth bias in the decomposition tree, we further apply runtime shaping (Eq. 15):

    rₜ=λ_d^hₜ rₜᵇᵃˢᵉ+I_stop,t bₛₜₒₚ,

    		(15)

    where

    rₜᵇᵃˢᵉ=\begincases-1.0,&invalid split or empty children, rₜᵍᵉᵒ,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(16)

    Here hₜ is the depth of the current node, I_stop,t indicates whether stopping criteria are satisfied at step t, and bₛₜₒₚ is the corresponding stop bonus. We use λ_d=0.9 as a tree-depth reward-shaping factor. The term λ_d^hₜ rescales the immediate geometric reward according to structural depth, so that obtaining the same local improvement only after additional recursive splits contributes less reward and unnecessarily deep decomposition trees are discouraged. This factor is distinct from the Bellman discount γ=0.95 used in Section III-E: λ_d acts on the current-node reward, whereas γ discounts the aggregated future value of the generated child states. Thus, the two parameters serve different roles and are not interchangeable. The stop flag and the terminal indicator are related but not identical: I_stop,t=1 marks a node that reaches a valid stopping state, whereas dₜ=1 marks any terminal node, including those terminated by candidate exhaustion or split failure. Every stopped node is terminal (I_stop,t=1⇒dₜ=1), but a node can be terminal without earning the stop bonus.

    III-D1 Evaluation Criteria and Meshability Indicator

    This section clarifies the model-level evaluation criterion used in SR and the operational meshability indicator used in the reward meshability term q_M.

    To guide the reinforcement learning agent toward valid geometric decompositions, we define an operational meshability indicator z_t,iᵐᵉˢʰ∈{0,1} (Eq. 14) for each decomposed child block B_t,i, evaluating its compatibility with the supported structured-hexahedral meshing families. Each compatibility function returns 1 if the corresponding conditions hold and 0 otherwise:

  • •

    Map compatibility cₘₐₚ: the volume must admit a logical-hexahedral organization with six logical sides and eight logical corners. A logical side may consist of multiple geometric surfaces; opposite logical directions must admit compatible interval constraints so that a structured i-j-k parametrization can be formed.

  • •

    Submap compatibility c_submap: a volume that is not directly mappable as one logical hexahedron may still be accepted when its boundary admits a consistent local i-j-k classification into mappable logical subregions. Boundary vertices are classified from the local interior-angle structure around nominal 90^∘ increments. The automatic classification uses a fixed fuzzy angular tolerance of 27^∘ for all datasets; this value is not tuned per dataset.

  • •

    Sweep compatibility c_sweep: the volume must admit topologically compatible source and target surfaces connected by continuous linking surfaces. The linking surfaces must support Map/Submap-compatible structured discretization, and multiple logical source-to-target paths must have consistent total interval counts so that the source mesh can be propagated along one logical sweep direction.

    • These predicates are operational compatibility tests for the supported structured-hexahedral meshing routes rather than necessary-and-sufficient conditions for arbitrary hexahedral meshability. Consequently, local compatibility is used only as the meshability-oriented reward signal, while actual downstream meshing success is evaluated separately.

    It is important to distinguish this intermediate reward signal from the final evaluation metric. While the block-level indicator z_t,iᵐᵉˢʰ drives the optimization of q_M during training, the model-level Success Rate (SR) reported in our evaluations is defined solely by successful completion of the final hexahedral meshing pipeline rather than by this operational indicator. Successful generation is defined for the entire input CAD model, including all final leaf volumes. For each dataset, SR=100N_success/200 is reported as a percentage. A case ending without a complete hexahedral mesh, including incomplete volume meshing or errors or timeouts that prevent completion, is counted as a failure and remains in the denominator. Scaled-Jacobian statistics characterize the generated elements; the reported fraction with Jₛ>0.8 is not an additional threshold defining SR. The current reward also does not directly optimize final element-wise hexahedral mesh quality. Such feedback could be incorporated in future work as a delayed terminal reward based on metrics such as scaled Jacobian, or through a learned mesh-quality surrogate. We keep it separate in the reported method because repeatedly generating a complete hexahedral mesh at intermediate decomposition steps would substantially increase training cost and couple the decomposition policy more tightly to the downstream mesher.

    III-D2 Global Conformity Across Shared Block Interfaces

    Block-level Map/Submap/Sweep compatibility is treated as a local operational meshability criterion, while global conformity is handled in a separate downstream meshing stage. After decomposition, the leaf volumes are assembled on shared CAD topology rather than meshed independently, so the final hexahedral mesh is generated on a common multi-block representation. Figure 8 illustrates shared-interface conformity through a manually constructed MAMBO M1 verification example.

    Coincident CAD interfaces are first subdivided into corresponding topological regions, and the matching surfaces, curves, and vertices are identified in the assembled model. For neighboring leaf volumes Vᵢ and Vⱼ sharing a two-dimensional interface Γᵢⱼ, conformity requires

    Mᵢ|_Γᵢⱼ=Mⱼ|_Γᵢⱼ=M_Γᵢⱼ.

    		(17)

    Here Mᵢ denotes the mesh of Vᵢ, and M_Γᵢⱼ is the common interface mesh. Equality means that both sides reference the same global node identifiers and quadrilateral connectivity. Each internal interface quadrilateral is incident on one hexahedron from each neighboring volume, with opposite boundary orientations. The interface mesh is generated once and reused by both volumes.

    Interval compatibility also includes volume constraints. For a Sweep-compatible volume with fixed source, target, and logical edge classifications, let nₑ be the number of intervals on logical boundary curve e∈E. The signed interval sums along two source-to-target paths Pᵣ and Pₛ must agree:

    ∑_e∈E(w_r,e-w_s,e)nₑ=0.

    		(18)

    The path coefficient w_r,e∈{-1,0,1} is +1 or -1 for traversal along or against the logical sweep direction, and 0 for transverse curves or curves outside Pᵣ. This condition couples the hexahedral layer counts along different paths, including paths inside holes and along the exterior boundary. Surface interval compatibility alone does not ensure volume sweep compatibility [18]. Equation (18) applies to Sweep volumes; other schemes contribute their own applicable constraints.

    For fixed meshing schemes and logical classifications, the surface and volume constraints are collected into a global integer feasibility problem [18]:

    \minₓf(x,g)(19)
    subject toAx=b, x∈ℤᵐ,
    ℓ≤x≤u.

    The vector x contains curve interval counts and any required auxiliary integers. The matrix A collects surface balances, volume constraints such as Eq. (18), applicable parity constraints, and explicitly fixed intervals; inequalities can be converted using bounded auxiliary variables. For example, a sum-even condition is encoded by ∑ₑnₑ-2k=0 with integer k. The bounds enforce admissible intervals, while g supplies the target-size goals. These goals are adjusted within the feasible set; the compatibility constraints remain hard requirements. Feasible interval assignment does not by itself certify successful geometric mesh generation or element quality.

    For Map-compatible leaves, structured discretization follows the logical i-j-k directions; Submap-compatible leaves use mappable logical subregions; and Sweep-compatible leaves propagate a quadrilateral source mesh toward a topologically compatible target through the linking surfaces. Final mesh generation and quality evaluation are performed downstream, without an additional learned mesh-quality optimizer. The manually constructed SALOME 9.16.0 verification example in Fig. 8 uses a common quadrilateral layout and consistent layer divisions, with interface nodes created once and reused by adjacent hexahedra [31]. The complete inspected interface contains 896 quadrilaterals and 1,008 distinct nodes; every interface quadrilateral has exactly two incident hexahedra with opposite outward face orientations. The complete mesh contains 27,392 hexahedra and 32,328 nodes, forms one face-connected component, and has no duplicate coincident-node groups at a tolerance of 10⁻⁹ model units. This example verifies shared-interface conformity and does not imply a general meshing guarantee from local compatibility alone.

    III-EDecompRL Optimization

    DecompRL is optimized with a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) formulation adapted to the candidate-conditioned decomposition setting. We use a masked candidate policy with twin Q-functions and soft target updates, together with the multi-child Tree-Bellman target below; thus, the method is not PPO and is not intended to be presented as a new generic RL algorithm. Relative to the controlled DRL substitutions used in our experiments, SAC differs from DDPG and TD3 by using a stochastic entropy-regularized policy rather than deterministic action selection with external exploration noise; TD3 additionally employs target-policy smoothing and delayed actor updates. PPO is on-policy and optimizes a clipped surrogate objective rather than using replay-based off-policy updates. These comparisons therefore hold the CAD environment and candidate interface fixed while changing the RL optimization mechanism.

    The value function itself follows the standard RL definition; the distinction in our setting lies in the transition structure used by the Bellman target. Since one split can produce multiple valid child solids, a standard single-next-state backup is insufficient for our decomposition tree. We therefore store tree transitions in replay and aggregate future value over all valid children generated by one split. Let Child(Bₜ,aₜ) denote the set of child solids produced by executing geometric action aₜ on the active solid Bₜ. The reward rₜ measures the immediate quality of the selected split at the current node, while V_ν̄(s^′) is the standard state-value estimate applied to each resulting child state. Accordingly, the training target combines immediate reward with discounted aggregated future value over all generated children:

    yₜ=rₜ+γ(1-dₜ) Agg ({V_ν̄(s^′)|s^′=ψₛₜₐₜₑ(B^′),.(20)
    .B^′∈Child(Bₜ,aₜ)}),

    where dₜ is the terminal indicator, V_ν̄ is the same target value network, and Agg(·) is an aggregation operator over child values. In our default setting, Agg(·) is the sum operator, so a split is evaluated by the combined utility of all generated children rather than by only one favorable branch.

    III-E1 Training Algorithm

    Algorithm 1 summarizes the training loop used for the Tree-Bellman optimization described above: state encoding from the B-Rep, scoring of explicit candidates, masked selection, geometric reward composition, depth discounting, tree-structured target construction, and updates for the reported DRL method.

    The key difference from a standard one-step MDP backup is the multi-child target: a single split can produce multiple child solids, so the value target aggregates over all resulting children rather than a single next state.

    IV Experiments

    We organize the experiments around four questions: Can DecompRL successfully decompose and mesh representative challenging CAD models with interacting features (RQ1)? Does it improve mesh quality and decomposition success rate over baselines under a unified evaluation setup across datasets (RQ2)? Are the proposed architectural components and reward terms reasonable for improving decomposition and meshing performance (RQ3)? And how efficient is it compared with the frame-field pipeline on aligned samples (RQ4)?

    IV-AExperiment Setting

    Datasets. Each training run comprises 5,000 episodes. At the start of each episode, one source CAD model is selected from the training pool of 1,400 models. For validation, we use four fixed sets of 200 CAD models each, one for each dataset (ABC [32], Fusion360 [33], NIST [34], and DeepCAD [35]). Unless otherwise specified, ablation experiments are conducted on ABC.

    Implementation Details and Compared Baselines. We compare the reported DecompRL instantiation with PPO [36], DDPG [37], and TD3 [38] as controlled algorithm substitutions within the same CAD decomposition task, rather than as application-independent baselines. These learned methods use the same CAD environment and geometric backend, solid-specific candidate-generation and feasibility-filtering pipeline, state/candidate observation interface, reward definition, split execution interface, hexahedral-meshing success criterion, and benchmark protocol. Their differences are therefore confined to the RL optimization scheme and algorithm-specific training machinery. We additionally compare with the prior decomposition method of Zhang et al. [21], which is evaluated with its original action families, and include the field-based LMFF method as the hexahedral-meshing baseline for runtime comparison [23]. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments use the CadQuery/OCP geometric backend and a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, and all learned DRL methods are optimized with Adam.

    Training configuration

    Unless otherwise noted, all learned DRL methods use the same hidden dimension. Table I reports the optimization settings and trainable parameter counts for each method. Off-policy methods additionally use replay buffers and soft target-network updates, while PPO uses clipped policy optimization with multiple epochs per rollout. DDPG and TD3 further use scheduled exploration noise. For the controlled comparison, DDPG and TD3 are adapted to the same finite masked candidate-selection interface rather than being used to output continuous geometric split parameters. Their actors score the same feasible candidates generated by the shared geometry pipeline; PPO likewise selects from the same masked candidate set. The comparison therefore isolates the RL optimization mechanism while keeping the geometric action interface fixed.

    Mesh size and shared settings

    For each input CAD model, we compute the target element size once from the original geometry before decomposition:

    e_size=√[3]V_\max(0.03+0.00045m_d^3.1), m_d=5.

    		(21)

    Here, V_\max is the largest solid volume in the original input model. The reference volume and target size are fixed for that input and reused across all methods in the benchmark Jacobian comparison, without recomputation from the child volumes after decomposition. Integer subdivisions may be adjusted to satisfy shared-interface and mapping/sweeping constraints; the common target size therefore does not require identical realized element counts. No additional mesh smoothing is applied in the main experiments.

    Metrics. Success Rate (SR, reported as a percentage of evaluated models), the percentage of elements with scaled Jacobian >0.8 (written as J>0.8 in tables), minimum scaled Jacobian (\minJₛ), and Mean Reward (written as R in tables). SR and the Jacobian metrics are the primary metrics, while Mean Reward is reported only as a supporting optimization signal. A model is counted as successful only if hexahedral meshing completes successfully. For the efficiency analysis, we report the runtime ratio for each sample, defined as Speedup=t_LMFF/t_DecompRL. Here, t_LMFF covers the complete LMFF procedure used in our experiments, whereas t_DecompRL covers CAD decomposition only and excludes subsequent hexahedral mesh generation. The quantity labeled Speedup therefore denotes this stage-specific runtime ratio, rather than an end-to-end meshing speedup. Mesh-quality statistics include only cases that successfully generate a complete globally conforming hexahedral mesh. For each successful case, we compute the proportion of elements with Jₛ>0.8 and the minimum scaled Jacobian, then average each metric with equal weight across successful cases. Thus, the reported \minJₛ is the average of per-case minima, and the reported J>0.8 value is the average of per-case proportions, rather than an element-count-weighted pooled statistic. Failed cases are excluded from quality averages without being assigned zero Jacobian values, but remain in the SR denominator.

    IV-BCase Study (RQ1)

    Fig. 9 visualizes representative successful decomposition outputs produced by DecompRL across diverse CAD models, with each color denoting one child solid generated by the selected split sequence. Fig. 10 then compares decomposition and hexahedral meshing results on six representative CAD models: its upper half shows the decompositions, where different colors denote sub-blocks, and its lower half shows the corresponding hexahedral meshes, colored by scaled Jacobian, where blue indicates better mesh quality and red indicates failure to generate hexahedral meshes.

    The six comparison cases were deliberately selected to cover different combinations of splitting actions and to illustrate the resulting partitions and meshes. Dataset-level performance is assessed separately on the complete evaluation sets.

    In the six-case comparison, DecompRL produces more refined and better aligned block partitions, especially for interacting features, and the resulting decompositions yield more complete, higher-quality hexahedral meshes. In the (2) T-junction case, it separates the orthogonal cylindrical branches and introduces an O-grid split to resolve the internal conflict. In the (4) cylindrical case, it isolates the wall block containing the hole from the regular cylindrical portion; in the (5) ellipsoidal case, it generates an O-grid-style decomposition suited to the curved outer shape; and in the (6) plier case, it separates the handle block from the remainder. These decompositions better resolve feature interactions and lead to clearer improvements in mesh quality in cases (2)–(5), with fewer red regions where hexahedral meshes cannot be generated. Although the less regular upper geometry leaves some red regions in case (6), DecompRL still produces the most complete and highest-quality mesh among the compared methods.

    Failure cases. Two ABC models illustrate different causes of failure. In Case 1 (Fig. 11), the rollout stopped with unresolved leaves. In Case 2 (Fig. 12), Boolean validation rejected the proposed cuts. The follow-up diagnostics are reported separately from the original policy outcomes.

    Coupled residual meshing (ABC 00013257). The perforated-plate and curved-sleeve model stopped after six accepted actions with 11 frontier leaves, four unresolved. Later case-specific processing produced 49 bodies, but only 40 contained hexahedra (10,853 elements), with nine elements below a scaled Jacobian of 0.2, including one inverted element; 41 interfaces remained incomplete. Some residual blocks could be meshed separately but not in the assembly, exposing coupled sweep and interval constraints.

    Geometric-validation failure (ABC 00012519). For the raised-lettering model, all three attempted actions were rejected. Each cut produced two positive-volume children, but the subsequent Boolean validation failed with a vertex-mapping error. Later feature-oriented repairs meshed 25 of 28 bodies with 2,608 hexahedra and a minimum scaled Jacobian of 0.2316 over the meshed subset. Three feature-cap bodies remained unmeshed and new central interfaces were unverified, so the model remained unsuccessful.

    IV-COverall Performance (RQ2)

    Main result comparison. Table III reports the endpoint comparison across datasets. DecompRL ranks first in mean SR on ABC, Fusion360, and NIST, with the largest margin observed on Fusion360. It also attains the best J>0.8 results on two of the four datasets and remains competitive in \minJₛ, even though no single method dominates this metric uniformly. Overall, DecompRL achieves higher SR on three of the four evaluated datasets, with the clearest improvement observed on Fusion360, while maintaining competitive mesh-quality metrics. The method of Zhang et al. [21] performs reasonably on ABC but degrades on the other datasets, likely due to its more limited action space. The DRL baselines remain competitive in selected metrics but generally trail DecompRL, supporting the value of its architectural and reward design.

    Statistical comparison. We assess cross-dataset SR differences between DecompRL and PPO, DDPG, and TD3 using two-sided Welch t-tests computed from the reported, rounded means and sample standard deviations over three random-seed runs per method (n=3). Holm correction is applied across all 12 comparisons (three RL baselines across four datasets). These are comparisons of seed-level SR summaries, rather than paired tests of individual model outcomes. Table II reports the comparison against the RL baseline with the highest mean SR on each dataset.

    On Fusion360, DecompRL exceeds PPO by 12.6 percentage points, and this difference remains significant at the 0.05 level after correction (p=0.000677). The smaller numerical gains on ABC and NIST are not significant after correction. On DeepCAD, DecompRL is 1.3 percentage points below DDPG, also without a significant difference after correction. A non-significant result does not establish equivalence between methods.

    IV-C1 Learning Progression

    Figure 14 shows complete-model SR during training on the same fixed Fusion360 evaluation set. At each evaluated episode t, SR(t)=100N_success(t)/Nₑᵥₐₗ, with a fixed denominator. A model counts as successful only if hexahedral meshing completes for the entire model, including all final leaves. DecompRL rises during early training and reaches approximately 60% toward the end of the plotted period.

    Figure 15 complements this curve with archived decomposition outputs for two models. These images come from a historical training/evaluation run distinct from the 5,000-episode benchmark runs. Solid counts change from 4 to 7 for 00006119 (episodes 50 and 250) and from 7 to 5 for 00026545 (episodes 50 and 125). Because evaluation seeds and terminal-verification settings differ across the historical snapshots, they illustrate changes in partition layout rather than controlled failure-to-success transitions. Block count alone does not establish improved meshing quality.

    IV-DAblation Study (RQ3)

    Table V summarizes two groups of ablations, covering architectural components and reward components, and reports their impact on SR and mesh quality. Each variant is trained with three random seeds, and the results are reported as mean±std.

    Main component ablations. Removing Tree Bellman backup degrades SR across all three seeds, supporting the role of multi-child aggregation in long-horizon decomposition. Disabling the advanced actions causes the largest drop, indicating that richer split primitives are directly relevant to hexahedral meshability. To isolate the learned candidate-scoring architecture from geometric pre-filtering, the early-fusion ablation keeps the same candidate generation, feasibility mask, and candidate set as the full model, but replaces the separate state/candidate encoders with a shared encoder over concatenated raw descriptors. Its lower SR therefore reflects the effect of the learned candidate-conditioned scoring architecture rather than removal of candidate pre-filtering.

    Fig. 13(a) compares the aggregation operator over child values in Eq. 20 on ABC, reporting mean SR over seeds 42, 43, and 44. We observe a ranking of sum > mean > max. This ordering matches the decomposition objective, in which overall utility depends on jointly strong child branches rather than a single favorable branch. Mean dilutes cumulative gains across branches, whereas max overemphasizes a single optimistic branch.

    IV-D1 Comparison with Non-Learning Selectors

    To examine the contribution of learned action selection, we compare DecompRL with a deterministic Greedy selector and Random-valid, which samples uniformly from valid candidates (Table IV). Only the action-selection strategy changes: all methods share the candidate-generation and feasibility-masking rules, execution pipeline, action budget, and complete-model meshing-success criterion, and are evaluated on the same fixed 200 CAD models per dataset. DecompRL uses the main benchmark means across three seeds; Random-valid is evaluated with seeds 42, 43, and 44 and reported as mean±standard deviation.

    For each dataset and each of the three DecompRL seeds, we perform a two-sided exact McNemar test against deterministic Greedy using discordant paired success/failure outcomes on the same 200 models. Holm correction is applied across all 12 tests (three seeds across four datasets). The table reports the largest adjusted p-value across the three seeds for each dataset. No statistical test against Random-valid is reported.

    DecompRL improves SR over Greedy by 24.6, 43.1, 28.1, and 49.5 percentage points on ABC, Fusion360, NIST, and DeepCAD, respectively. Its mean SR also exceeds Random-valid on all four datasets; this latter comparison is descriptive. These results support a contribution from learned action selection beyond the two tested non-learning selectors under the shared geometric proposal and feasibility-filtering pipeline.

    IV-D2 Action-Space Ablation

    While Table V removes all advanced actions jointly, we further ablate individual primitives to quantify the contribution of each action family. We conduct this study on a fixed Fusion360 subset (N=200). Fig. 13(b) shows that removing any single family lowers SR. Rotation and symmetry splits have the largest impact (ΔSR -9.46 and -8.00 percentage points), consistent with their role in resolving sweep-direction conflicts in ring-like structures. O-grid and feature-gap splits each reduce SR by 6.00 percentage points, confirming their importance for circular features and closely spaced misaligned features. Overall, all advanced primitives contribute to the final performance.

    Reward component ablations. Disabling individual reward terms hurts either success rate or mesh quality in each ablation variant. The angle-based terms mainly affect quality consistency, so both face-corner-angle and dihedral-angle regularization remain important. Removing the internal face-boundary-loop term decreases the decomposition success rate, suggesting that this regularization helps discourage structurally unfavorable intermediate blocks, whereas removing the extreme-geometry term lowers the fraction of high-quality elements. Excluding the meshability term degrades both SR and hexahedral mesh quality, indicating that block-level meshability information provides useful guidance beyond local split validity.

    IV-D3 Reward Weight Sensitivity

    Fig. 16 shows reward-weight sensitivity across the four reported metrics: SR, J>0.8, \minJₛ, and Mean Reward. Each heatmap organizes the results by reward term and scaling factor. The center band reports the default DecompRL value once, while the outer cells show the signed change induced by 0.7× and 1.3× scaling.

    IV-D4 Depth-Discount Sensitivity

    We compare depth-discount configurations on the fixed Fusion360 test set under identical environment settings and a decision budget of 8 steps (Table VI). The default configuration uses λ_d=0.90 and γ=0.95. Here, λ_d scales the immediate reward by tree depth, whereas γ discounts future child-state values. SR measures complete-model conforming all-hexahedral meshing success within the budget. Average tree depth is the mean of the maximum decomposition-tree depth per evaluated model, and average steps is the mean number of executed decision steps. The high-aspect-ratio leaf percentage is computed over all accepted leaf blocks across the evaluated models, counting those whose oriented-bounding-box dimensions satisfy \min(L)/\max(L)<0.05.

    Removing depth decay reduces SR from 59.6% to 47.2%, a decrease of 12.4 percentage points, while increasing mean maximum tree depth from 2.8 to 3.8 and mean decision steps from 5.77 to 7.2. The high-aspect-ratio leaf percentage also increases from 4.1% to 14.6%. Stronger depth decay (λ_d=0.80) yields an SR of 56.5%, while reducing γ to 0.90 with the default depth discount yields 58.2%. Among the tested configurations, the default achieves the highest SR, and configurations with depth decay produce shallower trees than the configuration without depth decay.

    IV-EEfficiency Analysis (RQ4)

    Fig. 17 compares DecompRL decomposition time with the complete measured LMFF procedure on the same CAD models. DecompRL timing excludes subsequent hexahedral mesh generation. Figure (a) shows that decomposition times concentrate in the 10¹-second range, whereas the LMFF procedure largely occupies the 10²–10³-second range. Figure (b), labeled Speedup, reports the corresponding runtime ratio. The ranked curve remains well above 1×, with a median ratio of 41.8× and a P90 ratio of 103.4×; the maximum ratio reaches two orders of magnitude. These ratios compare the stated stages and are not end-to-end meshing speedups. The LMFF comparison in this study is intended primarily as an efficiency reference. The available paired evidence does not support a dataset-wide quantitative comparison of final scaled-Jacobian distributions under identical successful-meshing conditions, so we do not infer mesh-quality superiority over LMFF from the runtime results. Quantitative SR and mesh-quality comparisons are therefore reported for the learning-based methods under the unified protocol, while LMFF is retained for runtime and representative qualitative meshing comparison.

    Fig. 18 compares refined and coarse meshes generated from the same CAD model. Once a valid block decomposition is available, adjusting mesh resolution becomes straightforward. In contrast, frame-field-based pipelines couple mesh resolution to field construction, integer-grid-map generation, and mesh extraction, so refinement is rarely a purely local modification and often requires rerunning part of the pipeline.

    Table VII reports per-dataset decomposition diagnostics under the fixed N=200 setting. Here, Steps denotes the decomposition length, Leaves the number of exported leaf blocks, and Valid ratio the fraction of generated candidates that pass feasibility filtering. Across ABC, Fusion360, and NIST, the policy averages roughly 5–6 steps, well below the step budget of 8, indicating that it learns to stop early rather than over-decompose. DeepCAD requires the fewest splits (1.96 on average), consistent with its simpler geometries and near-saturated SR.

    V Conclusion

    This paper presents DecompRL, a DRL framework for CAD model decomposition toward hexahedral meshing. Our approach combines topology-aware splitting actions with a meshability term in the reward, allowing the policy to progressively split complex CAD models into simpler sub-blocks that support hexahedral meshing. Experimental results on four public CAD benchmarks show numerically higher decomposition success rates for DecompRL on three datasets, with the largest gain on Fusion360 and more modest differences on ABC and NIST; DDPG achieves a slightly higher rate on DeepCAD. On successfully meshed outputs, DecompRL also maintains competitive hexahedral element quality.

    Several limitations remain. The design of the action space is important for hexahedral decomposition, and incorporating richer action primitives may further improve the coverage of geometric configurations that can be successfully decomposed. The current action generators are primarily designed for mechanical CAD with recognizable analytic geometric structures and do not include dedicated decomposition primitives for arbitrary free-form NURBS/B-spline regions. Extending candidate generation with curvature-aware patch analysis or feature-line structures is therefore an important direction. Similarly, although the O-grid action is geometrically related to O-block layouts used in CFD, the present method does not model CFD-specific requirements such as boundary-layer growth, wall-normal alignment, or anisotropic spacing; incorporating such constraints would be required for CFD-oriented use. In addition, future work could improve training efficiency, sample efficiency, and convergence stability, especially for deeper decomposition trees and more complex CAD models.

    These results should not be interpreted as a guarantee of complete, globally conforming hexahedral meshing for arbitrary CAD inputs. Local Map/Submap/Sweep compatibility does not alone establish model-level meshing success. A finite decomposition budget, early splitting decisions that restrict later feasible actions, partial geometric observations, and the limited coverage of the current action templates can all contribute to unresolved or non-meshable regions. Further work will include systematic failure analysis across geometric and topological complexity, validation of local compatibility labels against downstream meshing outcomes, and stronger resolution-aware shared-interface and interval-consistency checks.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 微软 Auto SR 正式上车掌机：1080p、Auto HDR，新增 Performance Mode 把上限从 60–75 拉到 120 FPS ｜ Auto SR Officially Launches on ROG XBOX Ally X and X20, Expands to Copilot+ PCs
item.description:
一句话：系统级 ML 超分从预览走向出货，指标是帧率而不是画质榜。

要点：

  • 状态变化：Automatic Super Resolution（Auto SR）从预览转为**正式发布**，首批落在 ROG XBOX Ally X / X20 与部分 Copilot+ PC（AMD Ryzen）
  • 新增能力：支持**掌机电池模式**下的运行、支持 **1080p** 游戏、兼容 Auto HDR
  • 新的 Performance Mode 把上限从约 60–75 FPS 提到**最多 120 FPS**，可在 Game Bar 里实时切换模式看帧率变化

为什么值得看：系统级 ML 超分不是研究话题，但它决定了「AI 渲染」在消费级硬件上的默认形态：走 OS 层、不走游戏引擎。对引擎团队来说，这意味着要和系统级方案共存——什么时候该用自家 TAAU/FSR，什么时候直接交给系统，是被这条新闻逼出来的工程问题。

中文摘要：微软的 Automatic Super Resolution（Auto SR）结束预览，正式在 ROG XBOX Ally X / X20 以及部分搭载 AMD Ryzen 的 Copilot+ PC 上发布。此次带来的能力包括：支持掌机拔电（电池）模式运行、支持 1080p 游戏、兼容 Auto HDR；此外新增 Performance Mode，把帧率上限从原先约 60–75 FPS 提高到最多 120 FPS，并可在 Game Bar 中实时切换模式观察帧率变化。值得注意的是这类 ML 超分走的是操作系统层而非引擎层，因此对引擎团队而言，真正的问题变成「何时用自家时域上采样、何时直接交给系统」。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：DirectX Dev Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-12

Product Manager II

We’re excited to officially bring Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR) out of preview on the ROG XBOX Ally X and the ROG XBOX Ally X20. AutoSR is also now available on select Windows Copilot+ PCs, powered by AMD Ryzen, with several major new features beginning to roll out today.  

This release brings handheld play (undocked on battery), support for games running at 1080p, compatibility with Auto HDR and a new Performance Mode that can run up to 120 FPS. Handheld play, expanded support for Windows Copilot+ PCs powered by AMD Ryzen, and 1080p support are available today, while Performance Mode and Auto HDR support will be rolling out with Windows updates so they may take a little time to reach your device.

Performance Mode: Up To 120 FPS

Until now, Auto SR topped out around 60 to 75 FPS. We hinted at increasing this capability in our last post, and today we’re introducing a new Performance Mode.It raises the limit to up to 120 FPS, almost double what was possible before, so fast-paced and competitive games can feel even smoother. 

Switch between modes on the fly in Game Bar and watch your framerate change in real time for the right balance for each game.

Screenshots and FPS numbers from Rocket League gameplay on ROG XBOX Ally X at 720p on high in-game graphics setting

First image: Auto SR in Quality Mode averaging 70 FPS.

Second image: Auto SR in PerformanceMode averaging115 FPS.

Play in Handheld Mode (Undocked/Internal Screen)

During the XBOX Insider preview, players could use Auto SR only while docked. We started there because that’s where Auto SR makes the biggest difference: 1440p-like detail alongside smooth framerates on larger screens where every frame matters. By popular demand, Auto SR now also works in handheld mode, right on your device’s built-in screen, even when you’re unplugged and playing on battery. The next time a demanding game feels a little choppy on the go, Auto SR can help smooth things out, no dock required.

Support for 1080p Base Resolution

Many games on your handheld run at 1080p by default to match the built-in screen. During the preview, you had to lower a game’s resolution before Auto SR could kick in, an extra step that was easy to miss and a common reason Auto SR didn’t turn on. Now Auto SR will work with games running at 1080p. Dock to a higher-resolution TV or monitor, and it can upscale your game up to 1440p for a sharper picture on the big screen, with fewer settings to change. 

*Note:When using 1080p in handheld mode (internal screen), performance may not be as optimal as other configurations, but you’ll still see visual quality improvements especially in older games.

Auto SR and Auto HDR now work together

Auto HDR is a Windows feature that brings brighter highlights and richer colors to games without native HDR support when you play on an HDR display. Until now, you had to choose between Auto SR and Auto HDR. Now they work together, so you can enjoy sharper, smoother gameplay and vivid HDR visuals at the same time, whether on an HDR TV, monitor or ROG XBOX Ally X20.

Help shape Auto SR

A huge thank you to the XBOX Insider community for using Auto SR since its entered preview. Your feedback directly shaped this release, and we’d love to keep hearing from you. 

How is it working in your games? How does the setup and control feel?

→ Tell us atautosr@microsoft.com

Issues: Report via Feedback Hub >Game Performance> add “Auto SR”in the title

Category

  • Auto SR
  • DirectX

    • Topics

  • DirectX
  • DirectX 12 Ultimate

    • Author

    Product Manager II

    Product Manager, AI Models

    Join the discussion.

    Sort by :Newest

    Stay informed

    Get notified when new posts are published.Follow this blog

Switch between modes on the fly in Game Bar and watch your framerate change in real time for the right balance for each game.

Screenshots and FPS numbers from Rocket League gameplay on ROG XBOX Ally X at 720p on high in-game graphics setting

First image: Auto SR in Quality Mode averaging 70 FPS.

Second image: Auto SR in PerformanceMode averaging115 FPS.

Play in Handheld Mode (Undocked/Internal Screen)

During the XBOX Insider preview, players could use Auto SR only while docked. We started there because that’s where Auto SR makes the biggest difference: 1440p-like detail alongside smooth framerates on larger screens where every frame matters. By popular demand, Auto SR now also works in handheld mode, right on your device’s built-in screen, even when you’re unplugged and playing on battery. The next time a demanding game feels a little choppy on the go, Auto SR can help smooth things out, no dock required.

Support for 1080p Base Resolution

Many games on your handheld run at 1080p by default to match the built-in screen. During the preview, you had to lower a game’s resolution before Auto SR could kick in, an extra step that was easy to miss and a common reason Auto SR didn’t turn on. Now Auto SR will work with games running at 1080p. Dock to a higher-resolution TV or monitor, and it can upscale your game up to 1440p for a sharper picture on the big screen, with fewer settings to change. 

*Note:When using 1080p in handheld mode (internal screen), performance may not be as optimal as other configurations, but you’ll still see visual quality improvements especially in older games.

Auto SR and Auto HDR now work together

Auto HDR is a Windows feature that brings brighter highlights and richer colors to games without native HDR support when you play on an HDR display. Until now, you had to choose between Auto SR and Auto HDR. Now they work together, so you can enjoy sharper, smoother gameplay and vivid HDR visuals at the same time, whether on an HDR TV, monitor or ROG XBOX Ally X20.

Help shape Auto SR

A huge thank you to the XBOX Insider community for using Auto SR since its entered preview. Your feedback directly shaped this release, and we’d love to keep hearing from you. 

How is it working in your games? How does the setup and control feel?

→ Tell us atautosr@microsoft.com
