一句话：各家引擎微分的数学对象并不相同，而文献常把两个不同问题混为一谈。

要点：

  • 用途链条：可微仿真把导数穿过物理模拟器，让动画、系统辨识、控制与计算设计都变成基于梯度的优化问题
  • 隐藏差异：不同引擎不仅在「模拟什么物理」上不同，更在**微分哪个数学对象**上不同
  • 综述把常被混淆的两个问题分开：导数归属于谁（实际执行的有限计算、它近似的收敛方程，还是背后的连续动力学），以及梯度是否真的正确

为什么值得看：可微仿真出现的「梯度看着能用但收敛到错地方」的问题，多半来自这两个问题被混着谈。做物理驱动动画或神经物理时，这份分类能当检查清单用。

中文摘要：可微仿真把导数穿过物理模拟器，使动画、系统辨识、控制与计算设计都能表述成基于梯度的优化。但不同引擎之间不仅「模拟的物理」不同，更隐蔽的差异在于它们**微分的数学对象**并不相同。这份综述把文献中常被混为一谈的两个问题拆开：一是引用对象（referent）——返回的导数究竟属于实际执行的那段有限计算、它近似的收敛方程，还是背后的连续动力学；二是梯度本身是否正确。把这两件事分开之后，「梯度能算但优化收敛到错处」这类现象才有可解释的分类。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-12

Same Physics, Different Gradients:
A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation

Lei Shu1, Zizhou Huang2, Yunuo Chen3, Yifei Li4, Tao Du5, Minchen Li6, Tuur Stuyck7, Miles Macklin7, Kui Wu8, Bo Zhu9, Yin Yang10, Ming C. Lin11, Alberta Longhini1, Rika Antonova12, Leonidas Guibas1, Gordon Wetzstein1, Jeannette Bohg1 and Chenfanfu Jiang3

1Stanford University2Courant Institute, New York University3University of California, Los Angeles4Massachusetts Institute of Technology

5Tsinghua University6Carnegie Mellon University7NVIDIA8LightSpeed Studios, Tencent America

9Georgia Institute of Technology10University of Utah11University of Maryland, College Park12University of Cambridge

Abstract

Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered.

Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth.

We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

Keywords: differentiable simulation, adjoint methods, automatic differentiation, physics-based animation, contact, inverse problems, survey.

.  Introduction

Physically based animation is built on a forward map. A scene is described by geometry and their parameters θ (masses, stiffnesses, rest shapes, friction coefficients, control signals, boundary conditions), and a time integrator advances a state sₜ to sₜ₊₁ until a trajectory has been produced. Four decades of graphics research have made this map fast, stable, and expressive enough to carry feature films and real-time games.

Most of the questions practitioners ask, however, run in the opposite direction. An animator wants the wind field that makes a piece of cloth do what the storyboard says, an engineer wants the gripper geometry that achieves a grasp, and a vision researcher wants the material parameters that explain a video of a falling object. Each of these is an inverse problem posed on top of a forward simulator, and simulator derivatives often make its solution substantially more efficient, particularly when the number of optimization variables is large.

Differentiable simulation is the practice of making those derivatives available. Spacetime constraints [WK88, Coh92] posed trajectory authoring as a constrained optimization over a discretized trajectory, and keyframe control of smoke and of particle systems [TMPS03, MTPS04, WMT06] differentiated the discrete fluid solvers directly and a cloth solver through a swapped integrator, both long before the term existed; the same period produced gradient-driven and sampling-driven methods for steering rigid-body simulations toward authored outcomes [PSE∗00, PSE03, TJ08]. More recently, general-purpose automatic differentiation (AD) frameworks [PGM∗19, BFH∗18], GPU-resident simulation, and domain-specific compilers [HLA∗19, HAL∗20] have expanded the scale and range of simulators for which derivatives can be computed efficiently, and a large, fast-moving literature has grown around the possibility.

Two gaps run through that literature, and together they organize this report. The first is between the derivative an engine computes and the derivative its user expects: differentiating the finite solver and differentiating the equation it approximates target different mathematical objects. Their agreement requires conditions on both the forward solution and its sensitivities. The second is between obtaining a derivative and obtaining useful optimization progress. Even an exact gradient can be ineffective for finite-step optimization, while pathwise derivatives can be biased estimators for stochastic objectives with discontinuities. Neither difficulty is universal; identifying the regimes in which a returned derivative is both appropriate and useful is a central purpose of this report.

The two gaps are not equally consequential. The first decides what a method is entitled to claim, and it is always a question of fact: an engine either returns the derivative of what it ran or it does not. How much that costs an optimizer is a separate matter, and our own measurement in Section 7 finds the cost concentrated at the tightest solver budgets, and how far above them it persists to depend on where the fitting target comes from. The referent decides what you may claim and whether a gradient check can pass, while the horizon, the contact treatment and the conditioning usually decide whether the optimization works.

Beyond its size, the literature is difficult to navigate because two papers may both claim to present “a differentiable simulator” for deformable bodies with contact, agree on the physical model, agree on the discretization, and still compute meaningfully different derivatives, because they differentiate different mathematical objects. Neither is thereby incorrect. One may backpropagate through every Newton iteration that was executed; another may apply the implicit function theorem to the equation those iterations were trying to solve. For a smooth, locally regular solution branch, the two sensitivities approach one another when both the iterates and their parameter sensitivities converge to that branch. A small forward residual alone does not establish agreement, and disagreement at a finite iteration budget is a consequence of the differentiated object rather than necessarily an implementation error. Comparisons that ignore this distinction end up attributing to the physics, or to the contact model, differences that originate in the differentiation strategy.

.1.  Scope

This report surveys differentiable physics simulation: methods that propagate derivatives through the numerical solution of the equations of motion of rigid bodies, articulated systems, deformable solids, cloth, and fluids. We treat differentiable rendering as adjacent rather than in scope. It is a mature subfield with its own surveys and courses [KBM∗20, ZJL20], its discontinuities are of a different character (visibility rather than contact), and the techniques developed for them [LADL18, LHJ19, VSJ22] address visibility boundaries; their applicability to contact requires separate analysis. Mitsuba 2 [NDVZJ19] provides infrastructure for differentiable rendering; visibility derivatives are addressed in separate work. We do discuss the seam where the two meet (Section 9.5), because video-to-physics pipelines require both and because the composition raises questions neither field answers alone.

We also distinguish differentiable simulation from learned simulation. Graph-network surrogates [BPL∗16, SGGP∗20, PFSGB21, LWT∗19, GBH23], structure-preserving networks [CGH∗20], and physics-informed networks [RPK19] often expose derivatives through their neural components, and a learned surrogate can serve as the forward model of a PDE-constrained inverse problem, with the inverse solved by gradient descent through the network [ZLW22]. Their rollouts may nevertheless require differentiation through numerical integration, and discrete structural operations may introduce additional difficulties. We reference these models where they interact with numerical solvers, as surrogates, correction terms, or baselines, but do not survey learned simulators as a separate class.

.2.  Contributions

This report contributes:

  • •

    A two-axis taxonomy (Section 4) separating the referent of a derivative from the realization of its backward pass. The referent defines the target for an exactness claim; the realization and a separate state-recovery policy determine the computational and storage costs. Crossing these choices explains why exactness and low memory are not fundamentally incompatible, and identifies the assumptions and costs of the methods that combine them.

  • •

    An orthogonal taxonomy of discontinuity treatments (Section 5) for contact, friction, and collision, classifying methods by the mathematical fiction they adopt where the true map is non-smooth, and by the bias and variance that fiction introduces.

  • •

    A critical account of gradient quality (Section 7) that separates derivative correctness from practical optimization progress, identifies four distinct mechanisms that impair gradient-based optimization, and maps published mitigations onto them.

  • •

    A cross-cutting comparison of physical model families (Section 6), systems techniques (Section 8), and engines (Table 7) on a common set of axes.

  • •

    A reporting checklist (Section 10) that would make differentiable simulators comparable, and a research agenda (Section 11) organized around the gaps the taxonomy exposes.

    • .  Related Surveys, Literature Selection, and Organization

    .1.  Related surveys

    Differentiable simulation has been reviewed before, most directly by Newbury et al.[NCH∗24], who discuss gradient construction, dynamics and contact models, integrators, engines, and robotics applications, and, as one strand of a broader tutorial treatment of physics-based deep learning, by Thuerey et al.[THH∗21]. We refine this mechanism-oriented view by separating derivative referents, backward realizations, and state recovery. These distinctions help explain computational cost, failure modes, and differences that are obscured by engine-level comparisons. They also remain useful as software packages change. We give particular attention to whether the returned derivatives improve the optimization for which they are computed, drawing on evidence of challenging regimes [MFSK21, SSZT22] rather than assuming that derivative availability guarantees useful progress.

    .2.  Literature selection

    Differentiable simulation is developed in parallel in graphics, robotics and machine learning, so we searched DBLP, Crossref, arXiv, the ACM Digital Library and Google Scholar for differentiable, gradient-based or adjoint combined with simulation, physics, solver, contact, cloth, fluid and related task terms, and then followed the references and citations of each included work. Expansion stopped when a full round added no new differentiation strategy, contact treatment or application class. A work was included if it contributes a differentiable simulator or component, provides evidence about one, or supplies background the argument depends on. Work that is differentiable only because it is a neural network, and applications that use an engine without reporting on its derivatives, were excluded.

    .3.  Organization of this report

    Section 3 fixes notation and reviews the material the rest of the report assumes: the simulation map, forward and reverse mode, and the distinction between continuous and discrete adjoints. Section 4 develops the first taxonomy, separating the referent of a derivative from the realization of the backward pass, and is the conceptual core of the report; Table 2 crosses the two axes and Section 4.4 gives guidance on choosing a cell. Section 5 develops the second, orthogonal taxonomy for contact and other discontinuities, summarized in Table 3. Readers interested only in the classification may stop after these two sections.

    Section 6 surveys the physical model families through the lens of the two taxonomies, and Section 7 takes up gradient quality, which we regard as the most consequential and least settled part of the subject. Section 8 covers systems and implementation and compares the major engines in Table 7. Section 9 surveys applications, Section 10 evaluation practice and our proposed reporting checklist, and Section 11 the open problems the taxonomy exposes.

    .  Background and Notation

    This section fixes the notation used throughout, collected in Table 1, and the two distinctions the rest of the report rests on: forward against reverse mode, and the continuous against the discrete adjoint.

    .1.  The simulation map

    We write a simulation as a composition of T time steps. A step advances the state sₜ∈ℝⁿ, typically positions and velocities sₜ=(xₜ,vₜ), under parameters θ∈ℝᵖ. We fold into θ whatever is being optimized, including a control sequence or the weights of a controller that emits one; in the latter case a step depends on θ through the control it receives, and the form below is unchanged:

    sₜ₊₁=Φ(sₜ;θ), t=0,…,T-1.

    		(1)

    Explicit time dependence is suppressed in the notation: Φ may denote Φₜ, for example when selecting the control at step t from a sequence. All step Jacobians below refer to that step’s map. An objective L is evaluated on the trajectory, either terminally or as a running cost, and the quantity we want is dL/dθ.

    A central difficulty is that the time step is often specified by equations that must be solved numerically. Explicit schemes evaluate update formulas directly, although stiffness can impose restrictive time steps. Many implicit schemes used for stiff cloth and constrained systems [BW98] instead define the next state through a residual equation,

    g(sₜ₊₁;sₜ,θ)=0.

    		(2)

    Semi-implicit schemes may use explicit sequential updates or linear solves and need not require a nonlinear solve. For variational formulations with an appropriate incremental potential, a step can instead be characterized as a selected local minimizer of E(s;sₜ,θ). This characterization is not equivalent to an arbitrary residual equation.

    A simulator runs neither of these directly. It runs a solver for them: Newton with a linear solve, projective dynamics [BML∗14], Gauss–Seidel or Jacobi sweeps, extended position-based dynamics (XPBD) projections [MMC16], block coordinate descent [CLYY24], or, for a grid fluid, a pressure projection whose Poisson system is solved by conjugate gradients to a tolerance. It runs for a finite and usually small number of iterations.

    The three referents of Section 4 diverge in this gap between (1) and (2), between the step we write down and the finite computation we execute.

    .2.  Forward and reverse mode

    Given the per-step Jacobians, the chain rule assembles the trajectory derivative. For now, assume that s₀ is independent of θ and that L depends on θ only through the trajectory. Writing Aₜ=∂Φ/∂sₜ and Bₜ=∂Φ/∂θ evaluated at step t, the sensitivity of the final state is

    (ds_T)/(dθ)=∑ₜ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹A_T-1A_T-2⋯Aₜ₊₁Bₜ,

    		(3)

    where the factors are ordered by descending index, as the non-commuting product requires. An empty product is the identity, so the t=T-1 summand is B_T-1. The two modes of accumulation differ in which end of that product they start from. Beginning at the parameter end, with Bₜ, and multiplying by each Aₖ as k increases is forward mode: it propagates an n×p sensitivity matrix alongside the state as time advances, costing O(p) simulation-equivalents but requiring no storage of history. Beginning instead at the objective end and multiplying backward in time is reverse mode, or the discrete adjoint: one introduces an adjoint state s̄ₜ=(dL/dsₜ)^⊤, the total derivative of the objective with respect to the state at step t including everything downstream of it. Initialize s̄_T=(∂L/∂s_T)^⊤ and θ̄=0, and sweep backward for t=T-1,…,0,

    s̄ₜ=Aₜ^⊤s̄ₜ₊₁+((∂L)/(∂sₜ))^⊤, θ̄\mathrel+=Bₜ^⊤s̄ₜ₊₁,

    		(4)

    where the second term is the direct dependence of a running cost on sₜ and vanishes for a terminal objective, costing O(1) simulation-equivalents independent of p, but requiring access to the forward trajectory in reverse order. If the initial state is parameterized, (3) additionally contains A_T-1⋯A₀ ds₀/dθ, and the parameter gradient includes (ds₀/dθ)^⊤s̄₀. If the objective is extended to include direct parameter dependence, also add (∂L/∂θ)^⊤ to the column gradient.

    For the inverse problems that motivate differentiable simulation, p is large (a per-element material field, a control sequence, a mesh parameterization) and L is scalar, so reverse mode is the relevant regime and its memory cost is the binding constraint. This asymmetry between computational work and storage motivates the systems discussion of Section 8; checkpointing [GW00] is a common way to make reverse accumulation feasible when a full tape cannot be retained (Table 7).

    A thorough treatment of AD itself is outside our scope; see Griewank and Walther [GW08] for the standard reference, and Baydin et al.[BPRS18] and Margossian [Mar19] for surveys; for the broader program of differentiable programming in scientific computing, see Innes et al.[IEF∗19] and the position piece of Ramsundar et al.[RKV21].

    .3.  Two adjoints: continuous and discrete

    The PDE-constrained optimization literature distinguishes two ways to form an adjoint, and the distinction recurs under other names throughout this report. One may differentiate then discretize: derive the adjoint PDE analytically from the continuous equations of motion, then discretize that adjoint. Or one may discretize then differentiate: take the discrete forward scheme as the definition and differentiate it exactly.

    A continuous adjoint is derived before choosing its discretization. For a scalar objective, its evaluation often costs a small number of forward solves and is largely independent of the number of design parameters, while still depending on mesh resolution, time stepping, and solver accuracy. A separately discretized continuous adjoint need not equal the derivative of the chosen discrete forward map. This mismatch can impair optimization and finite-difference agreement; it does not necessarily correspond to the gradient of another scalar objective. Consistent forward–adjoint discretizations can remove the mismatch in appropriate settings [MMY21].

    A discrete adjoint instead differentiates a specified discrete object. That object may be the discrete equations or the finite solver used to approximate them, which is the distinction developed in Section 4.1. McNamara et al.[MTPS04] explicitly select a discrete formulation, treating projection and diffusion as linear operators. Agreement with finite differences therefore depends on the differentiated object, solver accuracy, and the usual smoothness and finite-difference conditions.

    Most methods surveyed here differentiate discrete objects. In physically based differentiable rendering, methods such as Li et al.[LADL18] first derive the rendering-integral derivative, including visibility-boundary terms, and then construct Monte Carlo estimators. This provides a related example of differentiating before numerical estimation.

    .  A Two-Axis Taxonomy of Backward Passes

    This section states the organizing claim of this report. Consider a stiff implicit step: the integrator defines sₜ₊₁ as a root of (2), and a solver produces an approximation to that root in K iterations. Two questions are needed to interpret a returned gradient, and the literature often answers only the second while appearing to answer the first.

    Which object is the derivative of?

    The finite computation the solver actually executed, the exact root that computation was approximating, or the continuous dynamics the discretization itself approximates. We call this the referent, and it decides what “exact” can mean.

    How is the backward pass realized?

    By recording the forward computation and generating its reverse operations, by solving equation-level adjoint systems, or by supplying custom operator adjoints. We call this the realization; together with state recovery it determines the cost.

    These are distinct questions: a referent can admit several implementations, and a realization can serve more than one referent. Our realization labels are operational categories rather than an exhaustive Cartesian product of construction choices, as Section 4.2 makes explicit. Two methods can target the same derivative by different means, or target different derivatives while both referring to “the gradient.” Table 2 crosses the labels; we call this the referent/realization distinction.

    .1.  Axis A: the referent

    A1, the executed computation.

    Treat the step as the literal sequence of K solver iterations and differentiate that computation. On a differentiable execution branch, with correct derivative rules, this targets the sensitivity of the output produced by the forward pass whether or not the solve converged. It is the referent directly tested by finite differences of the production configuration, subject to truncation error, roundoff, and stability of the execution branch.

    One qualification is used throughout the tables. A step often contains a linear solve run to a tolerance, a pressure projection or the inner solve of a Newton iteration, whose derivative the backward pass takes as that of the exact linear operator rather than of the iterations that approximated it. We mark such methods A1*: exact for an idealized program in which the linear solves are exact operators, which is not the program that ran. How far the derivative of that idealization is from the derivative of the finite-tolerance program is not given by the solver tolerance alone, since the conditioning of the system and the sensitivity of the residual to the parameters enter as well, and it is to be checked at the production configuration like any other gap; a finite-difference check of an A1* method is subject to that gap as well as finite-difference and floating-point error. The unqualified label is kept for programs whose every solve is differentiated as it ran. The referent distinction of this section emphasizes truncated nonlinear iteration, where the sensitivities can differ substantially; the asterisk records that reading a linear solve as exact is an assumption.

    The guarantee is narrower than often stated: it is exact for the executed program, not for the physics. A program containing a branch, a discrete collision-detection query, or a non-differentiable primitive returns the derivative of the branch that was taken, or a convention chosen by the framework at a kink. Nor is such an object guaranteed to be a subgradient. With the common convention ReLU^′(0)=0, differentiating the identity written as ReLU(x)-ReLU(-x) returns 0 at the origin, where the function is differentiable with derivative 1; the composition rule is not required to land in the subdifferential of the composite. What AD returns at a kink depends on local derivative conventions and need not be a derivative of the composite function; calling it “the true sensitivity” without qualification overstates what was computed.

    A2, the converged equation.

    Treat the step as a selected root of (2). If the residual is continuously differentiable near that root and its state Jacobian is nonsingular, the implicit function theorem gives the local root sensitivity:

    (∂sₜ₊₁)/(∂θ)=-((∂g)/(∂sₜ₊₁))⁻¹(∂g)/(∂θ),

    		(5)

    with sₜ held fixed, so the left-hand side is the step Jacobian Bₜ of Section 3.2. Nothing about the solver trajectory enters. The following distinction is used throughout the report. At the exact root, (5) gives the sensitivity of that root branch. An implementation typically evaluates the formula at the state where the solver stopped and solves the adjoint system only to a finite tolerance. Three quantities must therefore be distinguished: the converged-root derivative targeted by A2, the vector returned by the implemented implicit backward pass, and the derivative of the finite computation targeted by A1. These quantities generally differ at finite tolerances, although equality is possible in special cases. Their discrepancy depends on local conditioning and residual sensitivities, as well as forward and adjoint solve accuracy. Jacobian modifications introduce another approximation; for example, DiffXPBD [SC23] projects derivative blocks to be positive definite. Section 7 compares the returned equation-level vector with the derivative of the executed computation and measures their optimization consequences.

    This is the referent of the optimization-layer literature, where OptNet [AK17] differentiates a quadratic program through its Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, cvxpylayers[AAB∗19] generalizes this to convex cones, deep equilibrium models [BKK19] differentiate a fixed point without unrolling it, and modular libraries [BBC∗22] package the pattern.

    In interactive simulation, the forward solver is often stopped at a small iteration budget. The resulting state is then the output of the finite solver, whereas A2 targets a root of its defining equation. Evaluating the implicit derivative at this state generally approximates that root sensitivity and need not match the derivative of the finite solver. Section 7 examines this distinction at the iteration budgets used by the forward simulation.

    The dependence on convergence is quantitative. Under appropriate local regularity conditions, inexact implicit differentiation and residual-correction analyses can bound the error using forward and adjoint residuals together with conditioning constants. For a smooth, uniformly attractive fixed-point map with suitable derivative regularity, Christianson [Chr94] shows that an adjoint iteration evaluated at the final forward state converges at a rate controlled by the contraction factor. This result does not establish derivative accuracy from the forward stopping tolerance alone. Reporting a bound or an empirical sensitivity check at the production solver configuration would make the practical approximation explicit.

    A3, the continuous dynamics.

    Derive the adjoint of the continuous equations of motion and then discretize that adjoint. A separately chosen adjoint discretization need not produce the derivative of the chosen discrete forward map, so agreement with finite differences of that map is not automatic. Appropriate paired discretizations can recover consistency [MMY21]. The continuous formulation remains useful when the discretization changes with the design or when the continuous problem is the intended optimization target.

    The early graphics adjoints should not all be assigned to A3. McNamara et al.[MTPS04] explicitly choose a discrete adjoint, treating their linear projection and diffusion solves as exact operators; this is A1* under our convention. Treuille et al.[TMPS03] differentiate the steps of their discrete fluid simulation. Wojtan et al.[WMT06] use an integrator-swapping approximation, deriving a fully implicit adjoint for a linearized-implicit cloth forward solver. Li et al.[LHB∗25] take a continuous route for flow maps. The classification follows what each method differentiates rather than its use of the word adjoint.

    Outside graphics the row is well populated, and the machine-learning literature has already compared continuous and discrete adjoints in practice. Neural ODEs [CRBD18] are an A3 method in the strict sense: rather than backpropagating through the ODE solver, which the paper considers and rejects for its memory cost, they treat the solver as a black box and use an approach that “computes gradients by solving a second, augmented ODE backwards in time”, an adjoint derived from the continuous dynamics and discretized afterward. Later work outside graphics shows the consequences of the referent distinction. Gholaminejad et al.[GKB19] showed that this “optimize-then-discretize approach may lead to divergent training due to inconsistent gradients for small time step sizes”, and proposed recovering consistency by differentiating the discretization instead, at the cost of storing or recomputing the forward trajectory; Zhuang et al.[ZDL∗20] reach the same conclusion from the checkpointing side, finding that “the adjoint method has numerical errors in reverse-mode integration” and recovering accuracy by checkpointing. These studies expose two distinct numerical issues: inconsistency between the continuous and discrete adjoints, and instability when reconstructing the forward trajectory by backward integration. Checkpointing addresses state reconstruction, while differentiating the discrete scheme or using a consistent forward–adjoint pair addresses the derivative mismatch. A fixed production discretization makes consistency with that discretization a natural objective; continuous adjoints remain useful when the continuous model is the desired target or the mesh changes with the design.

    .2.  Axis B: the realization

    The realization describes how the backward pass is organized. Two useful attributes are how derivatives are constructed (automatically, manually, or by a hybrid of the two) and what computation produces them, such as reversing operations or solving adjoint equations. Locality and state recovery are further attributes; neither follows from who writes the code.

    We retain three operational categories for the systems comparison: B1 for automatically generated differentiation, B2 for equation-level sensitivity or adjoint solves, and B3 for custom operator-level adjoints. These labels are not a Cartesian product of construction and locality. B2 includes both implicit derivatives of discrete equations and discretized continuous sensitivity or adjoint equations. When this equation-level solve organizes the backward pass, B2 takes precedence regardless of how its Jacobians are constructed. Exact linear primitives inside an otherwise differentiated program are recorded by A1*. Locality-aware AD [MGRKS26] illustrates that automatic construction can exploit mesh structure without by itself establishing a complete block-local simulator backward pass.

    Labelling rule.

    Tables 4 and 5 were labeled by the following procedure, stated so that it can be applied to an engine we have not seen.

  • 1.

    Unit. The label describes the organization of the backward pass of one time step as a whole, not every operator inside it. A hand-derived adjoint that calls automatic differentiation for a local Jacobian-vector product, or a tape that wraps a hand-written kernel, keeps the label of its organizing structure.

  • 2.

    Referent. Identify the nonlinear solve the step runs and ask whether the backward pass differentiates its iterations (A1), the equation it was solving, by the implicit function theorem at whatever iterate was reached (A2), or a continuous model (A3). A linear solve run to tolerance, the pressure projection of a fluid step or the inner solve of a Newton step, that the backward pass differentiates as the exact operator makes the label A1*, exact for the idealized program in which that solve is exact; this is how ΦFlow appears in Table 5, its pressure solve differentiated as converged and the rest of its step as executed. A backward pass that deliberately differentiates a different model or objective is marked surr.; its surrogate referent is described explicitly rather than assigned to A1, A2, or A3 for the production forward map.

  • 3.

    Realization. Use B2 when the backward pass is organized around equation-level sensitivity or adjoint solves, including discretized continuous adjoint equations. Otherwise, use B1 for a backward pass generated by an AD framework or compiler, and B3 for custom operator-level adjoints. For B3, state whether the operators reverse discrete operations or implement a continuous adjoint; a continuous adjoint counts as B3 rather than B2 when its discretization is built on the forward solver’s own maps and structures rather than solved as a separate equation. In the A1/A1* operation-mirroring case, the backward pass can reuse the forward solver’s structure, including transposed linear solves; this is not a guarantee for every B3 method.

  • 4.

    Components. If a step combines different referents or realizations, identify the component motivating the primary label and state the remaining components in the note. For example, de Avila Belbute-Peres et al.[BPSA∗18], Liang et al.[LLK19], and Qiao et al.[QLKL20] combine framework differentiation with an implicitly differentiated contact or collision-response layer. Their primary label describes that layer, while the note records the surrounding differentiation. Computational cost can motivate which component is emphasized, but does not make the remaining components share its mathematical referent. List both when a single label would obscure this distinction.

  • 5.

    State. Record separately what the backward pass keeps (the State column), since the realization does not determine it.

    • A third question, where the state the backward pass linearizes at comes from, is kept out of this axis. The state must be held, recomputed from a checkpoint, or recovered by running the map backward, and that choice sets the storage asymptotics. It is orthogonal to both of the questions above (two methods identical in construction and in backward computation can differ in it by a factor of the solver depth), so it is reported separately, as its own column in Tables 4 and 5. Memory does not follow from a realization label.

    B1, recorded.

    Generate the backward pass with an AD framework or compiler, retaining or recomputing the intermediate values it needs. Fully stored reverse mode is one implementation, and the category spans a spectrum of engineering. At one end, simulators are written directly in an array framework such as PyTorch or JAX and inherit its generated reverse pass and residual-storage rules [PGM∗19, BFH∗18]; JAX MD [SC21] and Brax [FFR∗21] are prominent examples, the latter built around simple rigid-body physics so that thousands of unrolled environments run on an accelerator. At the other end are domain-specific compilers that generate adjoint code by source transformation. DiffTaichi [HAL∗20] is the canonical instance in graphics: it extends the Taichi language [HLA∗19] with a “megakernel” reverse mode that preserves the arithmetic intensity and parallelism of the forward kernels, which operator-level taping can fail to preserve. Its reported gains over an equivalent formulation in a general-purpose array framework are attributed by its authors to this structural preservation rather than to any difference in the mathematics. NVIDIA Warp [Mac22] follows a similar compiled-kernel philosophy, and Tiny Differentiable Simulator and its successors [HMC∗21] take the recorded route while embedding learned augmentations inside the engine rather than as residual corrections outside it. The most recent engines consolidate: Genesis [Gen24] and Newton [The25] both build a multi-physics, GPU-resident stack, differentiable for part of their physics, on a compiled-kernel foundation, and Newton in particular is built on Warp, one of the systems in Table 7. That consolidation means the realization axis is being settled by infrastructure decisions: whichever backward pass the shared substrate supports is the one most downstream work will use.

    Without recomputation, retaining O(n) data for each of K iterations over T steps requires O(TKn) memory. The actual tape constants and problem size determine whether this exceeds device capacity. Checkpointing [GW00] stores selected states and recomputes intervening segments. The optimality of a binomial schedule assumes a specified storage and execution-cost model, including a known step count; the achievable trade-off also depends on recomputation cost, checkpoint size, and whether the horizon is known in advance. Thus O(TKn) describes fully stored unrolling, not an unavoidable property of B1.

    The same trade-off drives the adjoint formulation of neural ODEs [CRBD18], for which checkpointing variants, one of them adaptive, exist [GKB19, ZDL∗20]. Compiler-level quantization of simulation state [HLY∗21] suggests a possible route to reduced-precision trajectory storage. That work evaluates quantized forward simulation; using such storage for a backward pass additionally requires analysis of reconstruction and gradient errors. Checkpointing also interacts badly with solvers whose iterates are not reproducible, such as anything using atomics with nondeterministic ordering or randomized sweep orders, because the recomputed segment is then a slightly different trajectory than the one differentiated, and keeping the executed-computation guarantee literally would require reproducing it bit for bit.

    Tool-built differentiation can also exploit structure. Several works [FFLW∗26, HSK24, THB∗26] show that derivative generation for mesh-based computation can be made more efficient, YASPS by making the mesh relations explicit in a differentiable intermediate representation. Symbolic and mesh-aware derivative generation can accelerate forward solvers; extending these structures to trajectory-level sensitivities requires additional backward-pass machinery. et al.[MGRKS26] demonstrate automatic locality-aware differentiation of mesh-based computations on the GPU: derivatives are taken per element by forward-mode AD, confined to registers and shared memory, and assembled into sparse gradients and Jacobians, so the tool exploits the mesh’s locality rather than treating the computation as a flat trace. That narrows the gap between a recorded and a rederived realization from the recorded side, and suggests the two are better seen as ends of a spectrum in how much forward structure the backward pass is allowed to know about.

    B2, resolved.

    Obtain sensitivities or adjoints by solving linear equations derived from the defining model, rather than reversing the finite nonlinear solver. For A2, (5) is evaluated at the final state, so the nonlinear solver’s K iterates need not be stored. For A3, continuous sensitivity or adjoint equations are discretized and solved; their trajectory-state requirements depend on the time integration and recovery policy. Real2Sim [HBBC19] and neural ODEs [CRBD18] are examples of this latter organization.

    Solving an A2 adjoint system does not require assembling or factorizing it. A matrix-free Krylov method needs only Jacobian-vector and vector-Jacobian products, which for most simulators are as cheap as a forward force evaluation, and this is how the approach scales to problems where an explicit Jacobian would not fit. For the A2 case, the required adjoint solve is defined by the equation or subsystem differentiated implicitly, and its coupling range follows from that subsystem, not from the label. When the equation is the whole implicit step, as for DiffPD, ADD or DiffXPBD, the system (5) couples every degree of freedom at once, and even matrix-free each Krylov iteration is a product over the whole mesh. When it is a contact layer, the solve couples the active set: Qiao et al.[QLKL20] apply it per impact zone, whose extent depends on the connected contact structure. The cost that follows is therefore a property of the whole-step case, and there it is a loss for forward methods whose performance argument is that they never form a global system: a Gauss–Seidel, XPBD or block coordinate descent step visits one vertex or constraint at a time and never couples the whole mesh in a single operation, while an equation-level backward pass for the same step does. For a forward method that already assembles and factorizes a global matrix, as Newton or projective dynamics does, the backward can reuse factorization work, as in DiffPD [DWM∗22], while its additional cost depends on the adjoint iterations and contact treatment; for one designed to avoid the global system, the backward pass introduces a coupling and a cost profile that the forward pass avoids. B2 also requires local regularity for classical implicit differentiation. Buckling and degenerate constraints can produce singular or ill-conditioned Jacobians, while contact transitions may instead invalidate smoothness or active-set stability. These conditions must be checked for the actual time-discrete system; static buckling does not by itself imply a singular dynamic-step Jacobian.

    B3, rederived.

    Construct custom operator-level adjoints using the structure of the differentiated model. In the A1/A1* operation-mirroring case, let s⁽ʲ⁾=Uⱼ(s⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾;θ) for j=1,…,m, and define Uⱼ^*(s̄;s⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾)=[DₛUⱼ(s⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾;θ)]^⊤s̄. The reverse sweep applies these Jacobian-transpose actions in the order j=m,…,1:

    s̄⁽⁰⁾=[DₛU₁]^⊤⋯[DₛUₘ]^⊤s̄⁽ᵐ⁾,

    		(6)

    with each Jacobian evaluated at its own forward input. Each reverse update also accumulates [D_θUⱼ]^⊤s̄⁽ʲ⁾ into the parameter gradient. For block-local updates this can avoid assembling an additional global adjoint system. Custom operators implementing a continuous adjoint form a separate A3 case and need not mirror discrete forward operations.

    For the discrete operation-mirroring case, B1 and B3 can differentiate the same object while differing in how the backward pass is constructed. B1 obtains it from an AD framework or compiler; B3 supplies custom operator adjoints. The latter can avoid a generic primitive-level tape but may still store states, replay data, and control-flow decisions. McNamara et al.[MTPS04] provide an example: they derive the adjoints of fluid-step stages by hand and apply them in reverse order, treating projection and diffusion as exact linear operators. Under our convention this is A1*×B3. A compiler-generated version with the same operators and derivative conventions can target the same derivative; finite-iteration and finite-tolerance implementations need to be checked separately. ADD [GHZ∗20], by contrast, uses an equation-level adjoint and is B2.

    B3 is broader than the block composition. Most of the entries Tables 2, 4 and 5 place under B3 mirror some other structure: the operation sequence of a fluid step, the recursion of an articulated-body algorithm, or custom continuous-adjoint operators for flow maps. Many graphics solvers have no block structure. Newton with a sparse direct factorization, preconditioned conjugate gradients and multigrid are global by design, and they remain the norm offline. For these A1 still exists, as the derivative of the Newton or Krylov iterations that ran, and B3 still applies, as the adjoint of that iteration. Christianson’s reverse accumulation instead iterates the adjoint equation at the converged point and discards the executed iterates, so it sits with A2 [Chr94]. A Krylov recurrence or a multigrid cycle is a composition of matrix-vector products, smoothers and transfers, each with a transpose. The memory advantage is absent: the inputs of each iteration’s adjoint are global vectors, so there is no block-local object to shrink the stored state to, and the saving that block mirroring offers is specific to solvers that decompose, which Section 4.3 returns to. If an inner linear system is solved accurately and differentiated as an exact operator, A1* records that idealization. A direct factorization still incurs floating-point error. With an accurate inner solve, the truncated outer Newton iteration may dominate the difference between the finite-solver and root sensitivities, but its magnitude also depends on conditioning, residual sensitivity, and backward-solve accuracy.

    For the block-local operation-mirroring case, a custom adjoint can remove the need for a backward-only global system, but it does not remove the need for state. Each local Jacobian must still be evaluated at the input seen by its forward update, so that input must be retained, recomputed, or recovered. The reverse sweep for vertex block descent [SJW∗26] stores nine doubles, or 72 bytes, of replay data per active vertex per sweep. The reported approximately 4 KB per vertex per sweep uses a different accounting: it is an empirical peak of total allocations, including mesh and other data. The reported storage still scales linearly with K|V|. Removing that K dependence requires a state-recovery strategy, which a block decomposition does not supply. McNamara et al.[MTPS04] likewise hand-derive their operator adjoints while storing the forward trajectory.

    Custom adjoints are not tied to one referent. In the discrete case, the fluid adjoints of McNamara et al.[MTPS04] and Takahashi et al.[TLQL21] mirror the stages of a fluid step, while Qiao et al.[QLKL21b] differentiate the executed Gauss–Seidel iterations of an articulated-body contact solver. A transposed pressure solve treated as an exact linear operator is recorded by A1*, rather than by an unqualified claim of exactness for the finite solver; McNamara et al. are an explicit example. Custom continuous adjoints instead belong to A3.

    An equation-level adjoint is classified as B2, whether its ingredients are hand-derived or generated automatically. DiffPD [DWM∗22] and DiffCloth [LDW∗23] are examples: DiffPD reuses the factorized forward matrix in its local–global adjoint iteration. In DiffCloth, the contact-free adjoint uses the elastic step Hessian, while frictional contact adds contact-response derivative terms to the global system. ADD [GHZ∗20] solves an adjoint system built from its integrator residual; Nimble [WOL∗21] differentiates its contact problem; and DiffXPBD [SC23] assembles derivative blocks and uses conjugate gradients, with a positive-definite modification of those blocks. Solving a system iteratively does not change its equation-level target, although solver tolerances and matrix modifications affect the returned approximation.

    All of these methods use the solver’s structure, and they differ in which object they differentiate.

    The cost of a custom adjoint is implementation and maintenance effort. It needs derivative actions for the operations it uses, supplied analytically, by local AD, or by another suitable interface. Data-dependent branches and line searches require retaining or reproducing the executed decisions and differentiating the corresponding smooth branch; they do not by themselves rule out a custom adjoint. A black-box routine without a derivative interface remains an obstacle. Changing an integrator can require new custom derivative code, whereas a framework-generated realization can often reuse the framework’s differentiation support.

    .3.  The cells of the grid

    Table 2 crosses the two axes, and the following observations draw on it.

    Which cells are occupied, and why. Table 2 reflects both the methods surveyed and our operational labeling convention. Equation-level adjoints are assigned to B2 even when AD constructs their Jacobian products; automatic implicit differentiation already exists [BBC∗22]. Discretized continuous adjoint solves can also occupy A3×B2, as in Real2Sim [HBBC19]. B3 may instead organize a discrete or continuous adjoint as custom operator-level updates. An empty cell is therefore not, by itself, evidence of mathematical impossibility or an unimplemented construction. Methods should be compared by differentiated object, backward organization, and state requirements. The remainder of this section focuses on discrete custom adjoints that mirror forward operations.

    Exactness is assessed relative to a referent. A1 targets the finite executed computation, A1* an idealized program with exact linear primitives, A2 a selected root of the discrete equations, and A3 the continuous dynamics. A target does not guarantee that an implementation attains it: finite tolerances, discretization, modified Jacobians, and nonsmooth operations may introduce additional qualifications. The corresponding sensitivities generally differ, but can coincide in special cases. When two methods return different gradients for the same nominal simulator, both the referent and the accuracy of its implementation should therefore be checked.

    Memory is decided by state recovery. A1 does not imply a tape; that it usually has meant one is an artifact of how A1 has been realized. Nor does the realization settle memory on its own. A discrete operation adjoint needs the state its forward operation saw; continuous adjoints likewise need an appropriate forward-state representation. These states can be obtained by several policies: retain them, recompute them from checkpoints, or recover them by running the map backward. The state-recovery policy helps determine the storage asymptotics and is reported separately from both axes. Conflating it with the realization makes a constant-factor saving read as an asymptotic one.

    Discrete custom adjoints can mirror the forward solver’s operations without assembling an additional global system. They may retain the trajectory, as in the early fluid adjoints, or recover the required states by recomputation or reversibility. McNamara et al.[MTPS04] provide an A1*×B3 example because their linear stages are differentiated as exact operators; Qiao et al.[QLKL21b] reverse executed contact iterations. Two useful structures are reversible updates and block-local compositions, but neither replaces the need to specify the state-recovery policy.

    The first structure is reversible reconstruction. If an update has a usable inverse, its intermediate states can be recovered during the backward pass instead of retained. Recovering the same linearization states and using the same local derivative conventions can reproduce the derivative of the corresponding stored-state computation. Numerical instability, rounding, and non-injective updates can prevent this in practice. Related constructions have been developed in machine learning, numerical integration, and molecular dynamics.

    Reversible residual networks recompute activations instead of keeping them [GRUG17], which makes activation storage independent of the number of reversible blocks, while activations at non-reversible layers must still be stored. The symplectic adjoint method [MMY21] takes a related but distinct route for neural ODEs: it retains time-step states as checkpoints, discards the per-step computation graph, recomputes the required stages, and uses a matching discrete adjoint to recover the gradient of the numerical forward scheme. Its memory reduction comes from checkpointing and recomputation rather than from requiring the forward Runge–Kutta method to be reversible.

    Stam [Sta22] applies it to the adjoint of a physical simulation, with a bitwise-reversible integrator he traces to Levesque and Verlet and to Rein and Tamayo, one that retraces its own path bitwise, with the reverse step of the adjoint method as the stated application. His paper mixes fixed-point with floating-point arithmetic because a pure float trajectory is not exactly reversible. Greener’s reversible molecular simulation [Gre25] reconstructs molecular-dynamics states by reverse-time simulation and matches taped reverse-mode AD in the reported gradient checks at small step counts. Its force-field training experiments, however, use 200-step gradient truncation. This both limits exploding gradients and reduces reverse computation; for the water-model setup, losses spaced 2000 steps apart require reversing only one tenth of the forward steps under that truncation policy. The reported training cost should therefore not be read as the cost of exact full-trajectory differentiation.

    The reversible methods above are one construction that recurs across fields for the same reason. It was developed in machine learning, numerical integration and molecular dynamics rather than in graphics.

    The second is mirroring the solver’s block structure, as Shu et al.[SJW∗26] do on Vertex Block Descent [CLYY24]; analogous operator-level reverse implementations can be constructed for projective dynamics [BML∗14] and XPBD [MMC16], provided the derivatives of their local updates are defined. Projective dynamics additionally requires differentiating its global linear solve.

    The two structures have different requirements. Reversing an update requires both an inverse and sufficient numerical stability in the backward direction. A contraction sₜ₊₁=asₜ, with 0

    Their memory behavior depends on state recovery. Reversible reconstruction can keep a small active reverse workspace, but Greener [Gre25] also retains periodic coordinate/velocity snapshots and random seeds. With a fixed snapshot interval, total snapshot storage grows with the trajectory length; the method should not be described as strictly constant-memory for arbitrary horizons. Block-local adjoints reduce the data needed per update but do not remove it: the reported reverse-sweep replay storage remains linear in K|V|[SJW∗26]. Both structures can avoid a backward-only global system in suitable implementations, while their total memory must be compared under explicitly matched checkpointing, truncation, and replay policies.

    For the stiff, contact-rich solvers emphasized in this report, stable reverse reconstruction can be difficult, while block-local adjoints provide another way to reduce storage constants [SJW∗26], and per-step checkpointing with recomputation yet another [QLKL21b]. More generally, A1 and low memory are compatible through recomputation, at potentially substantial additional computational cost. Block structure and reversibility can improve this trade-off, but neither is necessary for an executed-computation derivative to use little memory. The breadth of efficient implementations across graphics solvers remains an open question.

    A custom adjoint need not mirror a discrete block decomposition. An A3×B3 method implements a discretized continuous adjoint, potentially exploiting structures already maintained by its forward solver; Section 6.4 discusses the flow-map example. Its consistency and state requirements must be assessed for that continuous referent rather than inferred from the discrete block-local case.

    .4.  Using the taxonomy

    The referent should follow the intended optimization problem and the solver regime. A2 is attractive when a root of the discrete equations is the intended target and the forward and adjoint solves approximate its sensitivity accurately. This requires checking conditioning and derivative accuracy rather than relying on a tight forward tolerance alone. When a fixed finite iteration budget is part of the model being optimized, A1 directly targets that computation. An approximate A2 gradient may still be useful, but its target and approximation should be stated and evaluated at the production solver configuration.

    The realization should follow the solver’s structure, development constraints, and memory budget. A custom adjoint can exploit regular structure but requires implementation and maintenance effort. Automatically generated differentiation is often convenient for rapidly changing solvers, and checkpointing can reduce its storage requirements. An equation-level sensitivity or adjoint solve is attractive when its target is appropriate and the required adjoint system can be solved efficiently, especially when forward factorizations or preconditioners can be reused. None of these labels alone determines locality or memory.

    Classifying an engine.

    First identify the derivative target: executed iterations, an idealized program with exact linear operators, a regular root of discrete equations, continuous dynamics, or a stated surrogate. Then identify the organizing computation: equation-level sensitivity or adjoint solves (B2), otherwise framework- or compiler-generated differentiation (B1), or custom operator-level adjoints (B3). Record automatic, manual, or hybrid construction and the relevant local or global operators separately. Finally, state what is retained or recovered: a tape, trajectory states, checkpoints, replay data, or reverse-reconstructed states. Mixed components and finite-tolerance qualifications belong in the notes to Tables 4 and 5. The diagnostic in Section 10 measures the resulting behavior at the production configuration.

    We do not offer a ranking. Every published comparison we examined that appears to establish one sets a particular implementation against another at a particular problem size, and the axes above suggest such results are evidence about a cell rather than about a method.

    .  Discontinuity: Contact, Friction, and Collision

    The taxonomy of Section 4 concerns how a derivative is obtained from a computation, assuming the relevant local derivatives exist. Contact can violate that assumption. This section develops an additional, orthogonal axis: what a method does where the simulation map is non-smooth. An engine makes a choice on each axis, and conflating them is a recurring source of confusion, because a paper that improves contact gradients and a paper that improves solver adjoints may both be described as “better gradients” while addressing different deficiencies. Figure 2 shows what a solver is asked to resolve in this regime, where individual contact laws and changes in the active set both matter. The section is restricted to discontinuity arising from contact, friction and collision in solids. Fluids have discontinuities of their own, in the merging and splitting of free surfaces and in the discrete operators that track them; McNamara et al.[MTPS04] met one in the fast-marching redistancing of a level set and derived its adjoint by observing that the algorithm is locally continuous, and we do not treat that class further.

    .1.  Sources of non-smoothness in contact

    At the position level, a discrete rigid-contact constraint can be written using the gap φ at the constrained configuration and the normal impulse λ over the step: 0≤φ⊥λ≥0, meaning that at each contact either the bodies are separated with zero normal impulse, or they are touching with a non-negative normal impulse. Velocity-level time-stepping formulations instead pair the impulse with a scheme-specific normal-velocity residual, which may include gap stabilization or restitution; the gap formula is not a universal time-stepping law. Coulomb friction couples tangential impulse to normal impulse through a cone, together with a maximum-dissipation or equivalent stick–slip condition. The resulting time-stepping schemes, in the tradition of Stewart and Trinkle [ST96] and Anitescu and Potra [AP97], are linear or nonlinear complementarity problems. The same formulation underpins contact-implicit trajectory optimization [PCT14], which optimizes through contact by treating the complementarity conditions as constraints rather than by differentiating a forward solve, and is a major alternative for contact-rich trajectory optimization.

    This creates three distinct obstacles, and different methods address different ones.

  • 1.

    Non-smoothness at fixed topology. Even with a fixed set of candidate contacts, the solution has distinct branches (separating, sticking, sliding). Locally unique, non-degenerate solutions admit branch derivatives, but derivatives can differ or fail to exist at mode boundaries.

  • 2.

    Discrete events. Contact modes and event times can change under parameter perturbations. Differentiating each step at its current active set can give the correct local derivative of the discrete trajectory when the branch sequence is stable. Matching continuous-time impact sensitivities also requires event-time dependence when the discrete contact treatment omits it. The earliest rigid-body control work already shows the effect: Popović et al.[PSE∗00] plot the simulation function of a particle bouncing off a polygonal obstacle as piecewise smooth, discontinuous wherever the impulse switches facet, and vary the surface normals to narrow the gaps between the smooth pieces of the feasible exit set, and use curvature-adapted polygonal approximations of curved obstacles so that a first-order prediction still serves. Positions may remain continuous in time while impact velocities jump; facet or event-sequence changes can also make the parameter-to-output map discontinuous. Saltation matrices and event-time sensitivities address isolated transversal events with a locally stable event sequence; grazing and simultaneous impacts require separate treatment.

  • 3.

    Gradient collapse in the model. Some physically meaningful sensitivities are zero or undefined regardless of the numerical treatment. A ball resting on a table has no gradient of final position with respect to initial height, once dropped from any height that leads to rest at the same place. The information is absent from the dynamics themselves rather than lost in discretization, so this is a modeling limit and no differentiation scheme recovers it.

    • Much of the literature’s disagreement about “correct” contact gradients comes from prioritizing different obstacles.

    .2.  Complementarity branch derivatives

    The most direct approach differentiates the complementarity formulation on a stable active set. For a locally unique, non-degenerate solution, the corresponding active-set equations define a smooth local solution map. De Avila Belbute-Peres et al.[BPSA∗18] embedded an LCP solver as a differentiable layer, computing gradients by differentiating the LCP’s complementarity conditions at the solution in the manner of [AK17]. Nimble [WOL∗21] develops analytic LCP derivatives that exploit active-set structure, together with optional complementarity-aware heuristic directions. These heuristics depart from the local derivative in some contact regimes, including cases where the true local gradient is zero, to provide an optimization signal.

    Zhong et al.[ZHB22] ask directly whether these gradients are correct in the sense their users assume. They examine what differentiable contact simulators return with respect to position, velocity and control, and find discrepancies that ordinary use does not reveal. Their checks complement the diagnostics of Section 7.

    The forward simulation in this family is a hard-contact simulation with no artificial compliance, an advantage when the downstream task depends on accurate contact mechanics. Velocity-level complementarity does not eliminate interpenetration in practice, since the constraint is imposed on velocities and drift is corrected by stabilization, but the penetration that remains is a discretization error rather than a modeling parameter traded against gradient smoothness. Under the stated regularity assumptions, the returned object is a branch Jacobian. At a mode boundary, the method must specify its generalized derivative or heuristic selection. A valid local derivative need not provide an effective direction for crossing into another contact mode.

    .3.  Compliant and penalty relaxation

    Another strategy relaxes hard contact. Penalty and spring-damper laws are simple examples; their differentiability depends on the chosen activation and friction regularization. The convex contact solver of MuJoCo [TET12] uses a relaxed optimization model, while the original Brax [FFR∗21] uses Baumgarte-stabilized velocity-level collision impulses. These are distinct contact models, rather than interchangeable spring-damper laws. Le Lidec et al.[LLJM∗24] compare the models of MuJoCo, Drake, Bullet, DART, ODE and RaiSim and the qualitative differences they induce. Analytically differentiable formulations such as ADD [GHZ∗20] use compliant contact with explicit friction smoothing to obtain analytical gradients by adjoint sensitivity analysis for multibody systems.

    The trade-off between compliance and gradient behavior depends on the system. Increasing stiffness can worsen conditioning in multiscale problems, with the effect depending on the time step, masses, constraint geometry, and preconditioning, so stiffness alone does not determine the condition number. Constraint formulations with compliance [TNGF15, MMC16] soften that trade for the forward solve by writing the constraint with its compliance α, the inverse of its stiffness, rather than with the stiffness itself: the multiplier system carries α/h² on its diagonal, which tends to zero as the constraint stiffens. At fixed time step and with bounded constraint and mass operators, this avoids the penalty matrix’s growing entries. The condition number can still be unbounded: with redundant or degenerate constraints the system approaches singularity as α→0, although that ill-conditioning comes from the constraint Jacobian rather than from growing penalty entries. DiffXPBD [SC23] constructs an adjoint for compliant constraint dynamics, but the works reviewed here do not establish a systematic comparison of backward conditioning between compliance-form and penalty-form equations. Paulus et al.[PGS∗26] address a different aspect: DiffMJX improves numerical gradient accuracy with adaptive integration, while contacts from distance (CFD) supplies modified contact derivatives. Section 5.7 discusses this forward/backward decoupling.

    .4.  Barrier and interior-point formulations

    A third family approximates contact with barrier potentials on the strictly feasible, non-intersecting domain. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) [LFS∗20] combines these potentials with continuous collision detection (CCD) and a feasibility-preserving line search to maintain intersection-free and inversion-free configurations. The codimensional extension [LKJ21] covers cloth, rods, and points.

    For differentiable simulation this is a convenient starting point, with the following regularity. On the feasible domain, the contact potential is C¹ and piecewise C², with pieces determined by geometric feature configurations. Away from feature-transition boundaries, a stationary point with a nonsingular Hessian admits implicit differentiation. At a smooth local minimizer the true Hessian is positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite if the minimizer is non-degenerate; the barrier alone does not ensure this. Nor does piecewise C² regularity alone guarantee Newton convergence. IPC modifies element Hessians to obtain descent directions and uses a CCD-filtered line search to keep iterates feasible [LFS∗20]; local convergence additionally depends on regularity and non-degeneracy.

    Those devices make the forward solve robust. They do not change the derivative of the minimizer, which is still given by (5) with the unprojected Hessian, and nothing in the backward pass calls for the projected one. The adjoint system is a linear solve rather than a descent step, so it needs the true Hessian to be non-singular rather than positive definite, and a pivoted symmetric or LU factorization handles an indefinite matrix, at the price of not reusing the forward solver’s Cholesky factors. The adjoint system should therefore be assembled from the unprojected Hessian. Huang et al.[HTG∗24] do this: their adjoint system is built from the stiffness and mass matrices of the discretization; projection is confined to the Newton update and applied only when the unprojected direction fails to descend, and the barrier stiffness is held fixed, since adapting it would require differentiating through the update. Under those choices, the conditions for exactness are the ones (5) always carries, a converged and non-degenerate minimizer. A backward pass that instead reuses the projected matrix the forward solver factorized returns an approximation to that derivative. With no projection it uses the original derivative system; otherwise the result is generally perturbed, with error depending on the projection, the right-hand side, and the conditioning of the original and modified systems. Reading that result as the exact derivative of some other object would require naming the residual whose Jacobian the projected matrix is, and we are not aware of a formulation that does so. The shortcut returns an approximation to the A2 derivative, and the reporting checklist of Section 10 asks for this to be stated. Barrier stiffness and small gaps can create widely separated curvature scales and difficult linear solves. IPC’s discussion of unnecessary ill-conditioning concerns the choice of barrier stiffness, rather than a universal loss of invertibility as a gap closes. Related barrier-based work on rigid bodies [FLS∗21], on affine bodies [LKL∗22], on projective dynamics with the barrier recast as a positional constraint [LMY∗22], on a geometric contact potential with localized support [HPF∗25], and on multibody systems in which contact, friction and nonlinear joint constraints are all potentials of one minimization [CLL∗22], uses related contact potentials on the feasible domain, subject to the geometric regularity qualifications above.

    Barrier width and stiffness affect both contact response and its sensitivities. Adaptive stiffness is common, while some differentiable implementations hold it fixed. If a parameter-dependent stiffness update is part of the computation being differentiated, its derivative must be included. Quantitative errors in contact-time sensitivities cannot be bounded by barrier width alone; impact transversality and conditioning also matter. Motivated by the locking of IPC’s CCD-filtered line search as much as by conditioning costs, recent work drops the barrier altogether, enforcing non-penetration as a constraint through an augmented Lagrangian solver fed by continuous collision detection [ZLL26]; that recovers the solver’s efficiency but reintroduces an explicit active set, and with it the question of Section 5.2 for whoever differentiates the step. Its sensitivities remain branch-wise under a stable active set, including when the constrained optimality conditions are differentiated implicitly; mode boundaries require an additional derivative convention or event treatment.

    .5.  Randomized smoothing and stochastic estimators

    Randomization can smooth an objective, a transition map, or a collision query; these choices generally define different optimization problems. For an objective f, one may consider 𝔼_ε[f(θ+ε)], which can be smooth even when f is discontinuous. A score-function or likelihood-ratio estimator [Wil92] differentiates this expectation without differentiating the simulator. A pathwise estimator instead uses simulator derivatives and is a distinct construction: it is unbiased only when differentiation and expectation can be interchanged without missing boundary contributions. Section 7 discusses this comparison [PRPD18, SSZT22].

    Le Lidec et al.[LLSM∗24] apply randomized smoothing to optimal control of non-smooth dynamical systems, and Montaut et al.[MLLB∗23] apply it specifically to collision detection, obtaining useful derivatives of a quantity that is combinatorial in nature. Pang et al.[PSYT23] study both randomized and deterministic smoothing of quasi-dynamic contact models, including a log-barrier formulation, for contact-rich manipulation planning. Their analysis illustrates how smoothing can supply informative slopes in otherwise flat regions. Smoothing local dynamics before rollout is generally different from smoothing the full rollout objective.

    Under suitable integrability conditions and a regular smoothing distribution, score-function estimators require no simulator derivatives. Sampling introduces computational cost and variance, whose magnitude depends on noise scale, dimension, objective, estimator, and baseline. Variance need not increase monotonically with the smoothing scale.

    .6.  Event-aware and time-of-impact gradients

    A smaller body of literature addresses event-time dependence directly. For an isolated transversal impact with a locally stable event sequence, trajectory sensitivity includes a contribution from dτ/dθ and the impact update. An event-time model or detector makes this contribution available; geometric collisions often use CCD, while simpler systems can use analytic event equations. Grazing and simultaneous impacts require separate treatment. Zhong et al.[ZHDB23] differentiate collision timing and geometry, and Werling et al.[WOL∗21] include an approximation to continuous-time elastic-collision sensitivities. Cloth methods [LLK19, LDW∗23] that differentiate the detected contact system can still have valid local discrete derivatives; agreement with continuous-time event sensitivities is a separate question.

    The works reviewed here provide fewer event-aware implementations than fixed-branch or smoothed contact derivatives. This describes the reviewed coverage only and does not rank the families’ maturity.

    .7.  Decoupling the forward and backward contact model

    One option cuts across the families above: the contact model used in the forward pass and the contact model differentiated in the backward pass need not be the same. Surrogate directions can provide optimization signals even when they differ from the gradient of the forward objective; their convergence properties require separate analysis. For example, CFD modifies contact derivatives while leaving the forward contact model unchanged [PGS∗26]. Dojo [HLCB∗22] provides a related equation-based construction: the forward solve approaches hard contact, while smooth sensitivities can be evaluated at a cached, more relaxed central-path state. These differentiate the relaxed equations rather than the final harder-contact step, so both complementarity parameters should be reported. The approach has reached hardware. Song et al.[SKS25] run the forward pass in a non-differentiable simulator and take the gradient from a simplified single-rigid-body model aligned to its state, and transfer the resulting quadrupedal policy to a real robot. Schwarke et al.[SKB∗25], who reach hardware with a single analytically smoothed simulator instead, note that decoupling separates the choices of forward realism and backward smoothing, but adds the cost of maintaining and aligning two models.

    The idea predates its contact-focused instances by two decades. Wojtan et al.[WMT06] introduce an integrator-swapping approximation so that the adjoint of a linearized implicit cloth step becomes tractable: the backward pass differentiates a different scheme than the forward pass runs, and is accepted on a consistency argument, the two schemes agreeing to second order with a local O(Δt³) discrepancy the authors quantify, rather than because it is the adjoint of the executed forward scheme. This earlier instance indicates that the decoupling is a general structural option, and one to expect in settings other than contact.

    The returned vector need not be the gradient of the forward objective, and it need not be a conservative field. A scalar surrogate objective should therefore not be assumed without establishing one. Standard exact-gradient convergence results do not apply directly: guarantees require additional conditions, such as sufficient descent alignment or controlled bias. Decoupling can improve optimization in the regimes discussed in Section 7, while requiring separate checks of derivative accuracy and optimization behavior.

    .  Physical Model Families

    With the taxonomy and contact treatments in place, we survey the model classes. Each subsection asks what the model’s structure implies for differentiation. The physics itself is covered by the standard simulation literature. Figure 3 shows the two families where that structure bites hardest.
